teile.einleitung: A paper aeroplane is a small aircraft that you build just by folding a sheet of paper. You need neither scissors nor glue, and yet it can glide surprisingly far and long through the air. While making it, you learn along the way how flying works.
wichtigste: For a paper aeroplane you need only a sheet of paper.
You build it by folding, similar to the Japanese folding art of origami.
Light, smooth paper works best.
If you bend the back edges of the wings up slightly, the nose goes up.
A wet paper aeroplane flies badly because it becomes heavy and soft.
Never aim at people, because the point can go into an eye.
The world record for the longest flight time of a paper aeroplane is 29.2 seconds.

abschnitte.text: A **paper aeroplane** is a toy aircraft made from a single sheet of paper. You fold it so that a pointed body and two wings are formed. This folding is related to **origami**, the traditional Japanese art of paper folding. There are hundreds of folding models, from the simple dart to the wide glider.

When you throw it, you give the aeroplane momentum; that is its only power. The air flowing past the wings creates **lift**, an upward force. At the same time **gravity** pulls the aeroplane down, and **air resistance** slows it down. That is why a good paper aeroplane glides slowly to the ground at a shallow angle, like a glider.

Light, smooth paper works best, for example an ordinary A4 sheet. The folds should be sharp and precise, and both wings must be the same size. If you bend the back edges of the wings up slightly, the nose goes up and the aeroplane glides for longer. Wet paper becomes heavy and soft, which is why it flies badly.

Pointed, narrow **darts** fly fast and far. Wide **gliders** with large wings, on the other hand, stay in the air longer. Some models loop the loop or turn if you bend the wing edges differently. The principle is the same as with real aircraft, which are steered with movable **flaps** on the wings.

There are even world championships and world records for throwing paper aeroplanes. The record for the longest flight time is 29.2 seconds, and in distance throwing, paper aeroplanes have already flown further than a football pitch is wide. Engineers sometimes test ideas with paper models too. What matters is: never aim at people or animals, because the **point** can go into an eye.

begriffe.erklaerung: Japanese art of folding figures from paper without cutting or gluing.
Force that pushes an aircraft upwards through the air flowing past.
Braking force of the air on anything that moves.
Aircraft without an engine that glides slowly down through the air.

gewusst: Paper was invented in China about 2,000 years ago, and paper kites were made there early on too.
A good paper aeroplane thrown in a hall can stay in the air for almost half a minute.
The first flying pioneers also tested their ideas with small models before building real aeroplanes.

teile.einleitung: A graphics processing unit, GPU for short, is a special computer chip that calculates images, videos and 3D graphics. It makes sure video games run smoothly and films appear sharp on the screen. Today it is also one of the most important machines for artificial intelligence.
wichtigste: GPU stands for graphics processing unit.
The main job of a graphics processor is calculating images and 3D graphics.
It has very many small processing cores that work in parallel.
A graphics card's own memory is called graphics memory or VRAM.
A graphics processor colours in the individual picture dots, the pixels.
60 fps means that 60 frames are shown per second.
Integrated graphics are built into the main processor.
Powerful GPUs are often used today to train artificial intelligence.

abschnitte.text: GPU is short for **graphics processing unit**, in German “Grafikprozessor”. Besides the main processor, the **CPU**, it is one of the most important chips in a computer. Its main job is to calculate images and 3D graphics. It sits either on its own **graphics card** or is built into the main processor. Mobile phones, games consoles and cars also have graphics processors.

A main processor has only a few processing cores, but they are very versatile. A graphics processor, on the other hand, has thousands of small **processing cores** that all work at the same time. This is called **parallel processing**. You can imagine it like a whole school class solving simple sums at the same time, instead of a single maths genius. For many similar calculations this is much faster.

A screen is made up of millions of tiny picture dots, the **pixels**. The graphics processor calculates what colour each pixel should be, with light, shadows and reflections. In a video game it has to do this many times per second. The figure **60 fps** means that 60 frames are shown per second. The higher the frame rate, the smoother the game looks.

A graphics card has its own fast memory, the **graphics memory** or VRAM. This holds, for example, the textures, that is, the surface images of characters and landscapes. Many laptops have no graphics card of their own but **integrated graphics**. This graphics part is built into the main processor; it uses less electricity but is usually less powerful. It is quite enough for office work and videos.

Because graphics processors can manage so many calculations at the same time, they are now also used for other tasks. They are especially important for training **artificial intelligence**, for which huge data centres with thousands of GPUs are built. Researchers also use them for weather forecasts or simulations. Well-known makers of graphics processors are Nvidia, AMD and Intel.

In the past the main processor calculated the images all by itself. In the 1990s special **3D accelerators** for computer games came onto the market. In 1999 the company Nvidia advertised its GeForce 256 as the first GPU. Since then graphics processors have become many times more powerful.

begriffe.erklaerung: Abbreviation for graphics processing unit.
Single picture dot on a screen.
Frames per second.
Separate fast memory on a graphics card.
Many calculations are done at the same time instead of one after another.

gewusst: A modern graphics processor has thousands of processing cores, while a main processor often has only a handful to a few dozen.
Many artificial intelligence programs are trained on graphics processors that were originally invented for games.
A 4K screen has over eight million pixels, which the graphics processor can recalculate for every frame.

teile.einleitung: A lever is a simple machine with which you can move heavy things using little force. It consists of a rigid bar that turns around a pivot. Levers are everywhere in everyday life, from door handles to bike brake levers.
wichtigste: A lever is a rigid bar that turns around a pivot.
The distance from the pivot to the point where the force acts is called the lever arm.
The further from the pivot you push, the less force you need.
In return you have to move a longer distance.
Archimedes is said to have claimed that with a lever he could move the world.
Door handles, bottle openers, crowbars and bike brake levers are levers.
Our arm also works like a lever.

abschnitte.text: A **lever** is a rigid bar that is supported at one point. This point is called the **pivot**. On one side acts the force with which you push or pull, on the other the load you want to move. The distance from the pivot to the force is called the **lever arm**. Together with the wedge, the pulley and the inclined plane, the lever is one of the simple machines.

A simple rule applies to the lever: force times effort arm equals load times load arm. If the effort arm is twice as long as the load arm, you need only half the force. But in return you have to move the end of the lever twice as far. So you save force, but not work. This **law of the lever** was already described by the Greek scholar **Archimedes** more than 2,200 years ago.

A **door handle** is a lever that pulls back the latch in the lock. With a **bottle opener** you lever off a crown cap with no effort. A crowbar helps to lever up heavy things. The brake lever on a bicycle, scissors, pliers and a wheelbarrow also work with levers. In the playground, the seesaw is a large lever with the pivot in the middle.

Our body uses levers too. When you lift a bag, your **forearm** is the lever and your elbow is the pivot. The muscles pull close to the joint, while the load hangs far away in your hand. That is why muscles have to exert much more force than the bag weighs. In return the hand can move quickly and a long way.

Archimedes lived in the 3rd century BC in **Syracuse** in Sicily. The saying “Give me a firm place to stand, and I will lift the world off its hinges” is attributed to him. He wanted to show how powerful a lever with a long arm is. In reality, of course, there would be no place for the pivot and no such long bar. But the ancient Egyptians already used levers to move heavy blocks of stone.

begriffe.erklaerung: The point around which a lever turns.
The distance from the pivot to the force.
Force times effort arm equals load times load arm.
A basic tool that saves force, such as a lever, wedge or pulley.

gewusst: With a crowbar a child can move a stone that they could never lift with their bare hands.
On a seesaw a light child can lift a heavy child if the light child sits further out.
A nutcracker is a lever in which the nut and the hand are on the same side of the pivot.

teile.einleitung: In laser cutting, a strongly focused beam of light becomes so hot that it cuts through metal, wood or plastic. The laser works very precisely and does not touch the material. In factories this is how car parts, signs and fine patterns are made in seconds.
wichtigste: LASER stands for light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation.
In 1960 Theodore Maiman built the first working laser.
The laser beam is focused by a lens onto a tiny spot, where it melts or vaporises the material.
A cutting gas blows the molten material out of the narrow kerf.
CO₂ lasers have a wavelength of about 10.6 micrometres.
Fibre lasers cut copper and brass better, because these metals absorb their shorter-wavelength light better.

abschnitte.text: A **laser** produces light that has only one colour and travels very straight and focused. The word is an abbreviation of light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation. The first working laser was built in 1960 by the American Theodore Maiman using a ruby crystal. Soon afterwards people realised that focused laser light can melt material.

A lens focuses the laser beam onto a spot that is often smaller than a millimetre. There the energy becomes so concentrated that the material melts or vaporises. At the same time a nozzle blows a **cutting gas** onto the spot and drives the molten material out downwards. The cutting head, controlled by a computer, follows exactly the desired shape. A narrow **kerf** is left behind.

In **laser flame cutting** of structural steel, oxygen is used, because the burning iron provides extra heat. In **laser fusion cutting** of stainless steel, nitrogen blows out the molten material and stops the edges discolouring. In sublimation cutting the material vaporises directly, for example with wood or acrylic glass. Depending on the material and thickness, the suitable process is chosen.

For a long time the **CO₂ laser**, with a wavelength of about 10.6 micrometres, was the most important cutting laser. Today **fibre lasers** are often used, whose light has a much shorter wavelength. Shiny metals such as copper and brass absorb this light better and reflect less of it back. Fibre lasers also use less electricity.

In industry, lasers cut sheet metal for cars, machines and building façades. Watch parts, medical instruments and electronics are also processed with lasers, which is important in Switzerland with its precision industry. In schools and workshops, the so-called **makerspaces**, smaller laser cutters cut wood, cardboard and acrylic glass. Because the laser beam can seriously injure the eyes, the machines work inside closed casings.

begriffe.erklaerung: A device that produces very focused light of a single colour.
The narrow gap created by cutting.
A gas that blows the molten material out of the cut.
The distance between two crests of a light wave, which decides what kind of light it is.
A thousandth of a millimetre.

gewusst: The light of a CO₂ laser is invisible to our eyes because it is in the infrared range.
A laser cut can be narrower than a tenth of a millimetre.
Lasers can be used not only for cutting but also for engraving, welding and drilling.

teile.einleitung: A nuclear power station produces electricity from the energy released when atomic nuclei are split. The heat produced makes water boil, and the steam drives a turbine. In Switzerland nuclear power stations supply a large part of the electricity, but they are also controversial.
wichtigste: In a nuclear power station, the splitting of uranium nuclei provides the heat.
The heat produces steam, which drives a turbine and a generator.
The white cloud above the cooling tower is water vapour.
In 2025 four nuclear reactors were in operation in Switzerland.
The Mühleberg nuclear power station was shut down for good in December 2019.
After the Fukushima accident in 2011, the Federal Council decided to phase out nuclear power step by step.
Radioactive waste is to be stored in a deep geological repository in the Nördlich Lägern region.

abschnitte.text: Inside the **reactor** there are fuel rods containing uranium. When a uranium nucleus is hit by a neutron, it splits and gives off heat and new neutrons. These split further nuclei, creating a **chain reaction**. Control rods absorb neutrons and keep the chain reaction under control. The heat warms water, which turns into steam.

The hot steam flows through a **steam turbine** and makes it turn. In this way the energy of the steam is converted into rotation. The turbine drives a **generator**, which produces electricity. Afterwards the steam is cooled and turns back into water. The big white cloud above the **cooling tower** is just water vapour and is not radioactive.

In 2025 four reactors were in operation in Switzerland: **Beznau I and II** and **Leibstadt** in the canton of Aargau, and Gösgen in the canton of Solothurn. Beznau I was connected to the grid in 1969 and is one of the oldest reactors still running in the world. Leibstadt is the youngest and most powerful nuclear power station in Switzerland and went into operation in 1984. The **Mühleberg** nuclear power station in the canton of Bern was shut down for good in December 2019. Together the nuclear power stations supply about a third of Switzerland's electricity (as of 2024).

Nuclear power stations emit hardly any CO2 while running. But in serious accidents radioactivity can escape, which endangers people and the environment. In 1986 the worst accident so far happened at **Chernobyl** in what is now Ukraine. In 2011 the **Fukushima** power station in Japan was badly damaged by an earthquake and a tsunami. After that the Federal Council decided on a step-by-step phase-out, and in 2017 voters approved an Energy Act that bans the construction of new nuclear power stations.

Spent fuel rods remain **radioactive** for a very long time, some substances for thousands of years. They are first kept in interim storage facilities, for example in Würenlingen. For decades Nagra has been looking for a safe place for a **deep geological repository** deep in the rock. In 2022 it proposed the Nördlich Lägern region between Aargau and Zurich. Whether new nuclear power stations should be allowed again in future is being debated in politics.

begriffe.erklaerung: The splitting of a heavy atomic nucleus, which releases energy.
A process in which each splitting triggers new splittings.
A heavy, radioactive metal used as fuel.
A tall tower in which water is cooled by evaporation.
A store for radioactive waste deep underground.

gewusst: A cooling tower is almost empty inside; it is mainly a huge tube through which air flows upwards.
A small uranium fuel pellet the size of a fingertip contains roughly as much energy as a tonne of hard coal.
After its shutdown, the Mühleberg nuclear power station is being dismantled piece by piece over many years.

teile.einleitung: A capacitor is an electronic component that can store electric charge, and therefore energy, for a short time. In its simplest form it consists of two metal plates separated by an insulating layer. Capacitors are found in almost every electronic device, from mobile phones to computers.
wichtigste: A capacitor stores electric charge between two conducting surfaces.
Its capacitance is measured in farads.
If you double the distance between the plates, the capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor halves.
A capacitor of 100 µF at 10 V stores an energy of 5 mJ.
An RC circuit with 10 kΩ and 100 µF has a time constant of 1 second.
After about 5 time constants a capacitor is considered practically fully charged.
Electrolytic capacitors are polarised and can be destroyed if connected the wrong way round.
As the frequency rises, the reactance of a capacitor becomes smaller.

abschnitte.text: A capacitor consists of two conducting surfaces, the **electrodes**, and an insulating layer between them, the **dielectric**. When a voltage is applied, positive charge collects on one side and negative charge on the other. The charge stays stored even when the voltage is removed. Unlike a battery, however, a capacitor can release its energy very quickly.

How much charge a capacitor can store is given by its **capacitance**. Its unit is the **farad**, after the English scientist Michael Faraday. One farad is a great deal, so ordinary capacitors have values in microfarads (µF), nanofarads or picofarads. In a parallel-plate capacitor, the capacitance is greater the larger the plates are and the smaller the distance between them.

The stored energy is calculated with the formula E = ½ · C · U². So a capacitor of 100 µF at 10 volts stores 5 millijoules. If you charge it through a resistor, it does not fill up immediately but slowly. The **time constant** is resistance times capacitance, and after about five time constants it is practically charged.

If you connect capacitors side by side, that is in parallel, the capacitances add up. In a series connection the total capacitance becomes smaller: two times 10 µF gives only 5 µF. Once a capacitor is charged, direct current can no longer flow through it, but alternating current can. The higher the frequency, the smaller its **reactance**.

In power supplies, capacitors smooth the voltage so that devices get an even supply of electricity. In a camera flash they release their energy in an instant. The touchscreen of a mobile phone often works capacitively, like a capacitor whose capacitance changes when a finger touches it. **Electrolytic capacitors** have especially high capacitances, but they are polarised and must be fitted the right way round.

One of the first capacitors was the **Leyden jar** from the middle of the 18th century. It was a glass jar coated with metal inside and outside. Scientists could use it to produce powerful electric sparks and gave spectacular demonstrations at the time. Today there are tiny capacitors smaller than a grain of sand.

begriffe.erklaerung: How much electric charge a capacitor can store.
Unit of capacitance, named after Michael Faraday.
Insulating layer between the plates of a capacitor.
Time equal to resistance times capacitance, which describes charging.
Capacitor with high capacitance that only works when connected with the right polarity.

gewusst: In large devices, capacitors can still hold a dangerous charge even after being unplugged.
A smartphone often contains hundreds of tiny capacitors.
The Leyden jar is named after the city of Leiden in the Netherlands.

teile.einleitung: The Large Hadron Collider, LHC for short, is the largest particle accelerator in the world. It lies in a ring tunnel about 27 kilometres long under the border between Switzerland and France near Geneva. Here researchers make tiny particles collide at almost the speed of light to study the smallest building blocks of the world.
wichtigste: The LHC belongs to the CERN research centre near Geneva.
Its tunnel has a circumference of about 27 kilometres.
From 1989 to 2000 the LEP accelerator used the same tunnel.
The superconducting magnets are cooled to about 1.9 kelvin.
On 4 July 2012 ATLAS and CMS announced the discovery of a Higgs boson.
Since 2022 the LHC has reached 13.6 TeV in proton-proton collisions.
In September 2008 a faulty electrical connection caused a serious incident.

abschnitte.text: The LHC was built by **CERN**, the European Organization for Nuclear Research, based in Meyrin near Geneva. The ring tunnel lies about 50 to 175 metres underground, partly in Switzerland and partly in France. Before that, from 1989 to 2000, the **LEP** accelerator ran in the same tunnel, accelerating electrons and positrons. The LHC started on 10 September 2008.

In the LHC two beams of **protons** circle in opposite directions through two pipes. Strong magnets keep them on their circular path, and electric fields give them more energy on every lap. The protons become almost as fast as light and go round the ring about 11,000 times per second. At four points the beams cross, and the particles collide.

The more than 1,200 large bending magnets are **superconducting**, which means their current flows without resistance. For this they have to be cooled with liquid helium to about 1.9 kelvin, roughly minus 271 degrees Celsius. That is even colder than empty space. In September 2008 a faulty electrical connection between two magnets melted and helium escaped, so the LHC was out of action for over a year.

At the crossing points stand huge detectors that record the debris of the particles like cameras. **ATLAS** and **CMS** are general-purpose detectors; ATLAS is as big as a building several storeys high. ALICE studies collisions of heavy lead nuclei and the quark-gluon plasma as it existed shortly after the Big Bang. LHCb uses b quarks to study the difference between matter and antimatter.

ATLAS and CMS announced the most important discovery at the LHC on 4 July 2012: a **Higgs boson**. Physicists had predicted this particle back in 1964; it is connected with the fact that other particles have mass. Peter Higgs and François Englert received the Nobel Prize in Physics for it in 2013. Thousands of researchers from more than 100 countries work on the LHC experiments.

The energy of the particles is measured in teraelectronvolts, TeV for short. Since 2022 the protons have collided with a total of 13.6 TeV, each one having 6.8 TeV. This makes a proton about 7,250 times heavier than at rest; this is called the Lorentz factor. Next, the LHC is being upgraded to the High-Luminosity LHC, which is to deliver many more collisions.

begriffe.erklaerung: A machine that brings tiny particles up to very high speeds.
A building block of the atomic nucleus with a positive charge.
A material that conducts electricity with no resistance at all when very cold.
A measuring device that detects and records particles.
An elementary particle that explains why other particles have mass.

gewusst: At CERN in 1989, Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web so that researchers could share their data more easily.
Before the start, some people feared the LHC could create dangerous black holes, but experts showed that there is no danger.
The experiments at the LHC produce so much data that it is spread across data centres all over the world.

teile.einleitung: Morse code is a code of short and long signals with which letters and numbers can be sent. It was invented in the 19th century for the electric telegraph. The best-known Morse signal is the distress call SOS: three short, three long, three short.
wichtigste: The Morse alphabet consists of dots and dashes, that is, short and long signals.
The well-known distress call SOS is sent as three short, three long, three short.
Morse signals can be sent with light or with sound.
The letter E is just a single short dot.
The letter T is a single long dash.
In the past Morse signals were sent over wires with the telegraph.
Radio amateurs still use the Morse alphabet as a hobby today.

abschnitte.text: In Morse code, every letter and every digit is represented by a sequence of short and long signals. The short ones are called **dots**, the long ones **dashes**. A dash lasts three times as long as a dot. Common letters have short signals, so E is just a dot and T just a dash, so that messages can be sent faster.

In the 1830s the American **Samuel Morse**, together with Alfred Vail, developed an electric telegraph and the matching code. In 1844 the first message was sent over a long telegraph line from Washington to Baltimore. Later the code was developed further into the international Morse alphabet. It is still used all over the world today.

With the **Morse key** you close a circuit for a short or long time. In the telegraph, current then flows through a wire, and at the other end a tone or a mark on a paper strip appears. But Morse signals can also be sent with a torch, a signal lamp, a whistle or by radio. In the past ships communicated at night with flashes of light.

The distress signal **SOS** was agreed internationally at the beginning of the 20th century. It is easy to send and hard to mistake: three dots, three dashes, three dots, with no pause in between. When the Titanic sank in 1912, its radio operators sent distress calls in Morse code. Until the end of the 1990s Morse radio was compulsory at sea; then it was replaced by satellite technology.

Today Morse is used mainly by **radio amateurs**, who make contact with people all over the world as a hobby. Scouts also often learn the Morse alphabet. Aviation radio beacons still send their identifier in Morse code today. For people who can hardly move, Morse sent by blinking or with a switch can be a way of communicating.

begriffe.erklaerung: A device that sends messages with electrical signals over wires.
A key with which you give short and long Morse signals.
A person who transmits and receives with their own radio equipment as a hobby.
A signal with which you call for help when in danger.

gewusst: Samuel Morse was originally a painter before he turned to the telegraph.
Experienced operators can send more than 30 words per minute in Morse and understand the signals by ear.

teile.einleitung: The connecting rod is a component in engines that connects the piston to the crankshaft. It turns the up-and-down movement of the piston into rotation. Without it, a car engine could not drive the wheels.
wichtigste: The connecting rod connects the piston and the crankshaft.
Its upper end moves up and down, its lower end in a circle.
It is connected to the piston by the gudgeon pin.
A four-cylinder inline engine has 4 connecting rods.
In car engines they are usually made of forged steel.
During combustion it has to withstand a large compressive force.
On a steam locomotive the corresponding part is called the driving rod.

abschnitte.text: The **connecting rod**, conrod for short, is a linking bar in a piston engine. Its upper end sits on the **piston**, its lower end on the **crankshaft**. The upper, smaller eye is called the small end, the lower, larger one the big end. The lower end is usually split and is fixed round the crankshaft with bolts.

The piston moves in a straight line up and down in the cylinder. The lower end of the connecting rod, on the other hand, runs in a **circle** around the axis of the crankshaft. In this way a back-and-forth movement becomes a rotation, similar to cycling, when your legs turn the pedals. With each turn of the crankshaft, the piston is moved once all the way down and once all the way up.

When the mixture in the cylinder burns, it presses on the piston with enormous force. The connecting rod must pass on this **compressive force** without bending. During intake, on the other hand, it is under tension. That is why it is usually made of **forged steel** and has a cross-section shaped like an I or H, which is stable and yet light.

Each cylinder has a piston and a connecting rod. So a four-cylinder inline engine has 4 connecting rods, all attached to the same crankshaft. The **gudgeon pin** connects the upper end to the piston so that it can move. Racing engines sometimes use titanium connecting rods because they are lighter.

Steam engines also have a kind of connecting rod. On the **steam locomotive** it is called the **driving rod**, and it connects the piston with the large driving wheels. You can see it clearly from outside when a steam locomotive pulls away. Coupling rods then connect several wheels with each other so that they all pull together.

begriffe.erklaerung: Turning shaft that takes up the movement of the pistons.
Movable part that slides up and down in the cylinder.
Pin that connects the connecting rod to the piston.
Rod that connects the piston with the wheel on a steam locomotive.

gewusst: If a connecting rod breaks, in the worst case it can punch a hole in the engine block.
Connecting rods in car engines often weigh only a few hundred grams, but have to withstand forces of several tonnes.
A sewing machine with a foot treadle also uses the principle of the crank and connecting rod.

teile.einleitung: Pilatus Aircraft is the largest aircraft manufacturer in Switzerland and is based in Stans in the canton of Nidwalden. The company, founded in 1939, is named after the nearby mountain Pilatus. Its aircraft fly all over the world, as trainers for military pilots, as bush planes or as business jets.
wichtigste: Pilatus has its headquarters in Stans.
The company was founded in 1939.
The PC-6 Porter is famous for taking off and landing on very short runways.
The PC-12 is a single-engine turboprop aircraft.
The PC-24 is Pilatus's first jet and can also land on unpaved runways.
The PC-7, PC-9 and PC-21 are mainly training aircraft.
The Swiss Air Force trains military pilots on the PC-21.
In 2024 Pilatus took over about 230 employees in Emmen from RUAG Aerostructures Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: Pilatus Aircraft was founded in 1939 and has its headquarters in **Stans** in the canton of Nidwalden, right next to Buochs airfield. It is named after the mountain **Pilatus** near Lucerne. Pilatus employs several thousand people and trains many apprentices. The company is one of the most important employers in central Switzerland.

The **PC-6 Porter** first flew in 1959 and became a legend. It can take off and land on very short runways, even on meadows or glaciers. That is why it was used in the mountains, in the jungle and in remote areas for transport and rescue flights. Parachutists like using it too.

The **PC-12** is a single-engine **turboprop**, that is, an aircraft with a propeller driven by a gas turbine. It has room for about nine passengers or for cargo. It is especially well known with rescue services, for example the Royal Flying Doctor Service in Australia, which uses it to fly doctors to patients in the outback. The PC-12 is Pilatus's best-selling aircraft.

With the PC-7, PC-9 and **PC-21**, Pilatus mainly builds training aircraft for training military pilots. Air forces in many countries learn to fly with them. The Swiss Air Force trains its pilots on the PC-21. The PC-7 Team, the Swiss Air Force's aerobatic display team, is also well known.

The **PC-24** is Pilatus's first jet aircraft and was delivered to customers from 2018. It is a business jet that can also land on short and even unpaved runways. This is very unusual for a jet. That is why it can reach places that otherwise only propeller aircraft can get to.

Pilatus has grown strongly in recent decades and supplies aircraft to many countries. In 2024 the company took over about 230 employees and the machinery in Emmen from **RUAG Aerostructures Switzerland**. Pilatus also has sites in the USA and Australia.

begriffe.erklaerung: An aircraft engine in which a gas turbine turns a propeller.
An aircraft driven by jet engines.
The take-off and landing strip of an airfield.
An aircraft with which pilots learn to fly.

gewusst: In 1960, during an expedition in the Himalayas, a PC-6 landed on a glacier at over 5,700 metres.
Many Pilatus aircraft have names and numbers with the letters PC, such as PC-6, PC-12 or PC-24.

teile.einleitung: Medical technology covers all the devices, instruments and materials with which doctors detect, treat or relieve illnesses. These include X-ray machines and CT scanners as well as pacemakers, hearing aids and dental implants. In Switzerland medical technology is an important branch of the economy.
wichtigste: Medical technology combines engineering, natural science and medicine.
In Switzerland the authority Swissmedic supervises medicines and medical devices.
In 1971 Godfrey Hounsfield built the first CT scanner used in hospitals.
In 1958 a pacemaker was implanted in a person for the first time, in Sweden.
Dental implants are usually made of titanium, because it grows firmly together with the bone.
The Lokomat walking robot was co-developed at the Balgrist University Hospital in Zurich.

abschnitte.text: With **imaging** devices, doctors can see inside the body without operating. In 1895 Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen discovered the rays named after him, which make bones visible. In 1971 the engineer Godfrey Hounsfield built the first **CT scanner** used in hospitals, which shows the body in cross-sectional images. On the Hounsfield scale, water has the value 0 and air the value minus 1,000. Ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging even manage entirely without X-rays.

A **pacemaker** gives the heart electrical impulses when it beats too slowly. The first was implanted in a person in Sweden in 1958. Dental implants are usually made of **titanium**, because this metal grows firmly together with the bone. Other examples are artificial hip joints, hearing aids and cochlear implants, which allow deaf people to hear.

A **pulse oximeter** is clipped onto the finger and uses red and infrared light to measure how much oxygen is in the blood. The ECG records the electrical signals of the heart. In intensive care units, monitors keep watch on pulse, blood pressure and breathing around the clock. Even the simple clinical thermometer is a medical device.

In operating theatres, **surgical robots** help, controlled very precisely by surgeons. After accidents or strokes, patients practise walking again with machines. The **Lokomat** walking robot was co-developed at the Balgrist University Hospital in Zurich and is now used in many countries. It guides the patients' legs on a treadmill in a natural walking movement.

Switzerland is an important location for medical technology, with many companies making, for example, implants, hearing aids and injection systems. The federal authority **Swissmedic** in Bern makes sure that medicines and medical devices are safe. Since 26 May 2021 Switzerland has been treated as a **third country** in the EU single market for medical devices, because the mutual recognition agreement was not updated. This means extra work for Swiss companies exporting to the EU.

begriffe.erklaerung: A device or material used in medicine for examination or treatment.
An X-ray method that shows the body in many cross-sectional images.
An artificial part that is placed in the body.
A small device that sets the rhythm of the heart.
Treatment that helps you get fit again after illness or an accident.

gewusst: In 1979 Godfrey Hounsfield received the Nobel Prize in Medicine for inventing computed tomography.
The first implanted pacemaker was about the size of an ice hockey puck.
Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen took one of the first X-ray pictures of his wife's hand.

teile.einleitung: A suspension bridge is a bridge whose deck hangs from thick cables. The cables run over tall towers and are firmly anchored on land. In this way suspension bridges can span huge distances over rivers, bays and gorges.
wichtigste: On a suspension bridge the deck hangs from large main cables.
The main cables are under tension, which means they are pulled apart.
The main cables run over tall towers, the pylons.
The ends of the cables are fixed in heavy anchor blocks on land.
Vertical cables, the hangers, connect the deck with the main cables.
Suspension bridges reach the longest spans of all kinds of bridges.
The longest span belongs to the Çanakkale Bridge in Turkey (as of 2026).

abschnitte.text: A large suspension bridge usually has two tall towers, the **pylons**. The thick **main cables** run over them from one bank to the other. Many vertical cables, the **hangers**, hang down from the main cables. The deck is attached to them. The ends of the main cables are set in huge concrete anchor blocks on land.

The weight of the deck and the cars pulls on the hangers and therefore on the main cables. So the cables are under **tension**. The pylons carry the weight down into the ground, so they are squeezed together. A freely hanging cable forms a **catenary**; under the even load of a deck it becomes roughly a parabola. Because steel cables can withstand a great deal of tension, they can be used to bridge especially long distances.

Long, light bridges can swing in the wind. In 1940 the **Tacoma Narrows Bridge** in the USA collapsed because the wind set it swinging more and more strongly. The disaster was filmed and is still famous today. Since then bridge shapes have been tested in a **wind tunnel**. Modern decks often have a flat, streamlined shape like an aircraft wing.

The **Brooklyn Bridge** in New York opened in 1883 and was one of the first with main cables made of steel wire. The **Golden Gate Bridge** in San Francisco has been a landmark since 1937; its main span is about 1,280 metres. In Japan the Akashi Kaikyō Bridge has spanned a strait since 1998. Today the record is held by the **Çanakkale Bridge** in Turkey, which opened in 2022 and has a free span of over 2,000 metres.

In the Swiss Alps there are many **pedestrian suspension bridges** over gorges and glacier streams. A very well-known one is the Charles Kuonen Suspension Bridge near Randa in Valais, which opened in 2017 and is almost 500 metres long. The Trift Bridge in the Bernese Oberland also attracts many hikers. Such bridges sway a little when you walk across. For big motorways, Switzerland tends to use other kinds of bridges.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tall tower over which the main cables run.
A vertical cable from which the deck hangs.
The free distance between two supports of a bridge.
A heavy concrete block that holds the cable ends in place on land.
A force that pulls something apart.

gewusst: The main cables of the Golden Gate Bridge are made of tens of thousands of thin steel wires bundled together.
The Golden Gate Bridge is not golden but painted in an orange-red colour.
The Incas already built simple suspension bridges from plant fibres in the Andes.

teile.einleitung: Programming means giving a computer exact instructions in a programming language. A program is a sequence of such commands that the computer carries out step by step. Apps, games, websites and even traffic lights only work thanks to programs.
wichtigste: Programming means giving a computer exact instructions.
Ada Lovelace is considered the author of the first computer program, for Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine.
A compiler translates the whole source code into machine code before it runs.
Guido van Rossum developed the programming language Python.
With 8 bits, 256 different values can be represented.
The hexadecimal number FF corresponds to the decimal value 255.
Binary search finds an entry in a sorted list in O(log n) steps.

abschnitte.text: A **program** is a list of instructions that a computer follows exactly. A computer understands nothing by itself; every little detail has to be laid down. The basic building blocks are commands, **loops** for repetitions and conditions such as “if, then”. Data is stored in **variables**. An exact set of instructions for solving a problem is called an algorithm.

Around 1843 the Englishwoman **Ada Lovelace** wrote a set of instructions for Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine. That is why she is considered the author of the first computer program, even though the machine was never finished. In the past computers were programmed with punched cards. In the 1950s the first high-level programming languages such as Fortran appeared. The Swiss computer scientist **Niklaus Wirth** developed the language Pascal at ETH Zurich.

There are hundreds of programming languages, for example Python, JavaScript, Java or C. **Python** was developed by the Dutchman Guido van Rossum and appeared in 1991. For children there are block languages such as **Scratch**, in which you fit commands together like puzzle pieces. A **compiler** translates the whole source code into machine code before it runs. An interpreter, on the other hand, runs the program line by line.

Internally computers calculate only with 0 and 1, a unit called a **bit**. With 8 bits, that is one **byte**, 256 different values can be represented. Programmers often write numbers in the hexadecimal system, with the digits 0 to 9 and A to F. The hexadecimal number FF corresponds to the decimal value 255. Colours on websites are often given this way too, for example FF0000 for red.

A good program not only solves a task correctly but also quickly. **Binary search** halves a sorted list with every step and therefore needs only O(log n) steps. In a list with a million entries, about 20 comparisons are enough. Mistakes in a program are called **bugs**, and looking for them is called debugging. In Switzerland many children take their first steps in programming at school in the subject Media and Computer Science.

begriffe.erklaerung: Exact step-by-step instructions for solving a problem.
A named storage place for a value.
A part of a program that is repeated several times.
Program that translates source code into machine code.
A mistake in a program.

gewusst: The word “bug” became famous when in 1947 a real moth caused a fault in a computer at Harvard University.
The programming language Python is named after the British comedy group Monty Python, not after the snake.
The programming language Ada was named in honour of Ada Lovelace.

teile.einleitung: Charging infrastructure is everything needed to supply electric cars with electricity: charging stations, plugs, cables and connections to the power grid. The more people drive electric cars, the more important a dense network of charging points becomes. There are slow charging stations for home and powerful rapid chargers on motorways.
wichtigste: In Europe the Type 2 plug is the standard for charging with alternating current.
For rapid charging with direct current, Europe mostly uses the CCS system.
A wallbox with three phases of 16 amperes each at 230 volts charges at about 11 kilowatts.
Rapid charging stations with 150 kilowatts and more are called high power charging, HPC for short.
Above about 80 per cent charge, rapid charging slows down to protect the battery.
The Federal Roads Office FEDRO had rapid charging stations installed at rest areas on the national roads.

abschnitte.text: **Charging infrastructure** includes charging posts on streets and in car parks, wallboxes in garages and large charging parks on motorways. On top of this come cables, plugs, power connections and payment systems by app or card. A single connection at which a car charges is called a **charging point**. So that everything fits together, manufacturers have agreed on shared standards.

The power grid supplies **alternating current**, but the battery in the car stores direct current. During slow charging, a charger in the car converts the current. In Europe you plug in the **Type 2 plug** for this. A wallbox at home usually charges at 11 kilowatts, because three phases times 230 volts times 16 amperes gives about 11,000 watts. That means a car is full again overnight.

In **rapid charging stations**, the converter is inside the post itself and supplies direct current straight into the battery. In Europe the **CCS** plug, the Combined Charging System, is used for this. Stations with 150 kilowatts and more are called high power charging. In about 20 to 30 minutes, a modern car can recharge a large part of its range this way. From about 80 per cent, the car reduces the power so that the battery does not overheat and ages less quickly.

For heavy electric lorries the **Megawatt Charging System** was developed, which allows outputs in the megawatt range. With **bidirectional charging**, the car can not only take in electricity but also return it to the house or the grid. In this way many parked cars together could act like one large electricity store. Researchers are also testing wireless charging using coils in the ground.

In Switzerland the number of public charging points has risen sharply in recent years. **FEDRO** had rapid charging stations built at rest areas along the national roads so that people can charge on long journeys too. Many municipalities, shopping centres and hotels also offer charging posts. Charging is especially environmentally friendly when the electricity comes from hydropower or solar energy.

begriffe.erklaerung: A single connection at which an electric car takes on electricity.
A charging station that hangs on the wall of a garage.
A unit of power, that is, how much energy flows per second.
A plug system for rapid charging with direct current.
In both directions, that is, taking in electricity and giving it back.

gewusst: A household socket supplies only about 2.3 kilowatts, which is why charging from it takes a very long time.
A 150-kilowatt rapid charger supplies about as much power as 75 kettles at once.
The Type 2 plug is sometimes called the “Mennekes plug” after the company that developed it.

teile.einleitung: NEST is a special research building in Dübendorf near Zurich. Here experts test new building materials, energy systems and ways of building not only in the laboratory but in real everyday life. The building works like a construction kit in which individual parts are swapped again and again.
wichtigste: NEST stands for “Next Evolution in Sustainable Building Technologies”.
The building was opened in 2016 in Dübendorf in the canton of Zurich.
It is run jointly by the research institutes Empa and Eawag.
A central backbone with open platforms carries exchangeable research modules, the units.
The units are actually lived in or used as offices.
Well-known units are “Urban Mining & Recycling”, the “DFAB HOUSE” and HiLo.
The aim is to bring new ideas from the laboratory to real building sites faster.

abschnitte.text: NEST stands on the **Empa** site in Dübendorf. Empa is the Swiss Federal Laboratories for Materials Science and Technology, and **Eawag** is the water research institute of the ETH Domain. Both run the building together. The name NEST also means “nest” in English, and indeed new projects keep “nesting” here.

The heart of the building is a fixed concrete **backbone** containing the stairs, the lift and all the pipes and cables for electricity, water and heat. Several open platforms on different floors branch off from it. The research modules, the **units**, are docked onto these platforms. When an experiment is finished, a unit can be taken down again and replaced by a new one.

The “Urban Mining & Recycling” unit opened in 2018. All the building materials used are meant to be reusable or recyclable later, **separated by type**. That is why the parts were slotted, clamped or screwed together rather than glued. In this way the unit shows how a house itself can become a store of raw materials. This idea is called **urban mining**, that is, mining in the city.

ETH Zurich's “DFAB HOUSE” was largely planned and built using **digital fabrication**. Robots, for example, built a curved steel mesh for a concrete wall, and ceilings were made with 3D-printed formwork. The **HiLo** unit, opened in 2021, is defined by a thin, doubly curved concrete shell roof. Such shells save a lot of material, because their shape distributes the forces especially cleverly.

People live in NEST, and others work there in offices. Meanwhile many sensors measure how much energy is used and how well the rooms work. In this way the researchers find out whether an idea also works in real life. Companies from the construction industry work closely with them so that good solutions reach the market quickly.

begriffe.erklaerung: Federal research institute for materials and technologies, based in Dübendorf.
Swiss research institute that deals with water and bodies of water.
An exchangeable research module that is docked onto NEST.
The idea of seeing buildings as stores of raw materials that can be reused.
Building with computer plans, robots and 3D printers.

gewusst: NEST is never finished, because it was deliberately planned as a building site for ever new ideas.
The roof of the HiLo unit is only a few centimetres thick and still supports itself.
Among other things, used and recycled materials were built into the “Urban Mining & Recycling” unit.

teile.einleitung: The Jaquet-Droz automata are three elaborate figures built in the 18th century in La Chaux-de-Fonds in the Neuchâtel Jura. The Writer, the Draughtsman and the Musician move like living people thanks to thousands of gearwheels and cams. They are considered masterpieces of Swiss watchmaking and early forerunners of the computer.
wichtigste: Pierre and Henri-Louis Jaquet-Droz built the automata with Jean-Frédéric Leschot between 1768 and 1774.
The automata are the Writer, the Draughtsman and the Musician.
The Writer consists of about 6,000 parts.
His text can be set freely using a wheel with exchangeable characters, which is why he is considered a forerunner of the programmable computer.
Among other things, the Draughtsman draws a portrait of King Louis XV of France.
The Musician plays a real organ with her fingers.
The automata served as advertising for their makers' watches at royal courts.
Today they are in the Musée d'art et d'histoire in Neuchâtel.

abschnitte.text: **Pierre Jaquet-Droz** was a watchmaker from La Chaux-de-Fonds in the canton of Neuchâtel. Together with his son **Henri-Louis** and the mechanic Jean-Frédéric Leschot, he built the three automata between 1768 and 1774. At that time the Jura was already a centre of watchmaking. The family wanted to show with the figures how well they could handle the finest mechanics.

The **Writer** is a boy sitting at a desk and writing with a goose quill. He dips the quill in the inkpot, shakes it lightly and follows the text with his eyes. He consists of about 6,000 parts. On a wheel, characters can be exchanged so that he can write a freely chosen text of up to about 40 letters, a kind of **program**.

The **Draughtsman** is also a boy and can draw four different pictures. These include a portrait of King **Louis XV** of France and a little dog. Now and then he blows the dust off his sheet. His movements are controlled by cams, in which the lines are stored like memories.

The **Musician** is a young woman who plays a real small organ. She really presses the keys with her fingers, so the notes do not come from a hidden music box. As she plays, her chest rises and falls as if she were breathing, and she moves her head and eyes. At the end of a piece she bows to the audience.

The Jaquet-Droz family travelled with the automata to kings and princes all over Europe. The audiences were amazed, and many afterwards bought the family's watches. So the automata were brilliant **advertising**. After changing hands many times, they were bought by the city of Neuchâtel at the beginning of the 20th century so that they would stay in Switzerland.

The three figures are now in the **Musée d'art et d'histoire** in Neuchâtel. After more than 250 years they still work and are demonstrated on certain days. Experts see the Writer as an early forerunner of the programmable computer. The automata show how advanced Swiss precision mechanics already was in the 18th century.

begriffe.erklaerung: Machine that carries out a sequence by itself.
Irregularly shaped disc that controls a movement as it turns.
Making very small, precise mechanical parts, as in watches.
Fixed sequence of instructions that a machine carries out.

gewusst: The Writer can be given a new text every time; you only have to exchange the characters on his wheel.
The Musician seems to breathe, because her chest rises and falls while she plays.
The word android for human-like machines was already used at the time of the Jaquet-Droz automata.

teile.einleitung: A hairdryer is an electrical device that blows warm air so that wet hair dries faster. In Switzerland it is usually called a “Föhn”, after the warm downslope wind in the Alps. Today there is one in almost every bathroom.
wichtigste: A hairdryer dries wet hair with a stream of warm air.
In Switzerland it is usually called a “Föhn”.
Inside there is a fan and a heating wire.
A grille at the back stops hair being sucked in.
The cool setting blows cool air and is kind to the hair.
A hairdryer must never fall into water, because there is a risk of electric shock.

abschnitte.text: Inside the casing, a small **electric motor** turns a fan. This sucks in air at the back and blows it out again at the front. In between is a **heating wire**, which glows when electricity flows through it and warms the air. Warm air can take up a lot of water vapour, so the water in the hair evaporates faster.

Most devices have several settings for the strength of the airflow and for the heat. With the **cool setting**, the hairdryer blows cool air so that a hairstyle holds. The narrow attachment at the front is called the **nozzle** and directs the air at one spot. A wide attachment with prongs, the **diffuser**, spreads the air gently and is often used for curls.

Electricity and water together are very dangerous. A hairdryer must therefore never fall into the bath or the washbasin, not even when switched off, as long as it is plugged in. In bathrooms a **residual current device** (RCD) protects against deadly electric shocks by switching off the current in a flash. Built-in overheating protection switches the device off if it gets too hot.

You should not hold the hairdryer right up against your scalp, because the hot air can burn. A distance of about a hand's width is good. Gently drying your hair with a towel first saves time and electricity. Every now and then you should clean dust and hair off the grille at the back so that the device does not overheat.

Around 1890 the Frenchman Alexandre Godefroy developed a large hairdryer for hairdressing salons. Small hand-held devices appeared from the early 20th century. The German company AEG registered the name **Fön** as a trademark. Because the name became so well known, many people still call every hairdryer a “Föhn” today.

begriffe.erklaerung: Warm, dry downslope wind in the Alps, and the Swiss word for a hairdryer.
A wire that gets hot when electricity flows through it.
Wide attachment that spreads the air gently.
Safety switch that cuts off the current immediately if current flows away the wrong way.

gewusst: In German-speaking Switzerland the hairdryer is named after a wind that blows in Swiss valleys such as the Reuss valley or the Rhine valley.
A hairdryer often uses about as much electricity as a kettle.
The first hairdryers in hairdressing salons were so big that you had to sit under a hood.

teile.einleitung: A loudspeaker turns electrical signals into sound that we can hear. Without it there would be no music from your phone, no announcements at the station and no sound on television. Inside, a magnet moves a thin membrane back and forth at lightning speed.
wichtigste: A loudspeaker converts electrical signals into sound.
In a dynamic loudspeaker, a voice coil moves in the field of a permanent magnet.
The coil drives a membrane that sets the air vibrating.
Woofers mainly reproduce bass, tweeters the high notes.
A crossover divides the signal between the individual loudspeakers according to pitch.
An amplifier makes the weak music signal strong enough for the loudspeaker.

abschnitte.text: A **loudspeaker** is a sound transducer: it turns electrical vibrations into vibrations of the air, which our ear perceives as sound. Sound is nothing other than rapid changes in pressure in the air. A young person hears sounds between about 20 hertz and 20,000 hertz. A good loudspeaker should reproduce as much of this whole range as possible.

The most common type is the **dynamic loudspeaker**. In it, a coil of wire, the **voice coil**, sits in the field of a permanent magnet. When the music signal flows through the coil, it is attracted one moment and repelled the next. The coil is attached to a **membrane** made of paper, plastic or metal, which therefore vibrates back and forth and moves the air.

Large membranes move a lot of air and are suitable for low notes; small membranes vibrate faster and are suitable for high notes. That is why good speakers contain several drivers: a **woofer** for the bass, often a midrange driver and a tweeter. A **crossover** divides the signal by pitch between the right drivers. For very deep bass there is also the subwoofer.

A membrane pushes the air forwards and at the same time backwards. When these two sound waves meet, they partly cancel each other out, especially at low notes. A **cabinet** separates the front sound wave from the back one so that the bass stays strong. That is why loudspeakers are almost always inside a box.

For **stereo** sound you need at least two loudspeakers, one for the left and one for the right. In cinemas and home cinemas, many loudspeakers provide surround sound. Tiny loudspeakers are found in headphones, mobile phones and hearing aids. Important: music that is too loud can permanently damage your hearing, so you should set the volume sensibly.

begriffe.erklaerung: A thin, movable surface that sets the air vibrating.
A coil of wire that moves in the magnetic field when current flows.
Unit of vibrations per second, which decides the pitch.
A circuit that divides high and low notes between different loudspeakers.
A device that makes weak electrical signals stronger.

gewusst: A loudspeaker can also work the other way round as a simple microphone.
Older people usually hear high notes less well than children.
The membrane of a tweeter vibrates back and forth many thousands of times per second for high notes.

teile.einleitung: Graphene is a form of carbon that is only a single layer of atoms thick. The atoms in it are arranged like a honeycomb of hexagons. Graphene is extremely thin, very strong and conducts electricity excellently, which is why it is considered a wonder material of the future.
wichtigste: Graphene consists of a single-atom layer of carbon atoms in hexagons.
The carbon atoms are sp² hybridised.
Graphene was first obtained in 2004 by peeling graphite with sticky tape.
Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov received the Nobel Prize in Physics for it in 2010.
A single layer of graphene absorbs about 2.3 per cent of visible light.
Ideal graphene has no band gap and a very high electron mobility.
Relative to its thickness, graphene has a record-breaking tensile strength.
Empa makes graphene nanoribbons to create a band gap.

abschnitte.text: Graphene is a special form of the element **carbon**. The atoms form a flat layer made entirely of hexagons, like honeycomb or a chain-link fence. This layer is only a single atom thick, which makes it one of the thinnest materials of all. If you stack many layers of graphene on top of each other, you get **graphite**, the material in pencil leads. So every pencil line contains tiny pieces made of a few layers of graphene.

For a long time people believed such a thin layer could not be stable at all. In 2004 **Andre Geim** and **Konstantin Novoselov** at the University of Manchester succeeded in making graphene. To do this they used **sticky tape** to peel thin layers off a piece of graphite again and again until only a single layer was left. This amazingly simple method made graphene world-famous. In 2010 the two received the Nobel Prize in Physics for it.

Relative to its thickness, graphene is considered one of the strongest materials of all and has an extremely high **tensile strength**. At the same time it is flexible and almost transparent, because one layer absorbs only about 2.3 per cent of visible light. It conducts heat and electricity excellently. The electrons move especially fast in it; this is called high **electron mobility**. The carbon atoms are sp² hybridised, that is, each is joined to three neighbours in one plane.

Ideal graphene has no **band gap**, so it cannot simply be used like silicon as a switch in computer chips. That is why researchers at Empa in Dübendorf make narrow **graphene nanoribbons**. They are built up atom by atom on surfaces through targeted chemical synthesis. Depending on the width and shape of the ribbons, a band gap is created. One day this could make tiny, fast electronic components possible.

Researchers are testing graphene for flexible screens, faster electronics, better batteries and light, stable composite materials. It is already found today in some sports equipment such as tennis rackets or bike helmets. It is also being researched as a filter for water or as a sensor. But making large, flawless sheets of graphene is still difficult and expensive.

begriffe.erklaerung: Chemical element that diamond and graphite are also made of.
Many layers of graphene lying on top of each other, for example in pencil leads.
Energy gap that makes a material a switchable semiconductor.
Very narrow strip of a material, only a few atoms wide.
How hard a material can be pulled before it tears.

gewusst: When you write with a pencil, you create tiny pieces made of a few layers of graphene.
The Nobel Prize for graphene started with an ordinary piece of sticky tape.
Before the Nobel Prize, Andre Geim also received a joke prize for making a frog float with magnets.

teile.einleitung: An insulator is a material or a component that conducts electric current not at all or hardly at all. Insulators protect us from electric shocks and hold high-voltage power lines safely on their pylons. Good insulators are, for example, glass, porcelain, plastic, rubber and dry air.
wichtigste: An insulator hardly conducts electric current at all.
Inside an insulator there are hardly any freely moving charge carriers.
Conductors such as copper, on the other hand, conduct electricity very well.
Overhead lines hang on insulators made of porcelain, glass or plastic.
The bare wires of an overhead line are insulated from each other by the surrounding air.
At very high voltage even air can become conductive, as lightning shows.
Dielectric strength shows up to what voltage an insulating material holds.

abschnitte.text: Electric current is the movement of charged particles, usually **electrons**. In metals such as copper or aluminium many electrons can move freely, which is why they are called **conductors**. In an **insulator** the electrons are tightly bound to their atoms. Because there are hardly any freely moving charge carriers, almost no current flows. In between there are semiconductors such as silicon, which are needed for computer chips.

Every cable in the flat consists of copper wires with a **plastic** coating. The coating means you can touch the cable safely. Plugs and sockets have plastic casings, and electricians wear insulating gloves and use tools with plastic handles. Rubber, glass, ceramics and dry wood also hardly conduct electricity. Water with dissolved substances, on the other hand, does conduct, which is why electrical appliances never belong in the bath.

High-voltage lines in Switzerland carry voltages of up to 380,000 volts. The bare cables hang on long chains of **porcelain**, glass or plastic that separate the cables from the steel pylon. The ribbed shape lengthens the path over the surface so that in rain no current creeps along the wet insulator. Between the cables themselves there is no coating; there the **air** insulates. That is why the cables must hang far enough apart.

Every insulating material only holds up to a certain voltage; this is called **dielectric strength**. If the voltage becomes too great, the insulation breaks down and a spark jumps across. **Lightning** shows that at very high voltage even air can become conductive. Dry air can withstand about 3,000 volts per millimetre before it breaks down. In thunderstorms, voltages of many millions of volts build up between clouds and the ground.

Insulation protects people from dangerous **electric shocks**. That is why you must never touch damaged cables with visible wires and should replace them immediately. With overhead lines the rule is: never climb pylons and never fly kites near power lines, because electricity can also jump across through the air. The word insulator is also used for materials that conduct heat poorly, such as polystyrene or glass wool. Many good electrical insulators are also good heat insulators.

begriffe.erklaerung: A material through which electric current can flow well, for example copper.
A tiny, negatively charged particle that carries the current in metals.
The force that drives the current, measured in volts.
How high a voltage an insulating material can withstand before a spark breaks through.

gewusst: Birds can sit on a high-voltage line because they touch only one cable and no current flows through them.
Completely pure water conducts electricity very poorly; only dissolved salts make it conductive.
The insulator chains of large high-voltage lines can be several metres long.

teile.einleitung: Carbon fibre reinforced plastic, CFRP for short or simply called carbon, is a material made of fine carbon fibres embedded in plastic. It is extremely light and yet very strong and stiff. That is why aircraft, racing cars, bicycles and sports equipment are made from it.
wichtigste: CFRP consists of carbon fibres embedded in a plastic such as epoxy resin.
Most carbon fibres are made from polyacrylonitrile (PAN).
A single fibre is only about 5 to 10 micrometres thick.
CFRP has a density of about 1.5 grams per cubic centimetre and is therefore much lighter than steel.
When overloaded, CFRP tends to break in a brittle way instead of bending like steel.
In 1981 the McLaren MP4/1 was the first Formula 1 car with a carbon fibre monocoque.
Because CFRP hardly expands, it is suitable for precision parts such as satellite structures.

abschnitte.text: CFRP is a **composite material**; it consists of two parts. The **carbon fibres** are very thin, only about 5 to 10 micrometres, much thinner than a hair. Thousands of them are bundled into strands and woven into mats. These fibres are embedded in a plastic, the **matrix**. In aircraft construction this is usually epoxy resin, which holds the fibres together and protects them.

Most fibres are made from the plastic **polyacrylonitrile**, PAN for short. PAN threads are heated strongly without air until almost only carbon is left. For components, **prepregs** are often laid in a mould; these are fibre mats pre-soaked with resin. They are stored cold so that the resin does not harden too early. Finally the parts harden in an **autoclave**, a kind of pressure oven.

CFRP has a density of only about 1.5 grams per cubic centimetre, steel on the other hand almost 8 grams. Even so, it is very strong and stiff in the direction of the fibres. That is why CFRP saves a lot of **weight** without losing stability. When overloaded, however, CFRP tends to break in a **brittle** way, without visibly bending first. In addition, it hardly expands with heat in the direction of the fibres, which is important for satellites and measuring instruments.

Modern airliners such as the **Boeing 787** or the **Airbus A350** are made to a large extent of fibre composite materials. In Formula 1, the McLaren MP4/1 of 1981 was the first car with a carbon fibre monocoque; today all racing cars are built this way. Racing bikes, ski poles, tennis rackets and the rotor blades of wind turbines are also often made of CFRP. The Swiss solar aeroplane **Solar Impulse**, which flew around the world in 2016, was especially light thanks to CFRP. Expensive sports cars often have body parts made of visible carbon.

CFRP is expensive, and making it uses a lot of energy. If CFRP is joined to **aluminium**, the parts must be electrically insulated. This is because carbon is more noble and would otherwise trigger galvanic **corrosion** in the aluminium. **Recycling** is also difficult, because fibres and resin are firmly bonded. Researchers are working on processes to recover the valuable fibres.

begriffe.erklaerung: A material made of two or more substances bonded together.
The plastic in which the fibres are embedded.
A fibre mat pre-soaked with resin.
A pressure oven in which CFRP parts harden.
The destruction of a metal by chemical processes, for example rust.

gewusst: A racing bike frame made of CFRP can weigh less than a kilogram.
The typical checked pattern of carbon comes from the woven fibre mats.
In the Boeing 787, about half of the weight of the structure is made up of fibre composite materials.

teile.einleitung: A light-emitting diode, LED for short, is a tiny electronic component that produces light when current flows through it. LEDs are economical, last a very long time and are found today in lamps, screens, traffic lights and bike lights. There was even a Nobel Prize for the invention of the blue LED.
wichtigste: LED stands for light-emitting diode.
The light is produced in a semiconductor crystal.
The two connections are called the anode and the cathode; the shorter leg is usually the negative terminal.
A series resistor limits the current so that the LED does not break.
In 2014 the Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded for the development of the blue LED.
White LED light is usually produced by a blue LED exciting a yellow phosphor.

abschnitte.text: A **light-emitting diode** is a special diode, a component that lets current through in only one direction. Its heart is a tiny **semiconductor crystal**. When current flows in the right direction, part of the electrical energy is converted directly into light there. The colour depends on the material of the crystal; there are red, green, yellow, blue and infrared LEDs.

An LED has two connections: the **anode** as the positive terminal and the **cathode** as the negative terminal. On new LEDs the cathode leg is usually shorter. Because an LED would otherwise draw too much current and burn out, a **series resistor** is connected in front of it. An example: an LED needs 2 volts and 20 milliamperes on a 9-volt battery, so 7 volts must drop across the resistor, and 7 divided by 0.02 gives 350 ohms.

The first LED with visible red light was developed by Nick Holonyak in the USA in 1962. For a long time there were only red, yellow and green LEDs, used mainly as small indicator lights. A bright **blue LED** was only achieved at the beginning of the 1990s by the Japanese researchers Isamu Akasaki, Hiroshi Amano and Shuji Nakamura. They received the Nobel Prize in Physics for it in 2014, because blue finally made white LED light possible.

Most white LED lamps contain a blue LED coated with a yellow **phosphor**. Part of the blue light is converted by the phosphor into yellow light. Our eye sees blue and yellow together as white. Depending on the phosphor, the light looks warmer or cooler.

For the same brightness, LED lamps use only a fraction of the electricity of an old light bulb. They last many years and hardly get hot. That is why light bulbs were gradually taken off the shelves in Switzerland and Europe. LEDs are found today in street lamps, traffic lights, car headlights, television screens and the torches of mobile phones.

begriffe.erklaerung: A component that lets current flow in only one direction.
A material that conducts electricity well only under certain conditions.
The positive terminal connection of the LED.
The negative terminal connection of the LED, usually the shorter leg.
A resistor that limits the current through the LED.

gewusst: Your television's remote control sends signals with an infrared LED whose light you cannot see.
With a mobile phone camera you can often make the invisible flashing of a remote control visible.
An LED can also work the other way round as a weak light sensor.

teile.einleitung: Photovoltaics is the direct conversion of sunlight into electric current. This happens in solar cells, which you now see on many roofs, façades and even dams. It is an important renewable energy source in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Most solar cells are made of silicon.
Peak output is given in kilowatts peak (kWp).
An inverter turns the direct current into alternating current for the household grid.
In 2024 photovoltaics supplied about 7 per cent of Switzerland's electricity.
Photovoltaics produces electricity, whereas solar thermal produces heat.
In Switzerland modules ideally face south.
Alpine installations supply more electricity in winter because they are above the fog and snow reflects light.

abschnitte.text: A **solar cell** usually consists of thin wafers of **silicon**. When light hits it, it frees electrons from their bonds, and an electrical voltage is created. This process is called the **photovoltaic effect**. Many cells together form a solar module, and several modules form a solar installation.

abschnitte.titel: From the roof to the grid
abschnitte.text: Solar modules supply **direct current**. But sockets in the house need alternating current, so an **inverter** converts the current. Whatever you do not need yourself flows into the public grid or into a battery. The output of an installation under standard conditions is given in **kilowatts peak**.

The photovoltaic effect was discovered by the French physicist Alexandre Edmond Becquerel in 1839. In 1954 researchers at Bell Labs in the USA built the first usable silicon solar cell. At first solar cells were used mainly for satellites in space. Only when they became much cheaper did they appear in large numbers on house roofs, from about 2000.

Photovoltaics is growing rapidly in Switzerland and supplied about 7 per cent of the electricity in 2024. In the Swiss Plateau there is often **fog** in winter, so installations there produce much more in summer. In the Alps the sun shines above the fog, and the snow reflects extra light. A well-known example is the installation on the **Muttsee dam** in the canton of Glarus.

Both technologies use the sun, but for different things. Photovoltaics makes **electricity**, while **solar thermal** heats water for the shower and heating. For the best yield over the year, modules in Switzerland face south and are tilted at about 30 degrees. East-west installations, on the other hand, supply more electricity in the morning and evening.

begriffe.erklaerung: Component that converts light directly into electricity.
Semiconductor material made from sand, from which most solar cells are made.
Device that converts direct current into alternating current.
Peak output of a solar installation under standardised test conditions.
Using the sun's heat, for example for hot water.

gewusst: In 2015 and 2016 the Swiss solar aeroplane Solar Impulse 2 flew around the world on solar energy alone.
Solar modules work better in the cold than in heat, which is why sunny winter days in the mountains are ideal.
Silicon, the material of solar cells, is the most common element in the Earth's crust after oxygen.

teile.einleitung: High-voltage direct current transmission, HVDC for short, is a technique for transporting very large amounts of electrical energy over long distances. Instead of alternating current, direct current at a very high voltage flows through the line. It is especially important for long submarine cables and for wind power produced far away from where it is used.
wichtigste: HVDC transports electricity as direct current at a very high voltage.
Over very long distances the losses are lower than with alternating current, and there is no reactive power.
Converter stations convert alternating current into direct current and back again.
The expensive converter installations at both ends are the biggest cost disadvantage.
HVDC can connect power grids that are not synchronised.
The first commercial HVDC link went into operation in 1954 between the Swedish mainland and Gotland.
Since 2021 the NordLink submarine cable has connected Germany and Norway.

abschnitte.text: In our power grids, **alternating current** usually flows; in Europe it changes direction 50 times per second. With HVDC the electricity is converted into **direct current** for transport, which always flows in the same direction. The voltage is often several hundred thousand volts. At the destination the electricity is converted back into alternating current.

The conversion takes place in large **converter stations**, which can be as big as factory halls. Older installations work with semiconductor components called thyristors. Modern voltage source converters, VSC for short, use **IGBTs**, which can switch very quickly. These installations are expensive, which is why HVDC is worthwhile mainly over long distances.

With alternating current, long lines and especially cables produce **reactive power**, which also flows back and forth and puts a load on the line. With direct current there is none, and transmission losses are lower. That is why long submarine cables with alternating current work only over short distances. In addition, HVDC can connect two power grids that do not run in step.

In 1954 the first commercial HVDC link went into operation between the Swedish mainland and the island of **Gotland**. Since 2021 the **NordLink** submarine cable has connected Germany with Norway so that wind power and hydropower can be exchanged. In Germany the SuedLink project is meant to bring wind power from the north to the south with underground cables. In China there are HVDC lines more than 3,000 kilometres long.

Switzerland lies in the middle of the European interconnected grid, which runs on alternating current in step. But HVDC technology is also developed by companies closely connected with Switzerland. Part of it comes from the history of ABB, which was formed in 1988 from the Swedish company ASEA and the Swiss company Brown, Boveri & Cie. in Baden. ASEA had already built the Gotland link.

begriffe.erklaerung: Current that always flows in the same direction, as from a battery.
Current that keeps changing direction, as from a socket.
Installation that converts alternating current into direct current or the other way round.
Current that swings back and forth in lines and does no useful work.
A semiconductor switch that can switch large currents on and off very quickly.

gewusst: In the 19th century Thomas Edison and supporters of alternating current argued about which kind of current should win.
An HVDC line needs fewer conductors than an alternating current line and can therefore be built narrower.
With HVDC cables on the sea floor, wind farms far out at sea can be connected.
