teile.einleitung: Traffic lights use coloured lights to control who may drive or walk at a junction. In Switzerland they are usually called a “Lichtsignal”, in Germany an “Ampel”. Red, amber and green make sure that cars, bicycles, trams and pedestrians do not get in each other's way.
wichtigste: In Swiss traffic language, traffic lights are called a “Lichtsignal”.
On traffic lights for cars, red is at the very top.
Red means stop; amber means stop if it is still safe to do so.
A flashing amber light means: drive especially carefully.
The world's first traffic lights stood in London in 1868.
At some traffic lights, pedestrians press a button.
For blind people the traffic lights tick or vibrate.

abschnitte.text: Traffic lights are an installation with coloured lamps that controls traffic at junctions and pedestrian crossings. For cars the lights are arranged one above the other: **red** at the top, **amber** in the middle, **green** at the bottom. Because red is always at the top, colour-blind people can also tell which light is on. Today most installations use economical LED lamps.

Red means: stop and wait. Green means: you may go, but you must still pay attention. Amber means you should stop if this is still possible safely. If red and amber light up together, it is about to turn green. A **flashing amber light** warns that you must drive especially carefully, for example when the installation is switched off.

Pedestrian signals show a red standing **figure** and a green walking one. At some installations you first have to press a button for it to turn green. For blind and partially sighted people, the signal ticks or a small arrow under the button vibrates when you may cross. That way everyone can cross the road safely.

The first traffic lights stood in **London** outside Parliament in 1868. They were lit by gas and operated by hand by a policeman, but soon exploded. Electric traffic lights appeared in the USA from 1914. In Europe they were introduced in big cities in the 1920s, as more and more cars were on the roads.

Modern traffic lights are controlled by computers. Loops in the road or cameras detect whether vehicles are waiting. With a **green wave**, several sets of lights are coordinated so that at the right speed you always have green. In Swiss cities such as Zurich or Basel, trams and buses often announce themselves by radio so that they get green sooner.

begriffe.erklaerung: The Swiss word for traffic lights.
A place where two or more roads meet.
Several sets of traffic lights switched so that you get green one after another.
White or yellow stripes on which you cross the road.

gewusst: In many Swiss cities, trams have their own signals with white bars and dots instead of coloured lights.
The pedestrian traffic light figures with hats from eastern Germany are so popular that you can buy them as souvenirs.

teile.einleitung: A magnifying glass is a curved glass through which small things look much bigger. With it you can watch beetles, leaves or stamps closely. In German it is called a “Lupe”.
wichtigste: A magnifying glass makes small things look bigger.
It consists of a converging lens, which is thicker in the middle than at the edge.
If you hold the magnifying glass too far from the object, the image becomes blurred.
You must not leave a magnifying glass lying in the sun, because it can start a fire.
Even a drop of water can magnify like a magnifying glass.
The detective Sherlock Holmes is often shown with a magnifying glass.
Watchmakers in Switzerland work with a magnifier right in front of their eye.

abschnitte.text: A **magnifying glass** is a glass for enlarging things, with a handle or a frame. The most important part is the **converging lens**, a glass that is thicker in the middle than at the edge. Because of its curve, the light rays are refracted, that is, bent. As a result the object looks two to ten times bigger to our eye.

To see sharply, the magnifying glass must be close enough to the object, namely closer than its **focal point**. Then you see an enlarged, upright image. If you hold the magnifying glass too far away, the image becomes blurred and can even be upside down. It is best to hold the magnifying glass close to your eye and move the object slowly until it is sharp.

A magnifying glass concentrates **sunlight** into a small, bright spot. There it gets so hot that paper or dry grass can start to burn, which is why it is also called a **burning glass**. That is why you must never leave a magnifying glass lying in the sun, for example on the windowsill. Also, you must never look at the sun through a magnifying glass, because that seriously injures the eyes.

With a magnifying glass you can look closely at beetles, ants, flowers, stones or snowflakes. Older people often use a **reading magnifier** to read small print. In Switzerland **watchmakers** wear a small magnifier right in front of the eye so that they can fit tiny gearwheels. Stamp collectors, jewellers and people studying nature also use magnifying glasses.

In ancient times people already knew that curved glasses or crystals can magnify. In the Middle Ages monks placed a **reading stone**, a polished half-sphere of glass or rock crystal, on the writing. Such lenses later developed into **spectacles**, the microscope and the telescope. In Arthur Conan Doyle's stories, the detective Sherlock Holmes looks for clues with a magnifying glass, which is why it is still seen as a sign of detectives today.

begriffe.erklaerung: Curved, transparent piece of glass or plastic that bends light.
Lens that is thicker in the middle and brings light rays together.
Point at which the concentrated light rays meet.
Magnifying glass used to concentrate sunlight so that it gets hot.

gewusst: A drop of water on a leaf works like a small magnifying glass and enlarges the leaf veins.
With a magnifying glass you can see that a screen is made of tiny red, green and blue dots.
The German word “Lupe” comes from French, where “loupe” means a magnifying glass.

teile.einleitung: A coffee machine is a device that makes coffee from ground coffee beans and hot water. They come in many forms, from the simple filter machine to the fully automatic machine. In Switzerland there is a coffee machine in very many kitchens and offices.
wichtigste: A coffee machine makes coffee from ground coffee and hot water.
Coffee is made from roasted and ground coffee beans.
In a capsule machine the coffee is inside a small capsule.
A fully automatic coffee machine grinds the beans itself with its grinder.
With the milk nozzle you can make milk froth for a cappuccino.
Coffee machines must be descaled regularly.
After making coffee, the coffee grounds are left over.

abschnitte.text: Coffee is made from the seeds of the **coffee plant**, which are called coffee beans. The beans are roasted, which gives them their brown colour and their aroma. Then they are ground. The coffee machine passes **hot water** through the powder. The water draws out flavour and colour, and the coffee is ready.

In a **filter coffee machine**, hot water slowly drips through ground coffee in a paper filter. The paper filter was invented by the German Melitta Bentz in 1908. An **espresso machine**, on the other hand, forces hot water at high pressure through finely ground coffee in a short time. This produces a strong, small espresso with a light brown layer of foam, the crema. Such machines were developed in Italy around 1900.

In a **capsule machine**, one portion of coffee is inside a small capsule made of aluminium or plastic. You put it in, press a button and get a coffee in seconds. The well-known Nespresso system comes from the Swiss company **Nestlé** and came onto the market in 1986. A **fully automatic coffee machine** grinds the beans fresh for every cup with a built-in grinder. At the push of a button it makes espresso, coffee or cappuccino.

Many machines have a **milk nozzle**, from which hot steam streams out. If you hold it in cold milk, fine milk froth forms. A **cappuccino** is espresso with lots of milk froth. A latte macchiato has even more milk and is often served in a tall glass. In Switzerland the “Schale” is also well known, a coffee with lots of milk.

Tap water contains dissolved **limescale**, especially in areas with hard water. When heated, the limescale settles in the machine and can block pipes. That is why a coffee machine must be **descaled** regularly, for example with a special descaling agent. The **coffee grounds** can go on the compost. In Switzerland used aluminium capsules can be handed in for recycling at many collection points.

Switzerland does not grow coffee itself, but it is an important country for the coffee trade and for coffee machines. Well-known manufacturers such as **Jura** and Thermoplan have their headquarters here. Swiss fully automatic machines and coffee capsules are sold to many countries. For many adults, drinking coffee is a fixed part of everyday life, for example at the mid-morning “Znüni” break. Coffee is not suitable for children because of the caffeine.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small, strong coffee made with pressure.
A part of the machine that grinds the beans into powder.
Removing limescale deposits from an appliance.
The wet coffee powder left over after brewing.
A substance in coffee that keeps you awake.

gewusst: The coffee bean is not actually a bean at all but the seed of a cherry-like fruit.
Melitta Bentz made the first coffee filter from the blotting paper of one of her son's school exercise books.
Coffee grounds can keep snails away in the garden and serve as fertiliser.

teile.einleitung: A helicopter is an aircraft with large rotating rotor blades on its roof. It can take off and land vertically and even stay still in the air. That is why it is ideal for rescues and transport in the mountains.
wichtigste: In Switzerland the word usually used is “Helikopter” rather than “Hubschrauber”.
The large main rotor creates lift and raises the helicopter into the air.
The small tail rotor stops the helicopter from turning in circles.
A helicopter can stay still in the air and needs no long runway.
In 1939 Igor Sikorsky built one of the first really usable helicopters.
In Switzerland you reach the air rescue service Rega on 1414.
Landing pads for helicopters are often marked with a large H.

abschnitte.text: The long **rotor blades** on the roof are curved like small wings. When they turn fast, they create **lift** and raise the helicopter. The pilot can change the angle of the blades. In this way the helicopter climbs, descends or flies forwards, backwards and sideways. It can even stay still in one place in the air.

abschnitte.titel: What is the small rotor at the back for?
abschnitte.text: When the big rotor turns in one direction, the body tries to turn in the other direction. The small **tail rotor** on the tail prevents this. It pushes the tail sideways and keeps the helicopter straight. Some helicopters instead have two main rotors that turn in opposite directions. Others use an enclosed tail rotor, which you can recognise by the round opening in the tail.

Around 1490 **Leonardo da Vinci** already drew a screw-shaped flying machine. But helicopters could only really fly in the 20th century. In Germany the Focke-Wulf Fw 61 flew in 1936. In 1939 the engineer **Igor Sikorsky** built one of the first really usable helicopters in the USA. After that, helicopters were quickly used for rescues, transport and the military.

In Switzerland helicopters are essential in the mountains. They bring **supplies and building materials** to mountain huts that no road reaches. They carry parts for cable cars and avalanche barriers. Mountain farmers sometimes have materials brought by helicopter too. Because helicopters need no long runway, they can land almost anywhere there is enough room for the rotor blades.

The Swiss air rescue service **Rega** was founded in 1952 and can be reached on **1414**. Its helicopters rescue injured people in the mountains, after accidents or in emergencies in remote places. With a **winch**, rescuers can also lift people off steep rock faces. Many hospitals have a landing pad on the roof. It is usually marked with a large H, which stands for helicopter.

begriffe.erklaerung: The turning blades that lift the helicopter into the air.
The small rotor at the back that stops the body from turning.
A force that acts upwards and carries the aircraft.
The Swiss air rescue service, emergency number 1414.
A device used to pull people up on a cable.

gewusst: A helicopter can fly backwards and sideways; an aeroplane cannot.
The word helicopter comes from Greek and means roughly “spiral wing”.
Rega is largely financed by patrons from the general public.

teile.einleitung: A clutch is a machine part that connects or separates two turning shafts. In a car with a manual gearbox, it separates the engine from the gearbox so that you can pull away and change gear. But clutches are also found in bicycles, chainsaws, machines and factories.
wichtigste: A clutch connects or separates two turning parts.
In a car with a manual gearbox it separates the engine from the gearbox.
The clutch pedal is on the far left.
The most common type in manual cars is the friction clutch.
If you let the clutch slip for a long time, the clutch plate wears out.
A centrifugal clutch only engages above a certain speed.
On a bicycle, the freewheel makes sure you can roll without pedalling.
A dual-clutch gearbox has two clutches for fast gear changes.

abschnitte.text: A car engine keeps turning even when the car is standing still. So that you can stop, pull away and change gear, the engine must be briefly separated from the **gearbox**. The **clutch** does this. When pulling away, you slowly connect the engine and wheels again so that the car rolls off gently and the engine does not stall.

In a car with a manual gearbox there are three pedals: the clutch on the left, the brake in the middle and the accelerator on the right. When you push the **clutch pedal** all the way down, the engine is disconnected and you can change gear. If you let it up slowly, the clutch gradually engages. Cars with automatic gearboxes have no clutch pedal.

Most manual cars have a **friction clutch**. A pressure plate with springs presses the **clutch plate** against the engine's flywheel, and the friction transmits the power. If you let the clutch slip for a long time, the surfaces rub against each other, get hot and wear down. As with brake pads, the clutch plate therefore has to be replaced at some point.

A **centrifugal clutch** engages by itself when the engine turns fast enough, for example on mopeds and chainsaws. Flexible rubber shaft couplings connect machine parts while cushioning shocks and vibrations. On a bicycle, the **freewheel** works like a one-way clutch: the pedals drive the back wheel, but the wheel can also keep rolling when you are not pedalling. That is where the typical clicking when freewheeling comes from.

A **dual-clutch gearbox** has two clutches, one for the even and one for the odd gears. While one gear is engaged, the next one is already prepared. This lets the gearbox change gear in a fraction of a second, almost without interrupting the power. Such gearboxes are found in many modern cars and in sports cars.

begriffe.erklaerung: Machine part with gearwheels that changes speed and force.
Disc with a friction lining that transmits the power in the clutch.
Force that pushes outwards during rotation.
Mechanism that transmits power in only one direction of rotation.

gewusst: The clicking of a freewheeling bicycle comes from small pawls in the freewheel.
Railway wagons and trailers are also connected with couplings, but that is a different kind of coupling.
Anyone who lets the clutch out too quickly when pulling away often stalls the engine.

teile.einleitung: A wedge is an object that is thin at the front and thick at the back. If you drive it into something, it pushes things apart with great force. The wedge is one of the oldest simple machines of humankind.
wichtigste: A wedge is thin at the front and thick at the back.
It converts a blow or push from behind into large forces to the side.
With a wedge you can split wood.
Knife blades, axe edges and nail points work like wedges.
A wedge can also hold something in place, for example a hammer head or a door.
The slimmer a wedge is, the more easily it goes in.
The wedge is one of the simple machines, like the lever and the inclined plane.

abschnitte.text: A **wedge** is a body with two sloping surfaces that meet at the front in a sharp edge. It is thin at the front and thick at the back. If you strike the back with a hammer, it goes into a material. In doing so it pushes the two sides **apart** with great force. You can think of a wedge as two inclined planes lying back to back.

With a **splitting wedge** and a heavy hammer you split thick pieces of wood. The blade of an **axe** is also a wedge. The edge of a knife is wedge-shaped too. A sharp knife cuts better than a blunt one because its edge is thinner. Chisels, needles and the point of a **nail** also work like wedges.

A long, slim wedge goes in with little force, but has to be driven in a long way. A short, thick wedge splits faster but needs more force. As with the lever: you save force, but have to cover a longer **distance**. The force the wedge exerts to the side can be much greater than the blow from behind. That is why the wedge is one of the **simple machines**.

Wedges can also hold things in place. A **door wedge** under the door keeps it open. A small wedge in the handle holds the head of a hammer in place. You put a **wheel chock** behind the wheels of a parked trailer so that it does not roll away. Wall plugs also hold on a similar principle.

Our **incisors** also work like wedges when we bite something off. Stone Age people used stone **hand axes** for cutting and scraping a very long time ago. In ancient Egypt wooden wedges were used to free stone blocks from the rock. They were driven into cracks and soaked with water; the wood swelled and split the stone. A plough and the bow of a ship also work on the wedge principle.

begriffe.erklaerung: A body that is thin at the front and thick at the back.
A basic tool that saves force, such as a lever, wedge or pulley.
The sharp, thin side of a knife or an axe.
A stone tool from the Stone Age.

gewusst: A zip works with small wedges in the slider that push the teeth together or apart.
Hand axes are among the oldest tools of humankind.
The pointed bow of an icebreaker also works like a huge wedge that splits the ice.

teile.einleitung: A camera is a device used to take photos or videos. It captures light through an opening with glass lenses and records the image. Today there is a camera in almost every smartphone.
wichtigste: With a camera you take photos and videos.
At the front of the camera is the lens with glass elements.
In the past cameras needed a film to record a picture.
Digital cameras store photos on a memory card.
The flash helps when taking photos in the dark.
Around 1826 Joseph Nicéphore Niépce took the oldest surviving photo in the world.
A selfie is a photo of yourself.

abschnitte.text: At the front is the **lens**, a tube with several glass elements that focus the light. The aperture in the lens controls how much light comes in. The **shutter** opens only very briefly when you press the button, often for just a hundredth of a second. At the back of the body, the film or a sensor captures the image. Through the viewfinder or on a screen you can see what will be in the picture.

The first cameras were big wooden boxes on a tripod. With one of them, **Joseph Nicéphore Niépce** took the oldest surviving photo in the world around 1826. Later cameras became smaller and easier to handle. In 1888 a simple camera from the company Kodak came onto the market that anyone could use. For many decades you needed a **film**, which was developed in a laboratory after the photos were taken.

In 1975 the engineer Steven Sasson at Kodak built the first **digital camera**. Instead of a film, an image sensor in it measures the light. The photos are stored as files on a **memory card**. This means you can look at pictures straight away and simply delete failed photos. From about 2000 digital cameras became more and more popular in everyday life.

Without light there is no photo. In the dark the **flash** helps, a very short, bright light. In the past magnesium powder was burned for this, which smoked and banged. Today an electronic flash or a small LED on the phone lights up. But good photographers often prefer to use natural light, for example in the evening when the sun is low.

Today there is a camera in almost every smartphone, often even several. With the front camera you take a **selfie**, a photo of yourself. There are also action cameras for sport, wildlife cameras in the forest and security cameras. On rovers on Mars and on space telescopes, cameras photograph alien worlds. Anyone who photographs other people should ask them first whether they agree.

begriffe.erklaerung: The front part of the camera with the glass elements.
Flap that opens briefly when you take a photo and lets light in.
Small card on which the photos are stored.
Stand with three legs that holds the camera steady.

gewusst: The first digital camera of 1975 was as big as a toaster and took about 23 seconds to store a picture.
In 2013 the word “selfie” was chosen as word of the year by the Oxford dictionaries.
The word camera comes from the Latin “camera”, which means chamber or room.

teile.einleitung: Pneumatics is the technology that works with compressed air. Squeezed air drives machines, opens doors, brakes trains or shoots capsules through tubes. The name comes from the Greek word “pneuma”, which means air or breath.
wichtigste: Pneumatics works with compressed air.
A compressor produces the compressed air.
In a pneumatic cylinder, compressed air moves a piston back and forth.
Because air can be compressed, pneumatics can hold loads less precisely than hydraulics.
Lorries and trains typically brake with air brakes.
Compressed air must be dried so that no rust forms.
In Swiss German a bicycle tyre is called a “Pneu” because it is filled with air.

abschnitte.text: In **pneumatics**, air is compressed and stored. If you let it flow out again, it can do work, rather like a balloon that whizzes across the room when you let go. A **compressor** sucks in surrounding air and squeezes it into a pressure tank. From there hoses and pipes carry the air to the machines.

The most important component is the **pneumatic cylinder**. In it the compressed air pushes a piston back and forth, which, for example, opens a flap or holds a workpiece in place. **Valves** control when the air flows where. Before use the air is filtered and dried, because water in it would cause rust.

Lorries, buses and trains have **air brakes**, which the American George Westinghouse patented in 1869. The doors of many buses and trams open with a typical hiss, also thanks to compressed air. On building sites the pneumatic drill rattles. In factories, pneumatic robot arms grip, push and sort thousands of parts a day.

With **pneumatic tube post**, capsules are shot through long tubes by air pressure. In many hospitals it carries blood samples and medicines from ward to ward in a flash. In the past big cities had whole pneumatic tube networks for letters. Some banks and shops also used them to move money safely.

**Hydraulics** works with oil instead of air. Oil can hardly be compressed, so heavy loads can be held very precisely with it. Air, on the other hand, can be compressed and gives a little. In return pneumatics is clean, fast and cheap, and escaping air pollutes nothing.

begriffe.erklaerung: Squeezed air that stores energy.
Machine that sucks in air and squeezes it together.
Tube with a piston that turns compressed air into movement.
Technology that works with liquids such as oil instead of air.

gewusst: As early as ancient Alexandria, the Greek Ctesibius built devices that worked with air pressure.
When the Gotthard railway tunnel was built in the 19th century, drilling machines driven by compressed air pushed forward through the rock.
The word “Pneu” for a tyre is short for pneumatic.

teile.einleitung: The mains frequency tells you how often the alternating current in our sockets changes direction per second. In Switzerland and almost all of Europe this is 50 oscillations per second, that is, 50 hertz. From this number you can tell whether exactly as much electricity is being produced in the grid as is being used.
wichtigste: In Europe the mains frequency is 50 hertz, in North America 60 hertz.
A large grid in which all generators run in step is called a synchronous area.
If more electricity is used than produced, the frequency falls.
A generator with one pair of poles turns 3,000 times per minute on the 50 Hz grid.
When there is a deviation, primary control reserve is activated automatically first.
In 1958, at the “Star of Laufenburg”, the grids of Switzerland, Germany and France were connected.
If the frequency falls to 49.0 Hz, consumers are switched off automatically.

abschnitte.text: The socket supplies **alternating current**, which means the current constantly flows back and forth. How often this happens per second is called the frequency, and it is measured in **hertz**. In Europe it is 50 hertz, in the USA and Canada 60 hertz. Japan is special: the east uses 50 Hz, the west 60 Hz.

The frequency is created in the large **generators** of power stations. A generator with one pair of poles turns exactly 3,000 times per minute on the 50 Hz grid. If more electricity is used than produced, the generators are slowed down and the frequency falls. If too little is used, it rises. That is why the mains frequency is like a pair of scales for the whole grid.

If a power station fails, the **inertia** of the many turning generators first slows the drop in frequency, rather like a heavy bicycle wheel that does not stop at once. Then, within seconds, **primary control reserve** kicks in, and power stations all over Europe automatically supply more electricity. Further reserves take over from them later. If the frequency still falls to 49.0 hertz, consumers are switched off automatically for protection.

Continental Europe forms a large **synchronous area** in which all generators run in step. It began in 1958 at the “Star of Laufenburg” in the canton of Aargau, where the grids of Switzerland, Germany and France were connected for the first time. Today the interconnected grid stretches from Portugal to Turkey. In Switzerland the company Swissgrid makes sure the grid stays stable.

Some clocks, for example in ovens or clock radios, count the oscillations of the grid to measure time. At the beginning of 2018, because of an energy shortage in the Serbia and Kosovo grid area, the frequency was slightly below 50 hertz for weeks. As a result such clocks in Europe ran up to about six minutes slow. By the way, the SBB runs on its own railway power grid, which has a frequency of 16.7 hertz.

begriffe.erklaerung: The unit of oscillations per second.
Current that keeps changing its direction.
A machine that converts movement into electric current.
A power grid in which all generators run exactly in step.

gewusst: Normally the mains frequency in Europe varies by only a few hundredths of a hertz around 50 hertz.
From audio recordings you can sometimes pick out the faint hum of the mains frequency and so work out when a recording was made.

teile.einleitung: The petrol engine, known in German as the Otto engine, is a combustion engine in which a mixture of air and petrol is ignited by a spark plug. For over 100 years it has powered cars, motorbikes and lawnmowers. It is named after the German inventor Nicolaus August Otto.
wichtigste: In a petrol engine, a spark plug ignites a compressed mixture of air and petrol.
The idealised reference process is the constant-volume (Otto) cycle.
The ideal efficiency depends mainly on the compression ratio.
With a compression ratio of 10 and κ = 1.4, the ideal efficiency is about 60 per cent.
Knocking is the uncontrolled self-ignition of parts of the mixture.
By definition, isooctane has an octane number of 100.
A three-way catalytic converter converts CO, hydrocarbons and nitrogen oxides when λ equals 1.

abschnitte.text: In 1876 **Nicolaus August Otto** built a successful four-stroke engine in Deutz near Cologne. It still ran on gas, but soon petrol was used too. Gottlieb Daimler, Wilhelm Maybach and Carl Benz developed light engines for vehicles from it. 1886 is considered the year the motor car was born.

A four-stroke petrol engine works in four steps. During **intake**, mixture flows into the cylinder; during **compression**, the piston squeezes it together. Then the spark plug ignites it, and the hot gas pushes the piston down; this is the power stroke. During exhaust, the exhaust gases leave the cylinder, and everything starts again.

In theory the petrol engine is described by the **constant-volume cycle**, in which combustion takes place in a flash with no change in volume. Its efficiency depends mainly on the **compression ratio**. With a compression ratio of 10 and κ = 1.4 it would be about 60 per cent. Real engines lose a lot of energy as heat and through friction, so they achieve much less, often around 35 per cent.

If the mixture is compressed too much, parts of it ignite by themselves before the flame reaches them. This **knocking** sounds metallic and can damage the engine. The **octane number** shows how resistant a petrol is to knocking. By definition isooctane has an octane number of 100; in Switzerland people usually fill up with unleaded 95 or 98.

For 1 kg of petrol you need about 14.7 kg of air; then the air ratio **λ equals 1**. The lambda sensor controls the engine to exactly this value. Only then can the **three-way catalytic converter** turn carbon monoxide, hydrocarbons and nitrogen oxides into less harmful substances at the same time. But it cannot remove the carbon dioxide produced by burning, which is why many countries today are also turning to electric cars.

begriffe.erklaerung: Component that ignites the mixture with an electric spark.
How strongly the mixture is squeezed together in the cylinder.
Measure of how resistant a petrol is to knocking.
Sensor in the exhaust that measures the oxygen in the exhaust gas.
Component that turns harmful exhaust gases into less harmful substances.

gewusst: Nicolaus Otto's first engine ran on coal gas, not on petrol.
A car engine at 3,000 revolutions per minute ignites 25 times per second in each cylinder.
Rudolf Diesel later invented an engine with no spark plug at all, the diesel engine.

teile.einleitung: A microwave oven, microwave for short, is a kitchen appliance that warms food with invisible electromagnetic waves. It is used mainly to heat up or defrost food quickly. It was invented by chance in a laboratory for radar technology.
wichtigste: The microwave oven is mostly used to heat up food quickly.
The microwaves mainly warm the water in the food.
A round glass plate turns so that the food warms more evenly.
Metal such as a spoon does not belong in the microwave.
The fine mesh in the door keeps the microwaves inside.
If you open the door, the appliance switches off immediately.

abschnitte.text: Inside the appliance, a component called a **magnetron** produces microwaves, usually at a frequency of 2.45 gigahertz. These waves make the **water molecules** in the food keep turning back and forth. In doing so they rub against each other, and heat is produced directly in the food. The dish itself gets warm mainly because the hot food warms it.

Microwaves are not spread equally strongly everywhere in the oven; there are hotter and colder spots. That is why in many appliances a round glass **turntable** rotates. Even so, food can still be cold inside and already hot outside. That is why you stir in between and let the food stand briefly at the end so that the heat spreads.

**Metal** such as spoons, aluminium foil or dishes with a gold rim can make sparks and damage the appliance. A raw egg in its shell can burst because steam forms inside. Water can also sometimes be heated above its boiling point and suddenly boil up when you take it out; this is called **superheating**. That is why you should take hot liquids out carefully and never run the appliance empty.

The walls of the appliance are made of metal and keep the microwaves inside. In the glass of the door there is a fine **metal mesh** whose holes are too small for the microwaves but big enough for light. So you can look in without any rays getting out. A **safety switch** turns the appliance off immediately when you open the door.

In the 1940s the American engineer Percy Spencer was working on radar equipment at the company Raytheon. He is said to have noticed that a chocolate bar in his pocket melted while he was standing next to a magnetron. He experimented further, and in 1947 the first appliance, called the **Radarange**, came onto the market; it was as big as a fridge. From the 1970s small microwaves for the kitchen at home became popular.

begriffe.erklaerung: Invisible electromagnetic waves, related to radio waves and light.
The component in the appliance that produces the microwaves.
The smallest particle of water.
When water gets hotter than 100 degrees without boiling and then suddenly bubbles up.

gewusst: Wi-Fi routers also transmit in a frequency range similar to microwave ovens, but with much lower power.
Frozen ice warms up much more slowly in the microwave than liquid water.
The first microwave appliance weighed over 300 kilograms.

teile.einleitung: Milk chocolate is a light brown, sweet chocolate that contains milk as well as cocoa. It was invented in Switzerland: in 1875 the chocolatier Daniel Peter in Vevey succeeded in making a milk chocolate that kept well. Today it is the most popular kind of chocolate in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Milk chocolate is made from cocoa beans, sugar and milk.
It is light brown and tastes milder than dark chocolate.
In 1875 Daniel Peter developed a famous milk chocolate in Vevey on Lake Geneva.
The problem was that milk contains a lot of water.
So Daniel Peter used condensed milk.
His neighbour Henri Nestlé helped him with his experiments.
In Bern Rodolphe Lindt invented the conche, which makes chocolate melt smoothly.

abschnitte.text: Milk chocolate consists of **cocoa mass**, **cocoa butter**, sugar and milk powder. The milk makes it light brown, and it tastes mild and creamy. Dark chocolate, on the other hand, contains more cocoa and no or hardly any milk. White chocolate has cocoa butter but no cocoa mass, which is why it is almost white.

Chocolate is made from the beans of the **cacao tree**, which grows in warm countries near the equator. Most cocoa beans today come from West Africa, above all from Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana. The beans are fermented, dried, roasted and ground into a mass. Then they are mixed with sugar and milk.

For a long time nobody managed to mix milk and chocolate well, because milk contains a lot of water, and water does not get on well with cocoa butter. The chocolate quickly went mouldy or lumpy. **Daniel Peter** in Vevey worked on this problem for years. With the help of his neighbour **Henri Nestlé**, he finally used condensed milk, from which a large part of the water has been removed, and succeeded in 1875.

In 1879 **Rodolphe Lindt** in Bern invented the **conche**, a machine that stirs and rubs the chocolate mass for many hours. This makes the particles finer, and unpleasant flavours disappear. Only then did chocolate become smoothly melting, as we know it today. Together with milk chocolate, such inventions made Switzerland a chocolate country.

Many famous chocolate companies were founded in Switzerland, such as Cailler, Lindt, Suchard and Tobler. Daniel Peter was married to a daughter of the chocolate pioneer François-Louis Cailler. The Swiss eat **about 11 kilograms** of chocolate per person per year (as of the 2020s), one of the highest figures in the world. A large share of Swiss chocolate is sold abroad.

Cocoa butter turns liquid just below our body temperature. That is why chocolate melts so pleasantly in the mouth. Unfortunately, on a hot summer's day in the sun it also melts in your hand or in your rucksack. It is best to store chocolate somewhere cool and dry, but not in the fridge.

begriffe.erklaerung: The pale fat from the cocoa bean.
Thickened milk from which some of the water has been removed.
A machine that stirs chocolate mass for a long time and makes it smooth.
A specialist who makes chocolate.

gewusst: Daniel Peter needed about eight years before his milk chocolate really worked.
When chocolate melts and sets again, it often gets a white coating, but this is harmless.

teile.einleitung: An integrated circuit, IC for short or simply a chip, is a whole electronic circuit on a tiny wafer of semiconductor material. Billions of transistors can fit on it. Today chips are found in almost every device, from mobile phones to washing machines.
wichtigste: An integrated circuit combines many electronic components on a single chip.
The first integrated circuit was made in 1958 and was made of germanium.
In 1959 the Geneva-born physicist Jean Hoerni invented the planar process.
Today chips are usually made of silicon on wafers 300 millimetres across.
A single chip piece sawn out of the wafer is called a die.
Special-purpose chips are called ASICs, freely configurable chips FPGAs.
A system on a chip combines almost a whole computer on one chip.

abschnitte.text: In the past, electronic circuits were built from many individual components connected by wires. In an **integrated circuit**, transistors, resistors and conducting tracks are all combined on a small **semiconductor wafer**. This saves an enormous amount of space and electricity. The circuits also become more reliable and cheaper. Almost all modern electronic devices are based on such chips.

In 1958 **Jack Kilby** at Texas Instruments built the first integrated circuit, made of germanium. Shortly afterwards **Robert Noyce** at Fairchild developed a chip made of silicon. This was made possible by the **planar process**, which the Geneva-born physicist Jean Hoerni invented in 1959. With it, flat, protected structures could be made on silicon. Jack Kilby received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2000.

Chips are made on **wafers**, thin silicon discs up to 300 millimetres across. In many steps, extremely fine structures are applied using photolithography, etching and coating. In this way hundreds of chips are made on one wafer at the same time. Then the wafer is sawn up; each individual piece is called a **die**. It is fitted into a package, for example a DIP with two rows of connecting legs.

An **ASIC** is a chip designed specially for a single task. An **FPGA**, on the other hand, can be programmed by the user after it has been made. A system on a chip combines a processor, graphics, memory control and more, as in mobile phones. There are also memory chips, sensor chips and many others. Chips with millions to billions of transistors are also called VLSI, for very large scale integration.

In 1965 Gordon Moore predicted that the number of transistors on a chip would double regularly. This **Moore's law** held for a surprisingly long time. Early chips had only a few transistors; today's top chips have many billions. That is why computers today are much more powerful and at the same time smaller than in the past. Chips have become so important that countries compete to make them.

begriffe.erklaerung: A material such as silicon that conducts electricity only under certain conditions.
A tiny electronic switch.
A thin silicon disc on which many chips are made.
A single chip piece sawn out of the wafer.
A chip built specially for a single application.

gewusst: Jack Kilby's first integrated circuit had only one transistor and was still connected with small wires.
The inventor of the planar process, Jean Hoerni, came from Geneva.
A modern car often contains more than a thousand chips.

teile.einleitung: An aerial cableway is a railway whose cabins hang from thick steel cables high above the ground. It takes people quickly and comfortably up mountains, across valleys and into ski areas. Switzerland is one of the countries with the most and the most spectacular cableways in the world.
wichtigste: The cabin of an aerial cableway hangs from thick steel cables.
The drive motor is usually in a station.
The tall frames over which the cable runs are called towers.
In an aerial tramway, one cabin goes up while the other comes down.
A gondola lift has many small cabins that circulate constantly.
The highest aerial cableway in Europe goes up the Klein Matterhorn near Zermatt.

abschnitte.text: An **aerial cableway** hangs from steel cables stretched between a valley station and a mountain station. Usually there are **track cables**, on which the cabin runs on rollers, and a **haul cable** that pulls it. The motor is in one of the stations and drives a large cable wheel. Along the way the cable runs over tall frames called **towers**.

An **aerial tramway** usually has two large cabins hanging from the same haul cable. When one goes up, the other comes down at the same time, and they pass each other in the middle. A **gondola lift**, on the other hand, has many small cabins that circulate constantly and detach from the cable in the stations so that you can get in comfortably. Chairlifts are also cableways.

On the **Titlis** near Engelberg, the cabin of the Rotair turns round once during the ride so that all passengers can enjoy the view. On the Stanserhorn there is the **CabriO**, where you can ride on the open roof of the cabin. Near Zermatt the highest aerial cableway in Europe goes up the Klein Matterhorn to over 3,800 metres. The cableways up the Schilthorn and the Pilatus are also well known.

Cableways are considered a very safe means of transport. The cables are regularly checked for damage with special equipment, and there are several independent **brakes**. In strong winds or thunderstorms the service is stopped. If a cabin does get stuck, there are emergency drives and rescue teams who can lower passengers on ropes if necessary.

For many mountain villages cableways are the most important link to the valley, and some places can only be reached this way. They are central to **tourism** and winter sport. Around the world, cableways are also being built in cities, for example in La Paz in Bolivia, where they serve as public transport. Swiss companies build cableways and cables that are supplied all over the world.

begriffe.erklaerung: A thick cable along which the cabin runs on rollers.
The cable that pulls the cabin along.
A tall frame over which the cable is guided.
A cableway, usually with two cabins, that travel back and forth.
A cableway with many small cabins that circulate constantly.

gewusst: In 1992 the Rotair on the Titlis was the world's first rotating aerial cableway cabin.
In Switzerland there are several thousand cableways and ski lifts, including many small ones for farmers and mountain villages.
The cabins of large aerial tramways often hold more than 100 people.

teile.einleitung: Pile dwellings are settlements from the Stone Age and Bronze Age that stood on lake shores and in moors. The houses were built on wooden piles driven into the soft ground. Switzerland has especially many traces of these villages, and they have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2011.
wichtigste: The pile dwellers built their houses on lake shores and in moors.
The piles protected the houses from the water.
The pile dwellings in Switzerland are several thousand years old.
Since 2011 the pile dwellings around the Alps have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Of the 111 sites in the World Heritage listing, 56 are in Switzerland.
The houses were made of wood, clay and reeds.
Wooden finds were very well preserved in the wet ground.
A dugout is a boat made from a hollowed-out tree trunk.

abschnitte.text: Pile dwellings are villages whose houses stood on wooden **piles**. People built them between about 5000 and 500 BC, in the Neolithic and the Bronze Age. The settlements lay on lake shores or in moors, where the ground was often wet. The piles raised the houses above the water and the damp ground.

The pile dwellers drove tree trunks into the soft lake bed. On these they built floors and walls of wood, branches and **clay**. They covered the roofs with **reeds**, straw or bark. A village often consisted of many houses in rows, sometimes with a fence of piles all round.

abschnitte.titel: Everyday life of the pile dwellers
abschnitte.text: The pile dwellers were farmers: they grew cereals such as barley and wheat and kept cattle, sheep, goats and pigs. They fished, hunted and gathered berries, nuts and apples. In a **dugout**, a boat made from a hollowed-out tree trunk, they travelled across the lake. They made tools of stone, bone and later bronze, made pottery and wove cloth from flax.

In the winter of 1853/54 the water level of Lake Zurich was very low. Near **Obermeilen**, many old piles and objects came to light. The Zurich researcher Ferdinand Keller interpreted them as the remains of pile-dwelling villages. After that, people searched eagerly for pile dwellings all over Switzerland, and the pile dwellers became a symbol of the country's early history.

Wood, seeds, cloth and even remains of bread often survived for thousands of years under water and in wet ground, because hardly any oxygen gets there. This allows **archaeologists** to study very precisely how people lived. With **dendrochronology**, counting and comparing tree rings, they can even work out in which year a tree was felled. That is why for some villages it is known exactly when they were built.

Since 2011 the **Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps** have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The listing includes 111 sites in six countries, 56 of them in Switzerland. Most of them lie invisible under water or in the ground. In museums such as the Laténium near Neuchâtel or in reconstructed pile-dwelling villages, you can experience the life of the pile dwellers today.

begriffe.erklaerung: The period when people settled down and farmed but did not yet use metals.
A specialist who searches the ground for traces of earlier people.
A boat made from a single hollowed-out tree trunk.
A method of dating wood using the growth rings of trees.
Places that UNESCO protects as especially valuable for all humanity.

gewusst: Today researchers know that many pile-dwelling houses stood on the shore and were only in the water during floods.
In pile-dwelling settlements, remains of bread and cereal porridge more than 5,000 years old have been found.

teile.einleitung: In nuclear fission, a heavy atomic nucleus, for example of uranium, breaks up into two smaller nuclei. This releases an enormous amount of energy. In nuclear power stations this energy is used to produce electricity.
wichtigste: In December 1938 in Berlin, Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann proved chemically that uranium had been split.
At the beginning of 1939 Lise Meitner and Otto Robert Frisch provided the physical explanation.
When a uranium-235 nucleus splits, about 200 MeV of energy is released.
On average about 2 to 3 new neutrons are produced.
Natural uranium contains only about 0.7 per cent uranium-235.
On 2 December 1942 the first controlled chain reaction was achieved in Chicago under Enrico Fermi.
The energy comes from the mass defect, because the fission products are more tightly bound.
A reactor core must still be cooled after shutdown, because the fission products produce decay heat.

abschnitte.text: Every atom has a tiny **nucleus** made of protons and neutrons. If a slow **neutron** hits a uranium-235 nucleus, the nucleus becomes unstable and bursts into two medium-weight nuclei. In the process 2 to 3 new neutrons fly out, and energy is released, mainly as heat. Each fission releases about 200 MeV, millions of times more than in the chemical burning of one atom.

In December 1938 in Berlin, the chemists **Otto Hahn** and Fritz Strassmann found that bombarding uranium with neutrons produced the much lighter element barium. At first they could not explain this. The physicist **Lise Meitner**, who as a Jew had had to flee Germany, and her nephew Otto Robert Frisch provided the explanation at the beginning of 1939. They realised that the uranium nucleus had been split.

The free neutrons can split further uranium nuclei, which in turn release neutrons. This creates a **chain reaction**. In a reactor it is controlled with control rods so that exactly one of the new neutrons triggers another fission. The first controlled chain reaction was achieved on 2 December 1942 in the Chicago Pile-1 reactor under Enrico Fermi.

abschnitte.titel: Where does the energy come from?
abschnitte.text: The two fragments together are a tiny bit lighter than the original nucleus plus the neutron. This missing mass is called the **mass defect**. According to Albert Einstein's formula E = mc², it is converted into energy. Even a tiny mass gives a great deal of energy.

In a nuclear power station the energy heats water, and the steam drives turbines and generators. Natural uranium contains only about 0.7 per cent fissile uranium-235, so it is enriched for many reactors. In Switzerland the Beznau, Gösgen and Leibstadt nuclear power stations are running; Mühleberg was shut down in 2019. Even after shutdown, the fission products still produce **decay heat**, which is why a reactor core must continue to be cooled.

In 1945 nuclear fission was also used for the atomic bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki. In accidents such as those at Chernobyl in 1986 and Fukushima in 2011, radioactivity escaped into the environment. The fission products are radioactive and must be stored safely as **nuclear waste** for a very long time. In Switzerland Nagra is looking for a site for a deep geological repository.

begriffe.erklaerung: Tiny centre of an atom made of protons and neutrons.
Particle in the atomic nucleus with no electric charge.
Process in which each fission triggers further fissions.
Mass that is missing after fission and is released as energy.
Property of some substances of giving off invisible, dangerous radiation.

gewusst: Otto Hahn received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the discovery of nuclear fission; Lise Meitner went away empty-handed.
The chemical element meitnerium is named after Lise Meitner.
One gram of uranium-235, if completely split, provides about as much energy as burning several tonnes of coal.

teile.einleitung: Guglielmo Marconi was an Italian inventor and businessman who made wireless telegraphy by radio known all over the world. In 1901 he achieved the first radio transmission across the Atlantic. Without his work there might be no radio, no ship radio and no mobile phones today.
wichtigste: Marconi was born in Bologna in Italy in 1874 and died in Rome in 1937.
He is known above all for wireless telegraphy by radio.
In 1896 he moved to Great Britain because he found support for his experiments there.
In 1901 he sent the Morse letter S across the Atlantic without wires.
In 1909 he received the Nobel Prize in Physics together with Ferdinand Braun.
When the Titanic sank in 1912, radio operators called for help with Marconi equipment.

abschnitte.text: Guglielmo Marconi was born on 25 April 1874 in **Bologna**. His father was an Italian landowner and his mother came from Ireland. Even as a teenager he was very interested in electricity and read everything about the **electromagnetic waves** that Heinrich Hertz had discovered. Around 1895 he began his own experiments on his family's estate near Bologna.

Marconi built a transmitter and a receiver and set them up further and further apart. With a high **aerial** and a connection to the earth, the range became much greater. Soon he could send signals over a hill, with no line of sight. But in Italy he found hardly any interest in his invention.

abschnitte.titel: A new start in Great Britain
abschnitte.text: In 1896 Marconi moved to **Great Britain**, where the British Post Office supported his experiments. There he applied for a patent and in 1897 founded his own radio company. In 1899 he achieved a radio link across the English Channel to France. His equipment was quickly fitted on ships, because a wireless connection was especially valuable there.

On 12 December 1901 Marconi attempted his biggest experiment: a transmitter at Poldhu in Cornwall (England) sent signals across the **Atlantic**. Marconi waited in Newfoundland in Canada and held the aerial up in the air with a kite. He heard the Morse letter **S**, that is, three short tones. Many experts had not believed that radio waves could follow the curve of the Earth.

In 1909 Marconi received the Nobel Prize in Physics together with the German physicist **Ferdinand Braun**. When the **Titanic** sank in April 1912, the radio operators on board sent distress calls with Marconi equipment. The ship Carpathia received the calls and rescued over 700 people. After that, radio became compulsory on large ships everywhere.

Marconi's radio telegraphy later developed into **radio** broadcasting, aircraft radio and mobile phones. That is why Marconi is considered one of the most important pioneers of radio technology. He died in Rome on 20 July 1937. Today streets, schools and an airport in Bologna bear his name.

begriffe.erklaerung: Sending messages over long distances, for example with Morse code.
Transmitting signals without cables using electromagnetic waves.
A code of short and long signals with which letters can be transmitted.
A metal rod or wire that sends out or receives radio waves.

gewusst: In Marconi's Atlantic experiment, the receiving aerial hung from a kite because the wind had torn away a balloon.
When Marconi died in 1937, many radio transmitters around the world fell silent for two minutes in his honour.
Marconi was only 35 years old when he received the Nobel Prize.

teile.einleitung: The motherboard is the large circuit board inside a computer on which all the important components sit. In German it is called the “Hauptplatine” (main board). It connects the processor, working memory, graphics card and all the other parts with each other.
wichtigste: The motherboard is also often called the mainboard.
Its main job is to connect all the components of the computer with each other.
The processor sits in a holder called a socket.
Fine copper tracks carry electricity and signals.
A button cell battery keeps the time and basic settings when the computer is switched off.
The start-up software BIOS or UEFI is stored on the motherboard.
Graphics cards are usually plugged into a PCI Express slot today.
ATX is a widespread standard format for motherboards in desktop computers.

abschnitte.text: The motherboard is a flat board made of plastic and glass fibre on which many electronic parts are mounted. You can compare it with the **nervous system** of a computer. All the components exchange their data through it. Without a motherboard, no part can work together with any other.

In the middle sits the **socket** for the processor, the computer's calculating centre. Next to it are slots for the **working memory**, into which long memory sticks are plugged. For graphics cards there are slots following the **PCI Express** standard. On top of this come connections for hard disks, fast M.2 storage and for USB, network and sound.

The fine lines on the board are copper **tracks**. They work like tiny roads for electricity and data. Often they lie in several layers on top of each other so that there is enough room. A special chip, the **chipset**, controls the traffic between the processor and the other connections.

A small memory chip holds the start-up software **BIOS** or its modern successor **UEFI**. When the computer is switched on, it checks the components and then starts the operating system. A small round button cell battery supplies the built-in clock with power. This means the computer still knows the time and date after being switched off.

So that motherboards fit into every case, there are fixed sizes. The best-known format for desktop computers is **ATX**, which the company Intel introduced in 1995. Smaller formats are called, for example, Micro-ATX and Mini-ITX. Laptops, tablets and mobile phones also have motherboards, but they are much smaller and tailored exactly to the device.

begriffe.erklaerung: The main circuit board of a computer, “Hauptplatine” in German.
The chip that does the calculating work in the computer.
Holder on the motherboard into which the processor is fitted.
Chip that controls the data traffic on the motherboard.
Modern start-up software that prepares the computer when it is switched on.

gewusst: A motherboard can consist of many layers of tracks on top of each other, even though it is only a few millimetres thick.
The button cell on the motherboard often lasts many years before it needs changing.
There is a motherboard inside a games console too.

teile.einleitung: The Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem is a basic rule of digital technology. It says how often you have to measure a signal such as music or speech so that you can reproduce it later without errors. Without this rule there would be no good CDs, mobile phone calls or music streams.
wichtigste: The sampling frequency must be more than twice the highest frequency in the signal.
Half the sampling frequency is called the Nyquist frequency; at 48 kHz this is 24 kHz.
If you sample too slowly, false tones arise; this is called aliasing.
A low-pass filter used as an anti-aliasing filter removes frequencies that are too high before digitisation.
Classic digital telephony according to G.711 works at 8 kHz.
Vladimir Kotelnikov formulated the theorem as early as 1933, independently of Shannon.
Wagon wheels turning backwards in films are an example of aliasing.

abschnitte.text: A microphone supplies an **analogue signal**, which changes constantly and smoothly. But a computer can only store individual numbers. That is why an analogue-to-digital converter measures the signal at very short, equal intervals; this is called **sampling**. How many measurements are taken per second is called the **sampling rate** or sampling frequency.

The theorem says: the sampling rate must be more than twice the highest frequency in the signal. Half the sampling rate is called the **Nyquist frequency**. If a telephone signal contains tones up to 3.4 kHz, 6.8 kHz is just not enough; you need more. That is why telephones use 8 kHz, and the music CD works at 44.1 kHz, because people hear at most about 20 kHz.

If you sample too slowly, frequencies arise that did not exist in the original at all. This is called **aliasing**. A tone of 7 kHz sampled at 10 kHz then appears as 3 kHz. In films you know the same effect: wagon wheels seem to turn slowly or even backwards, because the frame rate is too low.

To prevent aliasing, a **low-pass filter** is placed in front of the analogue-to-digital converter. This anti-aliasing filter lets low frequencies through and blocks frequencies that are too high. In audio devices with a sampling rate of 48 kHz, tones above 24 kHz must therefore be removed beforehand. Because real filters are not perfect, the sampling rate is usually chosen a little higher than necessary.

The name recalls **Harry Nyquist**, who did important groundwork in 1928, and **Claude Shannon**, who made the theorem famous in 1949. The Soviet engineer Vladimir Kotelnikov had already formulated it independently in 1933. The British mathematician Edmund Whittaker had also had similar ideas before. That is why it is sometimes also called the WKS sampling theorem.

begriffe.erklaerung: How many measured values per second are taken from a signal.
Half the sampling rate, the highest frequency that can be stored cleanly.
Distortion in which false frequencies arise because sampling is too slow.
Filter that lets low frequencies through and blocks high ones.
Unit of oscillations per second; 1 kHz is 1,000 oscillations per second.

gewusst: The music CD samples each channel 44,100 times per second.
Bat calls are often above 20 kHz, which is why especially high sampling rates are needed to record them.
Digital cameras can also show aliasing, for example as strange striped patterns on checked shirts.

teile.einleitung: A clean room is a room in which the air contains almost no dust. Computer chips, medicines or parts for satellites are made there, which could be ruined by even tiny specks of dust. People may only enter it in special protective suits.
wichtigste: The ISO 14644-1 standard divides clean rooms into classes by particles per cubic metre of air.
ISO 1 is the cleanest clean room class.
HEPA and ULPA filters hold back airborne particles especially effectively.
Many clean rooms have a laminar flow from the ceiling to the floor.
A slight overpressure stops unfiltered air getting in.
People are usually the biggest source of particles in a clean room.
In the lithography areas of chip factories the light is yellow.

abschnitte.text: In normal air there are countless tiny particles floating about, such as dust, flakes of skin or fibres. For making **computer chips** such **particles** are dangerous, because the structures on a chip are much smaller than a speck of dust. That is why in a **clean room** the air is constantly filtered. Temperature and humidity are also precisely controlled.

The international standard **ISO 14644-1** divides clean rooms into classes from ISO 1 to ISO 9. What is counted is how many particles of a certain size there are in a cubic metre of air. ISO 1 is the cleanest class, ISO 9 corresponds roughly to normal room air. Chip factories work in especially clean classes; hospitals and pharmaceutical companies often in somewhat less strict ones.

**HEPA** and **ULPA filters** in the ceiling hold back almost all airborne particles. The cleaned air flows evenly downwards without swirling; this is called **laminar flow**. It flushes particles down to the floor, where the air is sucked away. A slight overpressure makes sure that no unfiltered air flows in when a door is opened.

abschnitte.titel: People as a source of dust
abschnitte.text: People constantly lose flakes of skin, hairs and fibres from their clothes. That is why people are usually the biggest **source of particles** in a clean room. Anyone who wants to go in puts on overalls, a hood, a face mask, gloves and overshoes in an **airlock**. Make-up, perfume and paper are banned in many clean rooms.

In chip factories people work with **photoresist**, which reacts to short-wavelength, bluish light. That is why the lamps in these lithography areas shine yellow. The modern clean room with laminar flow was invented around 1960 by the American Willis Whitfield. In Rüschlikon, IBM and ETH Zurich have run the **Binnig and Rohrer Nanotechnology Center** with a large clean room since 2011.

begriffe.erklaerung: Tiny piece of matter such as dust that floats in the air.
Very fine air filter that holds back almost all airborne particles.
Even airflow without swirling.
Anteroom in which you change before entering the clean room.
Light-sensitive layer used to transfer patterns onto chips.

gewusst: In the cleanest clean rooms, a whole cubic metre of air contains fewer dust particles than a single breath outside.
The white protective suits in clean rooms are jokingly called “bunny suits” in English.
Parts for space telescopes are also built in clean rooms so that no dust clouds the sensitive mirrors.

teile.einleitung: The zip is a practical fastening made of two rows of small teeth that interlock. With a single pull, a jacket, bag or tent can be opened and closed. It is so taken for granted that people hardly think about how cleverly it is built.
wichtigste: In a zip, small teeth interlock.
The part you pull back and forth is called the slider.
In American English the zip is called a zipper.
The first forerunner was invented in the USA.
Gideon Sundback improved it so that it worked well.
The teeth are often made of metal or plastic.
If a tooth is missing, the zip can come open.

abschnitte.text: A zip consists of two fabric tapes to which small **teeth** are attached. Each tooth has a small bump on top and a hollow underneath. The **slider** brings the two rows together so that each tooth fits into the gap on the opposite side. At the ends, small stops prevent the slider from slipping off.

Inside, the slider is shaped like a **Y**. When you pull it up, it presses the teeth together at an angle from both sides, and they hook firmly into each other. When you pull it down, a wedge in the middle separates the teeth again. If a tooth is missing or the slider is worn, the fastening can open by itself.

In 1893 in Chicago the American **Whitcomb Judson** presented a hook fastening for shoes, a forerunner of the zip. But it often jammed and came open easily. The Swedish-born engineer **Gideon Sundback** made decisive improvements to the idea around 1913. His teeth interlocked reliably, and he also built machines to make them cheaply.

The English word **zipper** became known in the 1920s through rubber boots made by an American company. It imitates the sound made when you open it quickly. In German it is called a “Reissverschluss” (tear fastener), because you can rip it open and shut with a jerk. In Switzerland people sometimes simply say “Zipp”.

There are zips with teeth made of **metal**, of moulded **plastic** or with a coil of plastic thread. Metal is robust and suitable for jeans; coils are light and flexible for sportswear. Separating zips, as on a jacket, can be pulled completely apart at the bottom. The company **Riri**, based in Ticino, makes high-quality zips for fashion brands.

begriffe.erklaerung: Movable part that joins or separates the teeth.
Small links that hook into each other when closing.
American English word for a zip.
Zip whose halves can be pulled completely apart.

gewusst: The Japanese company YKK makes a large share of all the zips in the world.
Spacesuits and tents also have special, especially tight zips.
If a zip jams, a little pencil graphite or soap on the teeth often helps.

teile.einleitung: Regenerative braking, in German “Rekuperation”, means recovering energy. In electric cars, trains and trams, the motor becomes a generator when braking and turns the energy of movement back into electricity. In this way less energy is lost as heat in the brakes, and the vehicle can go further.
wichtigste: In vehicles, regenerative braking means recovering braking energy with the motor working as a generator.
A car weighing 1,500 kg at 72 km/h has 300 kJ of energy of movement.
360 kJ, half of it recovered, gives 0.05 kWh.
With one-pedal driving, the car brakes strongly through regeneration when you take your foot off the accelerator.
SBB electric locomotives usually feed braking energy back into the overhead line network.
In Formula 1 the KERS system was introduced in 2009.
With a full battery an electric car can hardly regenerate.
You recover especially large amounts of energy on a long descent from an Alpine pass.

abschnitte.text: The German word “Rekuperation” comes from the Latin “recuperare”, which means to recover. A moving vehicle has **energy of movement**, also called kinetic energy. With normal brakes it is turned into heat by friction and lost. With regenerative braking, the electric motor works as a **generator** and charges the battery with this energy.

Energy of movement is calculated with E = ½ · m · v². So a car of 1,500 kg at 72 km/h, which is 20 metres per second, has 300,000 joules or **300 kJ**. If a car recovers 50 per cent of 360 kJ when braking, that is 180 kJ. Because one kilowatt hour is 3,600 kJ, this corresponds to 0.05 kWh.

Many electric cars already brake when you take your foot off the accelerator. This **one-pedal driving** means you can often drive almost without using the brake pedal. On a long descent from an Alpine pass, an electric car recovers especially large amounts of energy. But if the battery is already full, it cannot take any extra energy, and then the normal brakes have to do more work.

Electric locomotives and trams have used regenerative braking for a long time. SBB locomotives usually return the braking energy to the **overhead line network**, where it powers other trains. On steep mountain lines such as the Gotthard or Lötschberg in particular, a lot of energy is gathered this way. Mountain railways and lifts can also recover electricity when going down.

In Formula 1 **KERS** was introduced in 2009, a system that stores braking energy and releases it as extra thrust at the push of a button. In a quarry near Biel the electric dumper truck **eDumper** operates. It drives up the hill empty and down fully loaded, and because it is heavier going down, it recovers more energy than it needs for the journey up. So it hardly ever has to be plugged in.

The word “Rekuperation” is also used in German for ventilation systems in houses. There the warm, stale air warms the fresh, cold air from outside before it flows into the house. In this way heat is recovered and heating energy saved.

begriffe.erklaerung: The energy a body has because it is moving.
A machine that turns movement into electricity.
A unit of energy used to measure electricity consumption.
The wire above the tracks that supplies trains with electricity.

gewusst: Thanks to regenerative braking, the brakes of electric cars wear out much more slowly than those of petrol cars.
Some e-bikes can also charge a little energy back into the battery when braking.

teile.einleitung: Hedy Lamarr was an Austrian-American film actress and inventor. She became world-famous as a film star in Hollywood, but on the side she tinkered with technical ideas. Together with the composer George Antheil she invented frequency hopping, whose principle is found today, for example, in Bluetooth.
wichtigste: Hedy Lamarr was born in Vienna on 9 November 1914 and died in the USA in 2000.
At first she was world-famous as a film actress in Hollywood.
With the composer George Antheil she developed frequency hopping.
The invention was meant to steer torpedoes by radio without interference.
Transmitter and receiver were to change frequency at the same time using identically punched paper rolls.
Today's radio technologies such as Bluetooth use the principle of changing frequency.
On her birthday Germany, Austria and Switzerland celebrate Inventors' Day.

abschnitte.text: Hedy Lamarr's real name was **Hedwig Kiesler**, and she grew up in **Vienna**. As a young woman she already acted in films in Austria and Germany. In 1937 she went to the USA, where a big film studio signed her up and gave her the name Hedy Lamarr. She acted in many Hollywood films and was considered one of the best-known actresses of her time.

As well as filming, Hedy Lamarr was very interested in technology. At home she had a workbench where she worked on ideas. During the **Second World War** she wanted to help the opponents of Nazi Germany. She thought about how remote-controlled torpedoes could be protected from interference.

A radio signal on just one frequency is easy for an enemy to find and jam. Lamarr's idea: transmitter and receiver keep changing **frequency** in the same rhythm. Anyone who does not know the sequence hears only fragments. This is how **frequency hopping** came about.

Her partner was the American composer **George Antheil**, who had written music for mechanical pianos. He suggested controlling the frequency changes with **punched paper rolls**, similar to a self-playing piano. Their system had 88 frequencies, as many as a piano has keys. In 1942 the two received a patent for it in the USA.

The American navy did not use the invention at the time. Only decades later did the principle become important in radio technology. Today **Bluetooth** and other radio methods use rapid frequency changes so that connections are stable and hard to disturb. Hedy Lamarr only received awards for her invention towards the end of her life, and since 2014 her name has been in the American National Inventors Hall of Fame.

begriffe.erklaerung: How often a wave oscillates per second; in radio, something like a channel.
Radio technique in which transmitter and receiver keep changing frequency together.
A right that protects an invention for a certain time.
Strip of paper with holes that a machine reads like a program.

gewusst: The 88 frequencies in Lamarr's patent correspond exactly to the number of keys on a piano.
Inventors' Day on 9 November was chosen because it is Hedy Lamarr's birthday.
Hedy Lamarr never sold her invention and earned no money from it.

teile.einleitung: A patent is a protective right for an invention. Whoever holds a patent may decide alone, for a certain time, who may make, sell or use the invention. In return the invention must be described publicly so that everyone can learn from it.
wichtigste: An invention must be new, inventive and industrially applicable.
In Switzerland a patent lasts at most 20 years from the application.
The Swiss Federal Institute of Intellectual Property in Bern is responsible.
In return, the inventor must describe the invention publicly.
The first federal Patent Act came into force in 1888.
As early as 1474 Venice passed one of the first patent laws in the world.
Albert Einstein worked at the patent office in Bern from 1902 to 1909.

abschnitte.text: A **patent** gives its holder a time-limited monopoly on a technical invention. During this time others may use it only with permission, usually in return for a fee, the **licence**. This makes it worthwhile to put time and money into new ideas. When the protection ends, everyone may use the invention freely.

An invention must be **new**, so it must not have been published anywhere in the world already. It must be based on an **inventive step** and must not simply be obvious to experts. It must also be industrially applicable. Ideas, rules of games or discoveries in nature itself cannot be patented.

In Switzerland patents are granted by the **Swiss Federal Institute of Intellectual Property** in Bern. A patent lasts at most 20 years from the application, and a fee has to be paid every year. Through the **European Patent Office** in Munich you can apply for protection in many European countries at once. Relative to its population, Switzerland files the most patent applications there (as of 2024).

In 1474 the city republic of **Venice** passed one of the first patent laws in the world. England and the USA followed later. Switzerland only introduced a federal Patent Act in 1888; before that, inventions could hardly be protected here. Since then the law has been renewed several times and adapted to international rules.

From 1902 to 1909 **Albert Einstein** worked as a technical expert at the patent office in Bern. There he examined patent applications, for example for electrical devices. On the side, in 1905, he wrote several famous papers, including the special theory of relativity. Later he said that the work at the office had helped him think clearly.

begriffe.erklaerung: Permission to use a protected invention in return for payment.
The right to be the only one allowed to do or sell something.
Rights to ideas, inventions, brands or works.
Public document that describes the invention exactly.

gewusst: Worldwide there are millions of valid patents, and hundreds of thousands are added every year.
Patent specifications are public, so anyone can read on the internet how protected inventions work.
At the Bern patent office, Einstein was first employed as a “technical expert, third class”.

teile.einleitung: A lorry, in Switzerland often called a “Camion”, is a large vehicle for transporting goods. Lorries bring food to the shops, gravel to building sites and parcels to distribution centres. Without them, a lot would be missing from our everyday life.
wichtigste: In Switzerland people often call a lorry a “Camion”.
In Switzerland a lorry with a trailer may weigh no more than 40 tonnes.
In principle, large lorries are not allowed to drive at night or on Sundays in Switzerland.
The blind spot is an area the driver cannot see.
For cyclists it is especially dangerous to be right next to a lorry on its right at junctions.
There are many special vehicles such as tippers, concrete mixers and container lorries.

abschnitte.text: A **lorry** has a cab for the driver and behind it a loading platform or a body for the load. It is usually driven by a powerful diesel engine, but more and more often by an electric motor. The first lorry with a combustion engine was built by Gottlieb Daimler's company in 1896. Today there are lorries in many sizes, from vans to heavy **articulated lorries**.

A **tipper** can tilt its loading platform so that gravel or earth slides out. A concrete mixer keeps turning its drum so that the concrete does not harden on the way to the building site. Other lorries carry **containers**, standardised metal boxes that can also be loaded onto ships and trains. There are also tankers, refrigerated lorries, dustcarts and car transporters.

In Switzerland a lorry with a trailer may weigh no more than 40 tonnes. Heavy lorries are subject to a **night driving ban** and a Sunday driving ban so that people can have peace and quiet. Since 2001 lorries have paid the performance-related heavy vehicle charge, **HVC** for short (LSVA in German), which is calculated by weight and kilometres driven. Among other things, this money helps to pay for expanding the railway so that more goods go by rail.

Anyone driving a lorry sits high up and, despite many mirrors, cannot see everything. The area the driver cannot see is called the **blind spot**. It is especially dangerous right next to the lorry on its right when it turns right at a junction. Cyclists and pedestrians should therefore wait behind a lorry and seek eye contact with the driver.

A large share of goods in Switzerland is carried by lorry for at least part of the way. Many lorries drive through the Alps between northern and southern Europe, which is why Switzerland wants to shift goods traffic to the railway. Manufacturers are developing **electric lorries** and hydrogen lorries so that fewer exhaust fumes are produced. Numerous electric lorries are already on the road in Switzerland, for example for retailers.

begriffe.erklaerung: Swiss word for a lorry, taken from French.
A tractor unit with a large trailer resting on it.
An area next to the vehicle that the driver cannot see.
A charge that lorries in Switzerland pay per kilometre and according to weight (LSVA).
A lorry that can tip its loading platform to unload.

gewusst: A fully loaded 40-tonne lorry weighs about as much as 25 cars.
Heavy lorries may drive at no more than 80 km/h on Swiss motorways.
A container is standardised so that it fits on ships, trains and lorries all over the world.

teile.einleitung: A hybrid drive combines two different kinds of drive in one vehicle, usually a combustion engine and an electric motor. In this way a car can save fuel, because the electric motor helps when pulling away and braking energy is recovered. The word hybrid means something like mixed or crossed.
