wichtigste: A hybrid drive usually combines a combustion engine with an electric motor.
In a series hybrid, the combustion engine only drives a generator.
The battery of a plug-in hybrid can be charged from the mains.
A mild hybrid with a 48-volt system usually cannot drive longer distances on electricity alone.
The Toyota Prius came onto the market in Japan in 1997 as the first mass-produced hybrid car.
Around 1900 Ferdinand Porsche built one of the first hybrid cars, the Semper Vivus.
In town traffic with frequent pulling away and braking, a full hybrid saves especially a lot of fuel.

abschnitte.text: A hybrid car has two hearts: a petrol or diesel engine and an **electric motor** with a battery. The computer in the car constantly decides which motor is working at the moment or whether both drive together. When braking, the electric motor works as a generator and charges the battery. This recovery of braking energy is called **regenerative braking**.

In a **series hybrid**, the combustion engine only drives a generator, and only the electric motor moves the wheels. In a parallel hybrid, both motors can act directly on the wheels. In a power-split hybrid, a **planetary gear** divides the engine's power between the wheels and the generator. Toyota, for example, uses this solution.

A **mild hybrid** usually has a 48-volt system and supports the engine only a little; it cannot manage longer distances on electricity alone. A full hybrid can drive short distances slowly on electricity only. In a **plug-in hybrid** the battery is bigger and can be charged at a socket or charging station. This often makes a few dozen kilometres possible on electricity alone.

A combustion engine works poorly when pulling away and at low load. That is exactly where the electric motor helps, which is why a full hybrid saves fuel above all in **town traffic** with many traffic lights. Many full hybrids use petrol engines based on the Atkinson or Miller principle, which are more economical thanks to a longer expansion of the gases. On the motorway at a steady speed, on the other hand, the advantage is smaller.

As early as around 1900, **Ferdinand Porsche** built one of the first hybrid cars, the Lohner-Porsche Semper Vivus. After that, pure petrol and diesel cars won out for a long time. In 1997 the **Toyota Prius** came onto the market in Japan, the first hybrid car to be built in large numbers. Today many buses, ships and even Formula 1 racing cars also run with hybrid drive.

begriffe.erklaerung: Recovering energy when braking in order to charge the battery.
Machine that converts movement into electric current.
The car can be plugged in and charged at a socket.
Gear with gearwheels that circle around a central wheel like planets.

gewusst: Semper Vivus is Latin and means always alive.
Many hybrid cars drive completely silently in car parks, because only the electric motor is running.
Diesel-electric locomotives work in a similar way to a series hybrid.

teile.einleitung: The scanning tunnelling microscope is a device with which individual atoms on a surface can be made visible. It was invented in 1981 in Rüschlikon on Lake Zurich. Instead of using light, it feels the surface with a tiny tip.
wichtigste: The scanning tunnelling microscope is based on the quantum mechanical tunnelling effect.
Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer invented it at IBM in Rüschlikon.
In 1986 they shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with Ernst Ruska.
Only electrically conducting samples can be examined.
Piezoelectric actuators move the tip with an accuracy of fractions of a nanometre.
In constant-current mode, a control system keeps the tunnelling current the same and records the height.
In 1989 Don Eigler wrote the letters IBM with 35 xenon atoms.

abschnitte.text: A normal light microscope cannot show atoms, because they are much smaller than the wavelength of light. That is why the **scanning tunnelling microscope** works quite differently. An extremely fine metal tip, which at best ends in a single atom, moves line by line over the sample. This line-by-line feeling is called **scanning**.

The tip does not touch the sample but stays about one nanometre away from it. If a small voltage is applied, electrons still jump across the gap; this is the **tunnelling effect** of quantum physics. The resulting **tunnelling current** depends very strongly on the distance. If the gap gets just 0.1 nanometres bigger, the current falls to about a tenth.

In **constant-current mode**, a control system always keeps the tunnelling current the same. To do this, the tip has to rise a little over each atom and sink in between. This movement in height is recorded, and the computer turns it into an image of the surface. The tip is moved by **piezo elements**, which expand by tiny amounts when a voltage is applied.

The German **Gerd Binnig** and the Swiss **Heinrich Rohrer** developed the device in 1981 at the IBM research laboratory in Rüschlikon. As early as 1986 they received the Nobel Prize in Physics for it. They shared it with Ernst Ruska, the inventor of the electron microscope. Today a nanotechnology centre in Rüschlikon bears both their names.

The tip can not only show atoms but also move them. In 1989 **Don Eigler** at IBM in California placed 35 xenon atoms on a nickel surface so that they formed the letters IBM. Because the device can only examine conducting samples, in 1986 Binnig developed the **atomic force microscope** with Calvin Quate and Christoph Gerber. Both inventions are seen as the starting signal for **nanotechnology**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Quantum effect in which particles overcome a barrier they should not really be able to jump over.
A billionth of a metre, about ten atoms side by side.
Crystal that expands very slightly when an electrical voltage is applied.
Research and technology with tiny structures made of individual atoms and molecules.

gewusst: Heinrich Rohrer came from Buchs in the canton of St Gallen.
The scanning tunnelling microscope works best in a vacuum and at very low temperatures.
Even a lorry on the road can disturb the measurement, which is why the devices stand on vibration-damped tables.

teile.einleitung: A QR code is a square pattern of small black and white squares in which information is hidden. With a mobile phone camera you can read it in a fraction of a second and, for example, open a website or pay a bill. It was invented in Japan in 1994.
wichtigste: QR stands for quick response.
The QR code was invented in Japan in 1994.
Originally it was used to track car parts in production.
The three large squares in the corners show the scanner the position and orientation.
Thanks to error correction, a QR code can often still be read when part of it is dirty.
The small squares of a QR code are called modules.
In Switzerland the QR-bill replaced the old red and orange payment slips.
Be careful with unknown QR codes, because they can lead to fraudulent sites.

abschnitte.text: A QR code is a **two-dimensional code** that stores information in rows and columns. An ordinary barcode in a shop stores data in only one direction and so holds much less. A QR code consists of many small squares, the **modules**. The smallest QR code has 21 by 21 modules, the largest 177 by 177.

The QR code was developed in 1994 by the Japanese company **Denso Wave**, which belongs to the car parts supplier Denso. The engineer Masahiro Hara wanted to use it to record and track **car parts** in the factory more quickly. The company decided not to charge licence fees, so anyone was free to use it. In this way it spread all over the world, especially since smartphones have had cameras.

The three large squares in the corners are called **position markers**. From them the camera can tell where the code is and how it is turned, which is why it can be scanned at an angle or upside down. Thanks to built-in **error correction**, the code stays readable even if, depending on the setting, up to about 30 per cent is damaged or covered. That is why you sometimes see QR codes with a logo in the middle.

Switzerland has had the **QR-bill** since 2020. It replaced the old red and orange payment slips, which could no longer be used from autumn 2022. A small **Swiss cross** is shown in the middle of the Swiss QR Code. You scan the code with the banking app, and the amount, recipient and reference are filled in automatically.

QR codes are found on posters, menus, train tickets, packaging and admission tickets. They can contain websites, contact details, Wi-Fi access or timetables. But fraudsters sometimes stick fake QR codes, for example on parking meters, that lead to forged payment pages. That is why, before opening one, you should check which address is shown and never simply enter passwords or card details.

begriffe.erklaerung: One of the small black or white squares of a QR code.
A device or app that reads a code.
Extra data with which missing or damaged parts are filled in.
A code made of lines, as found on products in shops.

gewusst: A QR code can store more than 7,000 digits.
The inventor is said to have got the idea for the position markers from the board game Go, which is played with black and white stones.

teile.einleitung: Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian painter, inventor and researcher of the Renaissance. He painted the Mona Lisa and drew flying machines centuries before people could fly. Because he achieved great things in art, technology and natural science, he is considered a polymath.
wichtigste: Leonardo da Vinci was born in Italy in 1452 and died in France in 1519.
He painted the Mona Lisa, which now hangs in the Louvre in Paris.
His mural “The Last Supper” is in a monastery in Milan.
He designed flying machines with flapping wings modelled on birds.
His aerial screw is considered an early forerunner of the helicopter.
The drawing “Vitruvian Man” shows a man in a circle and a square.

abschnitte.text: Leonardo was born on 15 April 1452 near the small town of **Vinci** in Tuscany, hence his name “da Vinci”, meaning “from Vinci”. As a teenager he went to Florence to train with the artist Andrea del Verrocchio. He lived in the time of the **Renaissance**, when artists and scholars rediscovered antiquity and studied nature closely. Leonardo was curious about almost everything and filled thousands of pages with notes and sketches.

His most famous painting is the **Mona Lisa**, a smiling woman whom he began painting around 1503. Today it hangs in the Louvre in Paris and is visited by millions of people every year. Between 1495 and 1498, in the monastery of Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan, he painted the mural **The Last Supper**, which shows Jesus with his disciples. Leonardo used soft transitions between light and shadow that make pictures look especially lifelike.

In his notebooks Leonardo designed flying machines with flapping wings that he had copied from birds. His **aerial screw** is considered an early forerunner of the helicopter. He also drew parachutes, bridges, canals, gear systems and war machines. Most of his inventions were never built in his lifetime, because the materials and engines were lacking.

Leonardo studied how water flows, how birds fly and how plants grow. He examined the human body very closely and drew muscles, bones and the heart. The drawing **Vitruvian Man** shows a man with outstretched arms in a circle and a square and deals with the proportions of the body. He often wrote in **mirror writing**, that is, from right to left.

Leonardo worked in Florence, Milan and Rome. In old age he accepted an invitation from the French king Francis I and lived in the Château du Clos Lucé near Amboise. He died there on 2 May 1519. Today he is seen as the very model of a **polymath**, a person who achieves great things in many fields of knowledge at once. His notebooks are spread across various museums and libraries around the world.

begriffe.erklaerung: Period in the 15th and 16th centuries in which art and science flourished anew.
A person who is an expert in many fields of knowledge at once.
Writing that is read from right to left, as in a mirror.
A picture painted directly onto a wall.
The size relationships of parts to each other.

gewusst: Leonardo was left-handed, which made his mirror writing easier.
The Mona Lisa measures only about 77 by 53 centimetres, smaller than many people expect.
In 1911 the Mona Lisa was stolen from the Louvre and only found again in Italy two years later.

teile.einleitung: Johannes Gutenberg was an inventor from Mainz who invented printing with movable metal letters in the 15th century. Suddenly books could be produced quickly and in large numbers, instead of every word being copied by hand. Many people consider his invention one of the most important in human history.
wichtigste: Johannes Gutenberg lived in the 15th century; he was born around 1400 and died in 1468.
He lived and printed in Mainz, which is in Germany today.
He invented printing with movable metal type.
His most famous work is the Gutenberg Bible.
About 180 Gutenberg Bibles were printed.
Besides books, he also printed letters of indulgence.
In Mainz the Gutenberg Museum remembers him.

abschnitte.text: Johannes Gutenberg's real name was Johannes Gensfleisch, and he was born around 1400 in **Mainz** on the Rhine. He took the name Gutenberg from a house belonging to his family, the “Hof zum Gutenberg”. He lived for some years in **Strasbourg**, where he worked with metal and probably already made his first printing experiments. Later he returned to Mainz, where he died in 1468.

Gutenberg's big idea was **movable type**: individual letters made of metal that could be put together into words and pages and then used again. With a **hand mould** he cast thousands of letters of the same size from a mixture of lead, tin and antimony. A **printing press**, similar to a wine press, pressed the paper onto the inked letters. For this he mixed a special oil-based printing ink that stuck well to the metal.

Around 1452 to 1454 Gutenberg printed the Latin Bible, now called the **Gutenberg Bible**. Each page has two columns, usually with 42 lines, and it runs to about 1,280 pages. About 180 copies were printed, most on paper, some on expensive parchment. Today about 49 of them still exist, and they are among the most valuable books in the world.

For his workshop Gutenberg needed a lot of money and borrowed it from the merchant **Johannes Fust**. In 1455 Fust demanded the money back, and after a legal dispute Gutenberg lost part of his workshop. With smaller jobs such as **letters of indulgence**, calendars and school books he earned extra money. Later he received a kind of honorary pension from the Archbishop of Mainz.

Within a few decades, print shops appeared all over Europe, including in **Basel**, which soon became an important printing city. Books became cheaper, more people learnt to read, and knowledge spread much faster. Without printing, the ideas of the **Reformation** would hardly have spread so quickly either. In Mainz the **Gutenberg Museum** remembers the inventor and shows original Bibles.

begriffe.erklaerung: Individual metal letters for printing.
Machine that presses paper firmly onto the inked type.
Expensive writing material made from treated animal skin.
Church document in the Middle Ages that could be obtained for money.
Church reform movement in the 16th century from which the Reformed churches arose.

gewusst: Nobody knows exactly what Gutenberg looked like, because there is no picture painted during his lifetime.
Before printing existed, monks often spent months or years copying a thick book by hand.
Gutenberg's Bible contains neither his name nor a printing date.

teile.einleitung: A hot-air balloon is an aircraft that flies without wings or an engine. It rises because the heated air in its huge envelope is lighter than the cool air outside. Balloon flights are one of the oldest ways in which people have got into the air.
wichtigste: The air in the balloon envelope is heated with a gas burner.
The passengers stand in a basket under the envelope.
The Montgolfier brothers built the first hot-air balloons in France.
In 1783 a sheep, a duck and a cockerel flew along as the first passengers.
In German, balloonists say “fahren” (to travel) instead of “fliegen” (to fly).
The direction is chosen by looking for winds at other heights.
Every winter a big balloon festival takes place in the mountain village of Château-d'Oex in Vaud.

abschnitte.text: Warm air expands and is therefore lighter than cold air. If the air in the **envelope** is much warmer than the surrounding air, **lift** is created that carries the balloon, basket and people upwards. If the pilot wants to climb, he heats more with the burner. If the air cools down, or he lets warm air escape through an opening at the top, the balloon sinks.

The envelope is made of light, tear-resistant fabric such as nylon or polyester and is often as tall as a house with several storeys. Below it hangs the **gas burner**, which burns propane from cylinders and produces loud, hot flames. The passengers stand in a **basket** made of woven willow or rattan. This material is light and stable and cushions the landing.

In 1783 the French brothers Joseph-Michel and Jacques-Étienne **Montgolfier** launched the first hot-air balloons. In September 1783, at Versailles in front of the king, a sheep, a duck and a cockerel went up and landed unhurt. In November 1783 people travelled in a hot-air balloon for the first time, in Paris. That is why a hot-air balloon is also called a **montgolfière**.

A balloon has no steering and drifts with the wind. Because the wind often blows from different directions at different heights, the pilot climbs or descends to find a suitable air current. Balloons usually take off early in the morning or in the evening, when the air is calm. A chase vehicle follows on the ground to collect the balloon and passengers after landing.

Every winter an international balloon festival takes place in the mountain village of **Château-d'Oex** in Vaud, where many colourful balloons travel over the snowy Alps. In 1999 the balloon Breitling Orbiter 3 also set off from there with the Swiss **Bertrand Piccard** and the Briton Brian Jones. They were the first to travel all the way round the Earth in a balloon without landing. Their balloon, however, was a mixture of a gas balloon and a hot-air balloon.

begriffe.erklaerung: Force that pushes something lighter upwards in air or water.
The big fabric bag of the balloon, which is filled with hot air.
Another name for a hot-air balloon, after the Montgolfier brothers.
A gas carried in cylinders and burned in the burner.

gewusst: In German, balloonists say “fahren” instead of “fliegen”, because the balloon drifts with the flow of the air like a ship.
The first passengers of a balloon were not people but a sheep, a duck and a cockerel.
In the basket you feel almost no wind, because the balloon drifts exactly as fast as the air around it.

teile.einleitung: A quantum computer is a computer that uses the strange laws of quantum physics to solve certain tasks much faster than normal computers. Instead of ordinary bits it calculates with qubits. Quantum computers are still research devices, but in future they could greatly change chemistry, medicine and encryption.
wichtigste: Quantum computers calculate with qubits instead of classical bits.
A qubit can be in a superposition of 0 and 1.
A register of 10 qubits covers 1,024 basis states.
Shor's algorithm efficiently breaks large numbers down into prime factors and so threatens encryption methods such as RSA.
Albert Einstein called entanglement “spooky action at a distance”.
Through decoherence a qubit loses its quantum properties.
Superconducting qubits are operated at a few millikelvin, almost at absolute zero.

abschnitte.text: A normal computer calculates with **bits**, which are either 0 or 1. A **qubit**, on the other hand, can be in a **superposition** of 0 and 1. Only when it is measured is it decided which value comes out. Several qubits together can represent many states at the same time. A register of 10 qubits covers 2 to the power of 10, that is 1,024 basis states.

Qubits can be **entangled** with each other. Then their measurement results are linked, even when they are far apart. Albert Einstein found this so strange that he called it “spooky action at a distance”. Today entanglement has been confirmed in many experiments. In 2022 Alain Aspect, John Clauser and Anton Zeilinger received the Nobel Prize in Physics for such experiments.

Quantum computers are not faster at everything, only at certain tasks. **Shor's algorithm** of 1994 can efficiently break large numbers down into prime factors. This would threaten today's encryption methods such as RSA, which is why new, secure methods are already being developed. **Grover's algorithm** searches unsorted data faster. For 1 million entries it needs only about 1,000 queries instead of up to a million.

Qubits are very sensitive. Even the slightest heat or vibration destroys their quantum properties; this is called **decoherence**. That is why **superconducting qubits** are operated at a few millikelvin, colder than in outer space. This requires large cooling devices that look like golden chandeliers. Other approaches use trapped ions or particles of light.

In 2019 Google claimed **quantum supremacy** for the first time with its **Sycamore** processor. The chip, with 53 usable qubits, solved a special calculation in about 200 seconds which, according to Google, would have taken a supercomputer much longer. Since then companies such as IBM and Google have been building ever larger quantum processors. In Switzerland, research into quantum technology is carried out at ETH Zurich, the University of Basel and IBM in Rüschlikon, among others. But there is still a long way to go to large, error-free quantum computers.

begriffe.erklaerung: Quantum bit that can be 0 and 1 at the same time in a superposition.
State in which a qubit contains several possibilities at once.
Mysterious connection between qubits whose measurement results are linked.
Loss of quantum properties through disturbances from the surroundings.
A thousandth of a degree above absolute zero, which is minus 273.15 degrees Celsius.

gewusst: The cooling of a quantum computer is colder than the space between the stars.
With 300 qubits there would be more basis states than there are atoms in the visible universe.
A quantum computer will never replace a normal laptop for surfing the web or writing.

teile.einleitung: The internet is a worldwide network that connects billions of computers, mobile phones and other devices with each other. Over the internet we send messages, watch videos, look for information and play together. An important part of it, the World Wide Web, was invented in Switzerland at CERN near Geneva.
wichtigste: The internet connects devices all over the world with each other.
Its forerunner is considered to be ARPANET, which was set up in the USA from 1969.
In 1989 Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web at CERN near Geneva.
With a browser you call up and look at web pages.
An IP address is a number that identifies a device on the network.
The “s” in “https” stands for secure.
Swiss internet addresses often end in .ch.

abschnitte.text: The internet consists of many networks connected by cable, radio and satellite. Each device has an **IP address**, a number that identifies it on the network, rather like a postal address. Data is split into small packets and sent separately. At the destination they are put back together. So that all devices understand each other, shared rules apply, the **protocols**, for example TCP/IP.

From 1969 **ARPANET** was set up in the USA; it is considered the forerunner of the internet. At first it connected only a few universities. In 1989 **Tim Berners-Lee** at CERN near Geneva proposed the World Wide Web, a system of linked pages. In 1991 the first website went online. From the mid-1990s the internet spread into many households.

The **World Wide Web** is the part of the internet with web pages connected by links. With a **browser** such as Firefox, Chrome or Safari you call up web pages. Every page has an address, the URL. If it begins with “https”, the data is transmitted encrypted; the “s” stands for secure. Search engines help you find the right page among billions.

Swiss internet addresses have the **country code** .ch, which comes from the Latin name Confoederatio Helvetica. The endings .ch and .li are allocated by the SWITCH foundation. Almost all households in Switzerland have internet today, many with fast fibre-optic lines. At **CERN**, research is still carried out at the forefront of science, and the first website can be viewed online there again.

On the internet you should not give personal data such as your address or passwords to strangers. A good **password** is long and is not used for several services. Not everything on the internet is true, so it is worth checking sources. Anyone who is treated nastily should turn to their parents or teachers. Shared rules for screen time help you use the internet sensibly.

begriffe.erklaerung: Number that identifies a device on the internet.
Program for looking at web pages.
Rules that let computers exchange data.
Connection that takes you to another page with a click.
Converting data so that only the recipient can read it.

gewusst: The world's very first website ran on a computer at CERN with a note stuck on it saying it must not be switched off.
Under the oceans lie hundreds of submarine cables that carry most of the world's internet traffic.
In 1993 CERN released the World Wide Web so that everyone could use it free of charge.

teile.einleitung: Moore's law states that the number of transistors on a computer chip doubles regularly, today usually given as about every two years. It is not a law of nature but an observation and prediction made by Gordon Moore in 1965. For decades it described surprisingly well why computers kept getting faster, smaller and cheaper.
wichtigste: In 1965 Gordon Moore published the article on which Moore's law is based.
Originally he predicted a doubling roughly every year.
Later he adjusted the forecast to about two years.
Moore's law is an empirical observation and forecast, not a law of nature.
In 1968 Moore founded the company Intel together with Robert Noyce.
Since about 2005 the clock speeds of processors have hardly risen because of too much heat.

abschnitte.text: **Gordon Moore** was an American chemist and businessman. In 1965 he wrote an article in which he noted that the number of components on a chip was roughly doubling every year. In 1968 he founded the company **Intel** together with Robert Noyce; it is still one of the largest chipmakers today. He died in 2023.

A computer chip contains tiny electronic switches, the **transistors**. Moore predicted that their number on a chip would grow regularly. In 1975 he adjusted his prediction to about one doubling every two years. An example: if a chip has 1 billion transistors and the number doubles every 2 years, after 10 years there are 32 billion. This kind of growth is called **exponential**.

The first microprocessor, the **Intel 4004** of 1971, had about 2,300 transistors. Today's processors in computers and mobile phones contain many billions of them. This became possible because transistors could be made smaller and smaller; some are now only a few nanometres in size. In this way computers became faster and at the same time cheaper and more economical.

For a long time **Dennard scaling** also applied: as chips were made smaller, the power density stayed the same, so the chips did not get hotter. Since about the middle of the 2000s this has no longer been true. That is why clock speeds hardly rose from about 2005, and manufacturers instead built several processing cores into one chip. In addition, chip factories are getting more and more expensive; according to **Rock's law**, their cost doubles about every four years.

Moore's law became a roadmap in the chip industry that companies followed. It explains why a mobile phone today has much more computing power than the large computers of earlier decades. Many experts agree that growth is slowing down because transistors are reaching physical limits. New ideas such as stacked chips or special **AI chips** are meant to keep increasing computing power nevertheless.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny electronic switch, the basic building block of every chip.
The calculating chip, the brain of a computer.
Growth in which an amount keeps doubling.
How many working steps a processor carries out per second.
Based on observation and experience, not on a law of nature.

gewusst: If transistors doubled every two years for 20 years, there would be more than a thousand times as many at the end.
Gordon Moore himself was surprised at how long his prediction held true.
The name “Moore's law” did not come from Moore himself but was coined later by others.

teile.einleitung: Semiconductors are materials that conduct electricity better than insulators such as glass, but worse than metals such as copper. Their conductivity can be controlled deliberately, and that is exactly what makes them so valuable. Without semiconductors there would be no computers, smartphones, LED lamps or solar cells.
wichtigste: Semiconductors conduct electricity better than insulators, but worse than metals.
Silicon is the most important basic material of the semiconductor industry.
Doping with foreign atoms such as phosphorus changes the conductivity.
As the temperature rises, a pure semiconductor conducts better.
A diode consists of a p-n junction and lets current through in only one direction.
In 1947 the first working transistor was demonstrated at Bell Labs.
In 1958 Jack Kilby built the first integrated circuit at Texas Instruments.

abschnitte.text: In metals many electrons can move freely, which is why they conduct electricity well. In insulators the electrons are tightly bound. In **semiconductors** an electron needs a small boost of energy to break free. This energy is called the **band gap**; for silicon at room temperature it is about 1.1 electronvolts. When a pure semiconductor gets warmer, more electrons are freed and it conducts better, unlike a metal.

Pure **silicon** conducts only a little. That is why tiny amounts of foreign atoms are mixed in; this is called **doping**. With phosphorus, extra free electrons are created; this is called n-doping. With boron, gaps called holes are created; this is p-doping. Where an n region and a p region meet, a **p-n junction** forms.

A **diode** consists of a p-n junction and lets current through in only one direction, like a valve. Light-emitting diodes, that is LEDs, give off light as they do so. A **transistor** can switch current on and off or amplify it; it is the basic building block of every computer. The first working transistor was demonstrated in 1947 at Bell Labs in the USA. John Bardeen, Walter Brattain and William Shockley received the Nobel Prize in Physics for it in 1956.

In 1958 Jack Kilby built the first **integrated circuit** at Texas Instruments, in which several components sit on a single piece of semiconductor. Today modern chips contain billions of transistors. They are made on thin silicon discs, the **wafers**. The most modern chips are made with EUV lithography, which uses light with a wavelength of 13.5 nanometres. The machines for this are built by the Dutch company ASML.

Semiconductors are found in mobile phones, cars, washing machines and **solar cells**. Silicon is obtained from quartz sand, one of the most common substances on Earth. Many of the most modern chips are made in Taiwan. In Switzerland, the semiconductor maker STMicroelectronics has its headquarters near Geneva. Because chips are so important, some people call silicon the “raw material of the digital age”.

begriffe.erklaerung: Energy an electron needs to move freely in a semiconductor.
Deliberately adding foreign atoms to change the conductivity.
Tiny electronic switch and amplifier.
Thin disc of silicon on which chips are made.
Component that lets current through in only one direction.

gewusst: Silicon Valley in California is named after silicon.
Chip factories must be much cleaner than an operating theatre, because even tiny specks of dust destroy a chip.
A single modern smartphone chip contains more transistors than there are people on Earth.

teile.einleitung: The PostBus (Postauto) is Switzerland's yellow bus, which also runs to remote villages and over high Alpine passes. With its three-tone horn it can be heard from far away on mountain roads. For many people in rural areas it is the most important link to the world.
wichtigste: PostBuses are yellow.
The first PostBus in Switzerland ran in 1906.
Before that, horses pulled the post coaches.
The typical horn with three notes is called the three-tone horn.
On mountain postal roads the PostBus has priority.
In the past the PostBus also carried letters and parcels.
PostBuses run especially often to villages and mountain valleys.

abschnitte.text: For a long time **post coaches**, pulled by horses, carried travellers and letters through Switzerland. Over the Gotthard the post coach ran until the railway tunnel opened in 1882. In 1906 the first PostBus in Switzerland ran, on a route near Bern. Gradually motor vehicles replaced the horses, including on the Alpine passes.

The famous PostBus horn plays three notes one after another, which is why it is called the **three-tone horn**. The tune comes from the overture to the opera “William Tell” by Gioachino Rossini. On winding mountain roads the PostBus sounds its horn before tight bends. In this way it warns oncoming vehicles, which can then pull over in time.

On some mountain roads there is a blue sign with a yellow **post horn**. It marks a **mountain postal road**. There the PostBus has priority, and other vehicles must make way for it. The drivers are especially well trained to steer large buses safely over narrow passes.

abschnitte.titel: On the move across the country
abschnitte.text: Today PostBuses connect hundreds of places, especially in **rural regions** and mountain valleys where no train runs. They take children to school, commuters to work and hikers to their starting points. In the past, as well as passengers, they also carried **letters and parcels**. Today this is mostly done by Swiss Post's own vans.

Trips over passes such as the Grimsel, Furka or Susten are very popular with tourists. The company PostBus belongs to **Swiss Post**. It is testing and using more and more buses with electric or hydrogen drives. The yellow colour makes the PostBus instantly recognisable everywhere.

begriffe.erklaerung: Horse-drawn carriage that carried post and travellers in the past.
PostBus horn with three notes in a row.
Road on which the PostBus has priority.
Old signal horn of the coachmen, now the symbol of Swiss Post.

gewusst: The three-tone horn is protected; private cars are not allowed to use it.
Almost every child in Switzerland recognises the tune of the three-tone horn after the first notes.

teile.einleitung: A microphone turns sound, that is, notes, voices and noises, into electrical signals. It is, so to speak, the electrical ear of a device. Microphones are found in mobile phones, laptops, hearing aids and on every concert stage.
wichtigste: A microphone converts sound into electrical signals.
A dynamic microphone works in principle like a loudspeaker in reverse.
Condenser microphones need a power supply, often called phantom power.
A cardioid microphone picks up sound mainly from the front.
If a microphone is too close to the loudspeaker, a loud whistling occurs: feedback.
Smartphones usually contain tiny MEMS microphones.

abschnitte.text: Sound consists of tiny changes in pressure in the air. In the microphone the sound hits a thin **membrane**, which vibrates along with it. This movement is turned into an electrical voltage that varies exactly in time with the sound. An amplifier then makes the weak signal stronger so that it can be recorded or played through loudspeakers.

In a **dynamic microphone**, a coil is attached to the membrane; it moves in a magnetic field and so produces current. It is robust and often used for singing on stage, and it works like a loudspeaker in reverse. In a **condenser microphone**, the membrane forms a capacitor with a metal plate, and the distance between them changes in time with the sound. It needs power, often supplied as **phantom power** through the microphone cable, and sounds especially fine and accurate.

Not every microphone hears equally well in all directions. An omnidirectional microphone picks up sound from everywhere. A **cardioid microphone** hears mainly to the front and hardly at all to the back; its sensitivity is shaped like a heart. Shotgun microphones with a long tube even pick up sounds from a greater distance in a targeted way, for example in filming.

If you hold a microphone in front of a loudspeaker, it picks up its own sound again, which is amplified and picked up once more. This creates a loud whistling, **feedback**. When recording vocals, a **pop filter** made of fine fabric often hangs in front of the microphone. It dampens bursts of air on sounds such as P and B, which would otherwise be heard as a popping noise.

Smartphones contain tiny **MEMS microphones**, which are made on a chip. Modern phones often have several of them so that background noise can be filtered out. For television interviews, a small **clip-on microphone** is attached to the clothing. Alexander Graham Bell's telephone of 1876 contained one of the early forms of the microphone.

begriffe.erklaerung: A thin, movable disc that is set vibrating by sound.
A loud whistling when the microphone picks up its own sound from the loudspeaker.
Power for the microphone that is supplied through the audio cable.
A microphone that picks up mainly from the front.
A screen in front of the microphone that catches bursts of air when speaking.

gewusst: Some microphones are so sensitive that they can pick up a person breathing in the next room.
In an emergency, headphones can also be used as a simple microphone, because they are built like small loudspeakers.
The word microphone comes from Greek and means roughly “small sound”.

teile.einleitung: James Watt was a Scottish inventor and engineer who made decisive improvements to the steam engine. His engines drove the Industrial Revolution. The unit of power, the watt, is named after him.
wichtigste: James Watt came from Scotland and lived from 1736 to 1819.
He improved the older steam engine of Thomas Newcomen.
With the businessman Matthew Boulton he built steam engines in large numbers in Birmingham.
The first Boulton & Watt engines mainly pumped water out of mines.
In his double-acting steam engine, the steam pushes the piston alternately from both sides.
To compare engines, he used horsepower.
The unit of power, the watt, bears his name.

abschnitte.text: James Watt was born in 1736 in **Greenock** in Scotland. He learnt the trade of instrument maker. At the University of Glasgow he repaired scientific equipment. One day he was given a model of **Thomas Newcomen's** steam engine to repair. In doing so he noticed how much energy this engine wasted.

In Newcomen's engine, the cylinder was cooled and heated again with every stroke. This cost a great deal of coal. Watt had the idea of a **separate condenser**, in which the steam is cooled while the cylinder stays hot. In 1769 he patented his invention. His engine needed only about a quarter of the coal that Newcomen's engine used.

From 1775 Watt worked with the businessman **Matthew Boulton** in Birmingham. Their company, Boulton & Watt, built steam engines in large numbers. At first these mainly pumped **water out of mines**. Later Watt developed the double-acting steam engine, in which the steam pushes the piston alternately from both sides. With a rotary motion, the engines could now also drive spinning mills and other mills.

To show customers how powerful his engines were, Watt compared them with horses. This gave rise to the unit **horsepower**, hp for short. After his death he was honoured with a unit of his own. The **watt** is today the unit of power, for example for light bulbs, hairdryers or power stations. From 2011 Boulton and Watt also appeared on the British 50-pound note.

Watt had many talents. In 1780 he invented a **copying press** to duplicate letters. He also improved measuring instruments and worked on chemistry. His steam engines drove the **Industrial Revolution** and changed work and life throughout Europe. James Watt died in 1819 near Birmingham.

begriffe.erklaerung: A machine that works with the power of hot steam.
Here, a container in which steam is cooled and turns back into water.
A movable cylinder that is pushed back and forth by steam pressure.
An old unit for the power of engines, hp for short.
Today's unit of power.

gewusst: Watt is said to have had the idea of the separate condenser while out on a Sunday walk.
One metric horsepower equals about 735 watts.
Watt received a patent for his steam engine that lasted so long that other inventors could hardly compete for decades.

teile.einleitung: The Paul Scherrer Institute, PSI for short, is the largest research institute for natural sciences and engineering in Switzerland. It lies on the River Aare near Villigen and Würenlingen in the canton of Aargau. With huge installations, experts here research materials, energy and the human body, and even treat cancer with protons.
wichtigste: PSI is in the canton of Aargau.
It was formed in 1988 from the institutes EIR and SIN.
It is named after the physicist Paul Scherrer, who in 1916 developed the Debye-Scherrer method with Peter Debye.
Since 1984 eye tumours have been treated with protons at PSI.
The spot-scanning radiation technique was developed at PSI.
PSI's neutron source is called SINQ.
In 2010 the radius of the proton was measured surprisingly precisely at PSI.
Next to PSI is the innovation park Park Innovaare.

abschnitte.text: PSI lies on both sides of the Aare near **Villigen** and Würenlingen in the canton of Aargau. It was formed in 1988 from two older institutes, the Federal Institute for Reactor Research (EIR) and the Swiss Institute for Nuclear Research (SIN). PSI belongs to the **ETH Domain**, together with ETH Zurich and EPFL in Lausanne. It employs more than 2,000 people (as of the 2020s).

Paul Scherrer (1890 to 1969) was a well-known Swiss physicist and professor at ETH Zurich. In 1916, together with Peter Debye, he developed the **Debye-Scherrer method**, which uses X-rays to study how the atoms in a powder are arranged. He did a great deal for nuclear physics in Switzerland. That is why the new institute was named after him.

The centrepiece is a proton accelerator with a large **ring cyclotron**, which brings protons up to 590 MeV. It is used to produce neutrons in the **SINQ** source and muons for experiments. The Swiss Light Source (SLS) supplies extremely bright X-ray light, and the X-ray laser SwissFEL makes lightning-fast processes visible. Researchers from all over the world come here to use measuring time on these installations.

Since 1984 tumours in the eye have been treated at PSI with **proton therapy**. Protons release their energy very precisely at a certain depth and spare the healthy tissue. **Spot scanning** was developed at PSI; in it, a fine proton beam scans the tumour point by point. Today this technique is used all over the world, and children are also treated at PSI.

In 2010 researchers at PSI used muonic hydrogen to measure the **radius of the proton** and found a smaller value than expected. This triggered new measurements and discussions worldwide. PSI also researches batteries, solar fuels, safe energy and new materials for computers. In the neighbouring Park Innovaare, companies and researchers work closely together.

At the **psi forum** visitor centre, school classes and families can experience how research at PSI works. In the iLab student laboratory, young people carry out their own experiments. The aim is to awaken enthusiasm for science and technology.

begriffe.erklaerung: An installation that makes tiny particles very fast.
An accelerator in which particles get faster and faster on a spiral path.
A cancer treatment in which protons destroy the tumour.
An uncharged particle in the atomic nucleus.
Invisible rays with which you can look inside materials.

gewusst: The Swiss Light Source is a ring almost 300 metres round that looks like a giant doughnut.
PSI's ring cyclotron is one of the most powerful proton accelerators in the world.

teile.einleitung: An oscilloscope is a measuring instrument that makes electrical voltages visible as a curve on a screen. With it you can see how a signal changes in fractions of a second. For experts in electronics it is as important as a stethoscope is for a doctor.
wichtigste: On the vertical axis the oscilloscope shows voltage, on the horizontal axis time.
The trigger makes a periodic signal appear as a still image.
The frequency is calculated from the width of one period and the timebase.
A usual 10:1 probe reduces the measured signal by a factor of 10.
Classic analogue oscilloscopes had a cathode-ray tube at their heart.
In XY mode, two sine signals produce Lissajous figures.
The bandwidth shows at what frequency a sine wave is displayed attenuated by 3 dB.

abschnitte.text: The oscilloscope draws a graph in real time. **Voltage** is shown vertically, and **time** runs horizontally. The screen is divided into squares, the divisions. With knobs you set how many volts and how many milliseconds one division stands for.

If one period is 4 divisions wide and the **timebase** is set to 5 ms per division, it lasts 20 ms. That gives a frequency of 50 Hz, exactly the frequency of our power grid. If a sine wave is 6 divisions high from peak to peak at 2 V per division, it measures 12 V peak to peak. The **amplitude**, the height from the middle to the peak, is then 6 V.

Without help, the curve would race across the screen and flicker. The **trigger** always starts recording at the same point in the signal, for example when the voltage passes a certain level. As a result all the sweeps lie exactly on top of each other. In this way a repeating signal appears as a calm, still image.

Early oscilloscopes used a **cathode-ray tube**, which Karl Ferdinand Braun had invented in 1897. In it, the measured voltage deflects a beam of electrons that draws a trace on a glowing screen. Today most devices are **digital storage oscilloscopes**. They convert the signal into numbers, store it and display it on a flat screen.

The signal enters the device via a **probe**. A usual 10:1 probe reduces it by a factor of 10 and so disturbs the circuit being measured less. The **bandwidth** shows how fast a signal the device can still display correctly. At this frequency a sine wave is already shown attenuated by 3 dB, that is, to about 70 per cent.

begriffe.erklaerung: Setting for how much time one horizontal square represents.
Release that always starts recording at the same point in the signal.
Greatest deflection of an oscillation from the centre line.
Measuring tip with a cable that carries the signal to the oscilloscope.
Looping pattern that appears when two oscillations are plotted against each other.

gewusst: Old televisions worked with the same tube technology as early oscilloscopes.
With Lissajous figures you can compare two frequencies without doing any sums.
Good modern oscilloscopes can record billions of measured values per second.

teile.einleitung: In a parallel circuit, electrical devices are connected side by side so that the current divides between several paths. Each device is connected directly to the same voltage source. This is how almost all the lamps and sockets in your home are connected.
wichtigste: In a parallel circuit the same voltage is across all branches.
The total current is the sum of the currents in the individual branches.
The total resistance is always smaller than the smallest individual resistance.
Two resistors of 10 ohms each give 5 ohms in parallel.
If one lamp blows, the others keep shining.
In the household, appliances are connected in parallel so that each gets the full voltage.
Kirchhoff's current law describes how the currents divide.

abschnitte.text: In a **parallel circuit** there are several current paths lying side by side. You can imagine it like a road that divides into several lanes and later joins up again. The points where the wires split or join are called **nodes**. Each path between two nodes is a **branch**.

Exactly the same **voltage** is across each branch, namely that of the source. The current, on the other hand, divides. If 2 amperes flow through one branch and 3 amperes through the other, 5 amperes flow in total. This is described by **Kirchhoff's current law**: what flows into a node must also flow out again.

In parallel circuits you add the reciprocals of the resistances: 1 over R total equals 1 over R1 plus 1 over R2. For 6 ohms and 3 ohms this gives 1/6 plus 2/6, that is 3/6, and the **total resistance** is 2 ohms. Each extra branch is another path for the current. That is why the total resistance gets smaller the more resistors you add in parallel.

Sockets, lamps and appliances in a flat are connected in parallel. In Switzerland each appliance therefore gets the full 230 volts. You can switch each one on and off individually without disturbing the others. But because the total current grows with each appliance, a **fuse** protects the wires from overloading.

If one lamp fails in a parallel circuit, the others keep shining, because their current path is not broken. This is practical for Christmas lights and street lamps. A disadvantage is that many appliances together draw a large current. If you plug too many powerful appliances into a multi-socket adaptor, the fuse can trip.

begriffe.erklaerung: A single current path in a parallel circuit.
Point at which wires split or join.
How strongly a component slows down the current, measured in ohms.
Rule that as much current flows into a node as flows out of it.

gewusst: If you connect many identical resistors in parallel, the resistance is divided by their number.
Your body also has many parallel paths: blood vessels branch in a similar way to current branches.
Gustav Robert Kirchhoff formulated his rules as early as 1845, while still a student.

teile.einleitung: The central processing unit, CPU for short, is the calculating centre of a computer. It carries out the instructions of all programs, from games to word processing. It is often called the “brain” of the computer.
wichtigste: CPU stands for central processing unit, “Hauptprozessor” in German.
The processor carries out the instructions of the programs.
Billions of tiny switches, the transistors, work in a modern processor.
The clock speed is given in gigahertz.
A quad-core processor has four processing units that can work at the same time.
The cache is a very fast buffer memory directly inside the processor.
Processors are made mainly of silicon and need cooling.

abschnitte.text: Every program consists of many simple **instructions**, for example “add two numbers” or “store this value”. The central processor fetches these instructions from the working memory and carries them out one after another. This happens incredibly fast, billions of times per second. The processor works closely with the **working memory** and the graphics card. Without a processor, a computer could do nothing at all.

A processor works in a fixed rhythm, the **clock**. The clock speed is measured in gigahertz; one gigahertz means a billion clock cycles per second. Modern processors have several **cores**, that is, several processing units on one chip. A quad-core processor can work on four tasks at the same time. This helps, for example, when you listen to music, surf the web and load a game at the same time.

A processor is a **computer chip** made of silicon. On it there are billions of tiny electronic switches, the **transistors**. They can only have two states, on or off, that is, one or zero. From many such switches, arithmetic units, control units and memory are built. The **cache** is an especially fast buffer memory directly inside the processor, where frequently used data is kept ready.

When calculating, a processor produces a lot of **heat**. That is why there is usually a metal heat sink with a fan on top of it. Thermal paste goes between the processor and the cooler so that the heat can flow away well. If a processor gets too hot, it slows itself down to avoid damage. Mobile phones have no fan; their processors are built to be especially economical.

In 1971 the company Intel brought out the **Intel 4004**, one of the first microprocessors. It had only about 2,300 transistors; today's processors have billions. Most processors for Windows PCs come from **Intel** and **AMD**. Mobile phones and many Apple computers contain processors with the economical ARM design. Today small processors also work in cars, washing machines and coffee machines.

begriffe.erklaerung: Abbreviation for central processing unit.
A tiny electronic switch.
How many working steps per second the processor manages.
A processing unit in the processor that can work independently.
A very fast buffer memory in the processor.

gewusst: The transistors in modern processors are so small that thousands would fit side by side across the thickness of a hair.
The first microprocessor of 1971 was originally intended for a desktop calculator from Japan.
A mobile phone today has more computing power than the computers used to control the Moon landing in 1969.

teile.einleitung: In a series circuit, electrical components are connected one after another, like beads on a necklace. The current has only one single path and must flow through all the components in turn. You know this circuit from batteries in torches and from old strings of fairy lights.
wichtigste: In a series circuit the current is the same everywhere.
The partial voltages across the components add up to the total voltage.
The total resistance is the sum of the individual resistances.
10 ohms and 30 ohms in series give 40 ohms.
Three 1.5-volt batteries in series supply 4.5 volts.
If one lamp blows, all the lamps go out.
Two identical lamps in series shine less brightly than a single lamp.

abschnitte.text: In a **series circuit** all the components are connected one after another in a single circuit. There are no branches. The current flows from the source through the first component, then through the second and so on, until it gets back to the source. It is also called a **series connection**.

Because there is only one path, the **current** is the same at every point. The **voltage**, on the other hand, is shared between the components, and the partial voltages add up to the total voltage. So two identical lamps on 12 volts each get 6 volts. That is why they both shine less brightly than a single lamp on the same battery.

You get the **total resistance** by adding up all the resistances. So 20 ohms and 40 ohms give 60 ohms. If they are connected to 12 volts, according to **Ohm's law** a current of 12 volts divided by 60 ohms flows, that is 0.2 amperes. Each extra resistor makes the total resistance larger and the current smaller.

If you put batteries one after another, positive terminal to negative terminal, their voltages add up. Three 1.5-volt batteries give 4.5 volts this way. That is why many torches and toys have several batteries in a row. A car battery also consists inside of six **cells** of about 2 volts each, connected in series.

One disadvantage of the series circuit is: if one component fails, the whole circuit is **broken**. With old strings of fairy lights you therefore had to check every bulb to find the broken one. One advantage is that series circuits can be used to divide or increase voltages. A **switch** is also always connected in series with the lamp so that it can open the circuit.

begriffe.erklaerung: Closed path along which electric current flows.
What drives the current, measured in volts.
How much electricity flows, measured in amperes.
Rule: current equals voltage divided by resistance.

gewusst: A light switch is always connected in series; otherwise it could not switch the lamp off.
In electric cars, hundreds of small battery cells are combined in series and in parallel.
A fuse is also connected in series so that it breaks the whole circuit if too much current flows.

teile.einleitung: A paddle steamer is a ship driven by large paddle wheels. A steam engine in the belly of the ship turns these wheels. Magnificent paddle steamers from around 1900 still sail on Swiss lakes today.
wichtigste: Paddle steamers are driven by large paddle wheels.
A steam engine turns the wheels.
The steam is produced from heated water.
On Swiss paddle steamers the paddle wheels are at the sides of the ship.
Five paddle steamers sail on Lake Lucerne today.
One of them is called Schiller, after the poet Friedrich Schiller.
On Lake Geneva a fleet of beautiful paddle ships from the Belle Époque sails.

abschnitte.text: Water is heated in the boiler, in the past with coal, today often with oil. The **steam** produced is under high pressure and pushes pistons back and forth in the **steam engine**. Via a crankshaft they turn the **paddle wheels**. The paddles dip into the water and push the ship forwards like a paddle.

In 1807 the American Robert Fulton ran one of the first successful steamships on the Hudson River. Soon afterwards paddle steamers were sailing on rivers and lakes in Europe. In 1823 the “Guillaume Tell” became the first steamship in Switzerland, on **Lake Geneva**. At sea, paddle steamers were later replaced by ships with a **propeller**, because these work better in rough water.

Five paddle steamers sail on **Lake Lucerne** today: Uri, Unterwalden, Schiller, Gallia and Stadt Luzern. The Uri of 1901 is the oldest of them. The Schiller bears the name of the poet Friedrich Schiller, who wrote the play “William Tell”. The ships are lovingly cared for and overhauled in the shipyard in winter.

On **Lake Geneva** a whole fleet of paddle ships from the **Belle Époque**, the period around 1900, sails. Paddle steamers also run on Lake Zurich, Lake Thun and Lake Brienz. Altogether Switzerland has one of the largest paddle steamer fleets in the world. Many of the ships are listed historic monuments.

On many Swiss paddle steamers the **engine room** is open and can be seen through glass or over a railing. Passengers can watch the gleaming pistons and rods at work. It often smells of warm oil and steam. On departure the steam whistle sounds, and you can feel the steady pounding of the engine.

begriffe.erklaerung: Large wheel with paddles that pushes the ship through the water.
Machine that moves pistons with steam pressure.
The “beautiful era” around 1900 with magnificent architecture.
Screw under the water that drives most ships today.

gewusst: The paddle wheels of Swiss lake steamers are often hidden in semicircular paddle boxes that are beautifully decorated.
To go backwards, the engineer simply runs the steam engine, and therefore the paddle wheels, the other way round.
On the Mississippi in the USA, many paddle steamers have their paddle wheel at the back, on the stern.

teile.einleitung: A ball bearing is a small but incredibly important machine part. In it, smooth steel balls roll between two rings and make sure that wheels and shafts turn with almost no resistance. Without ball bearings there would be no smooth-running bicycles, skateboards or electric motors.
wichtigste: A ball bearing reduces friction on turning shafts.
Instead of sliding friction, a ball bearing has much smaller rolling friction.
Ball bearings belong to the group of rolling bearings.
The cage keeps the balls evenly spaced.
In 1869 the Paris bicycle mechanic Jules Suriray received an early patent for a ball bearing.
In a bicycle, ball bearings are found, for example, in the wheel hubs.
Grease in the bearing reduces friction and wear.

abschnitte.text: A ball bearing consists of an **inner ring**, an **outer ring** and many balls in between. The inner ring sits on the turning shaft, and the outer ring is fixed in the housing. The balls roll in grooves between the two rings. A **cage** made of sheet metal or plastic keeps them evenly spaced so that they do not touch each other.

When two surfaces slide over each other, there is a lot of friction and things get hot. When something rolls, on the other hand, the resistance is much smaller. The ball bearing makes use of this difference between **sliding friction** and **rolling friction**. You know this from everyday life: you struggle to push a heavy box, but on castors it moves almost by itself.

Ball bearings belong to the **rolling bearings**, that is, bearings with rolling parts. The most common is the deep groove ball bearing. A **thrust bearing** takes mainly forces along the direction of the shaft, a radial bearing forces across it. Instead of balls, small cylinders can also roll; this is called a cylindrical roller bearing, which can carry larger loads.

Around 1500 Leonardo da Vinci already drew ideas for bearings with balls. In 1869 the Paris bicycle mechanic **Jules Suriray** received a patent for a ball bearing on a bicycle. After that it became important to make balls perfectly round in large numbers. At the end of the 19th century ball grinding machines were developed for this, for example in Schweinfurt in Germany.

Ball bearings are found in bike hubs, bottom brackets, inline skates and skateboard wheels. Washing machines, fans, cars and trains also need them. In many Swiss automatic watches, the rotor turns on a tiny ball bearing. So that everything lasts a long time, the bearings are lubricated with grease and often protected from dirt with seals.

begriffe.erklaerung: The resistance that arises when two surfaces move against each other.
A turning rod in a machine that passes on power.
A bearing in which balls or rollers roll between two rings.
The wearing down of parts through use.

gewusst: The balls in good bearings are so round that they often deviate by less than a thousandth of a millimetre.
A fidget spinner only spins for so long because there is a ball bearing in its middle.

teile.einleitung: A crank is a lever fixed to an axle with which you turn something in a circle. It turns the force of your hand into rotation. Whether on a bicycle, a barrel organ or a winch: cranks are found in many machines, often quite unnoticed.
wichtigste: A crank turns a hand force or a back-and-forth movement into rotation.
The longer the crank arm, the less force you need, because the lever arm is bigger.
In return, with a long crank the hand has to move a longer distance.
On a bicycle, the arms the pedals are attached to are called cranks.
In a car engine, the crankshaft turns the up-and-down movement of the pistons into rotation.
Early cars were started at the front with a starting handle.

abschnitte.text: A crank consists of an **axle**, an arm and a handle at the end. When you turn the handle, your hand describes a circle and the axle turns with it. The crank is one of the oldest machines of humankind and a form of **lever**. As early as the Middle Ages, cranks were used to drive grindstones, well winches and spinning wheels.

The lever rule applies to the crank: force times lever arm stays the same. If the crank arm is twice as long, you need only half the force to turn the same axle. In return the hand travels further. A handle 0.5 metres from the axle covers a **circumference** of about 3.1 metres in one turn. That is why heavy winches often have especially long cranks.

On a bicycle the pedals sit on two **cranks** fixed opposite each other on the same axle. When one leg pushes down, the other pedal comes back up. The cranks turn the front chainring, and the chain passes the rotation on to the back wheel. On adult bicycles the cranks are usually about 17 centimetres long.

In a combustion engine the **pistons** move rapidly up and down. They are connected by connecting rods to the **crankshaft**, which is set turning as a result. In this way a straight movement becomes a rotation, which drives the wheels via the gearbox. On the first cars you had to insert a starting handle at the front and turn it hard to start the engine. Later the electric starter motor replaced this tiring and sometimes dangerous job.

A **barrel organ** plays music when you turn its crank, because this pumps air into the pipes and plays the tune. On a **winch**, the crank winds up a rope to pull or lift heavy loads. Windows in old cars, sun blinds, hand-turned coffee mills and pencil sharpeners also work with cranks. There are even torches and radios that you charge with a crank.

begriffe.erklaerung: An arm on an axle with which you turn something in a circle.
The distance between the axle and the point where you push or pull.
A bent shaft in the engine that turns the movement of the pistons into rotation.
The arm on a bicycle to which the pedal is screwed.
A drum onto which a rope is wound to pull loads.

gewusst: On some old cars the starting handle could kick back when starting and injure the driver's arm.
A barrel organ needs no electricity either, just a person turning the crank evenly.
Even an ordinary key in a lock works a little like a small crank when you turn it.

teile.einleitung: The Grande Dixence is a huge dam in the canton of Valais and, at 285 metres, the highest gravity dam in the world. Behind it lies the reservoir Lac des Dix, whose water produces electricity in power stations. The installation is one of the most important hydropower plants in Switzerland.
wichtigste: The Grande Dixence stands in the canton of Valais at the end of the Val des Dix.
Behind the dam lies the reservoir Lac des Dix.
The highest water level is at about 2,360 metres above sea level.
The dam is made of concrete and is 285 metres high.
As a gravity dam, it holds back the water by its own enormous weight.
Part of the water is pumped here from valleys as far away as near Zermatt.
In 2019 the Bieudron power station produced more electricity than any other Swiss hydropower station.

abschnitte.text: The Grande Dixence lies high up in the **Val des Dix**, a side valley of the Val d'Hérens in the canton of **Valais**. It is not far to the next larger valley and to Sion, but all around there are glaciers and peaks over 3,000 metres. Behind the dam stretches the reservoir **Lac des Dix**, whose water level when the lake is full is at about 2,360 metres above sea level. In summer you can take a small cable car up to the top of the dam and walk along the lake.

The dam was built in the 1950s and completed in 1961. It is 285 metres high, almost as high as the Eiffel Tower, and consists of about 6 million cubic metres of **concrete**. As a **gravity dam**, it holds back the water pressure purely by its enormous weight, which is why it is very wide at the bottom. Inside there are passages in which experts regularly check the dam.

The reservoir holds about 400 million cubic metres of water. It comes mainly from the **meltwater** of glaciers, which flows plentifully in summer. Because its own valley does not supply enough, tunnels collect water from neighbouring valleys. With **pumping stations**, water is even carried up from the area near Zermatt and through the mountains to the Lac des Dix.

In winter, when a lot of electricity is needed, the water flows down through steep **penstocks** into the Rhône valley. There it drives turbines in power stations such as Fionnay, Nendaz and **Bieudron**, which turn generators. Bieudron uses a head of almost 1,900 metres, which was a world record when it opened in 1998. After an accident in 2000 it stood still for about ten years, but in 2019 it produced more electricity than any other Swiss hydropower station.

In Switzerland hydropower supplies about half to almost two thirds of the electricity. Storage lakes such as the Lac des Dix are especially valuable because they collect water in summer and supply the electricity only in winter. That is why they are also called the **batteries of the Alps**. Because of **glacier retreat**, the amount of meltwater the installations receive will change in future.

begriffe.erklaerung: Wall that blocks a valley and holds water back to form a lake.
Dam that holds back the water purely by its weight.
Reservoir that collects water to produce electricity later.
Thick pipe in which water flows steeply down to the turbines.
Wheel that is turned by water and drives a generator.

gewusst: More concrete went into the Grande Dixence than stone into the Pyramid of Cheops.
During construction, over a thousand workers lived in their own settlement high up in the valley.
In spring the Lac des Dix is often almost empty and only fills with glacier water in summer.

teile.einleitung: Louis Chevrolet was a Swiss racing driver and car designer after whom one of the best-known car brands in the world is named. He was born in La Chaux-de-Fonds in 1878 and made his career in the USA. His story shows how a watchmaker's son from the Jura became a car pioneer.
wichtigste: Louis Chevrolet was born in La Chaux-de-Fonds in the canton of Neuchâtel in 1878.
His father was a watchmaker.
In 1886 the family moved to France.
In the USA he first became known as a successful racing driver.
In 1911 he founded a car company in Detroit with William Durant.
An SBB Intercity tilting train bears his name.

abschnitte.text: Louis Chevrolet was born on 25 December 1878 in **La Chaux-de-Fonds**, a watchmaking town in the Neuchâtel Jura. His father was a **watchmaker**. Because the family had little money, they moved in 1886 to France, to the area around Beaune in Burgundy. There young Louis worked in a bicycle workshop and soon became interested in engines.

Around 1900 Louis emigrated to North America. In the USA he worked as a mechanic and quickly became known as a daring **racing driver**. He set speed records and raced for the Buick company. His brothers Arthur and Gaston also became racing drivers.

On 3 November 1911 Louis Chevrolet founded the Chevrolet Motor Car Company in Detroit with the businessman **William Durant**. Louis designed the first cars, but he and Durant often disagreed about what kind of cars to make. Durant wanted cheap cars for many people, Louis preferred bigger and better ones. In 1915 Louis left the company, which later became part of **General Motors**. The Chevrolet brand still bears his name today.

After leaving, Louis founded the racing car company **Frontenac** with his brothers. In one of their cars, his brother Gaston won the famous 500-mile race at **Indianapolis** in 1920. Shortly afterwards Gaston died in a racing accident. Louis himself never became rich; he died in Detroit on 6 June 1941.

In Switzerland people like to remember the famous son of La Chaux-de-Fonds. The SBB named one of its **Intercity tilting trains** “Louis Chevrolet”. In his home town there are memorial plaques and exhibitions about him. The Chevrolet brand with its bow-tie logo is known all over the world, but few people know that the man it is named after was Swiss.

begriffe.erklaerung: Someone who developed important things in the early days of the car.
A craftsman who makes and repairs watches and clocks.
To leave your home country to live in another country.
A train that leans to the side on bends and can therefore travel faster.

gewusst: A few years after it was founded, the Chevrolet company became part of General Motors, one of the largest car groups in the world.
Louis Chevrolet sold his shares in his own company and earned hardly anything from its later success.
La Chaux-de-Fonds, the watchmaking town where he was born, is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

teile.einleitung: ITER is a huge experimental reactor meant to show that energy can be obtained from nuclear fusion. In it, atomic nuclei are to fuse together, as happens in the sun. It is being built in Cadarache in southern France by several countries together.
wichtigste: ITER is an international experimental reactor for nuclear fusion.
It is being built in Cadarache in southern France.
Seven equal partners are involved, including the EU, China, India, Japan, South Korea, Russia and the USA.
The ITER agreement was signed in Paris in 2006.
ITER is meant to produce ten times more fusion power than is put in for heating.
The Latin word “iter” means “the way”.
According to the 2024 schedule, experiments with deuterium and tritium are planned from 2039.

abschnitte.text: In the sun, light atomic nuclei fuse into heavier ones, releasing a lot of energy. This process is called **nuclear fusion**. ITER is meant to fuse nuclei of **deuterium** and **tritium**, two kinds of hydrogen. To do this they have to be heated to well over 100 million degrees, much hotter than inside the sun. At this heat the gas becomes a **plasma**.

No material can withstand such hot plasma. That is why in ITER it is held suspended by strong **magnetic fields**. The installation has the shape of a ring and is called a **tokamak**. The large toroidal field coils are made of the superconductor niobium tin and are cooled almost to absolute zero. The plasma is to have a volume of about 840 cubic metres.

ITER is meant, for the first time, to obtain more energy from fusion than is put in for heating. The goal is a **gain factor Q** of 10. This means that 50 megawatts of heating power should become 500 megawatts of fusion power. ITER is not yet meant to supply electricity to the grid. It is an experiment that should pave the way for later **fusion power stations**.

The agreement for ITER was signed in Paris in 2006. Seven partners work together as equals: the **European Union**, China, India, Japan, South Korea, Russia and the USA. The components are made in many countries and brought to southern France. Construction is taking much longer and costing much more than originally planned. According to the 2024 schedule, experiments with deuterium and tritium are to begin from 2039.

Deuterium can be obtained from ordinary seawater. Tritium hardly occurs in nature. In future fusion power stations, it is therefore to be bred from **lithium** in a layer around the plasma, the **blanket**. Fusion produces no CO2 and no long-lived radioactive waste like nuclear fission. In Switzerland, the Swiss Plasma Center of EPFL in Lausanne researches fusion with its own tokamak.

begriffe.erklaerung: The fusing of light atomic nuclei, which releases energy.
Extremely hot gas in which atoms break up into nuclei and electrons.
A ring-shaped installation that holds plasma in place with magnetic fields.
A material that, when cooled, conducts electricity without any resistance.
A special, heavy form of hydrogen.

gewusst: The plasma in ITER is to become about ten times hotter than the core of the sun.
Just a few metres away from the plasma at over 100 million degrees, the magnet coils are almost as cold as outer space.
A single gram of fusion fuel could supply as much energy as several tonnes of coal.

teile.einleitung: Power-to-gas means turning electricity into gas. Surplus electricity is used to split water and produce hydrogen or methane. In this way energy from the sun and hydropower can be stored and used later.
wichtigste: The first step is the electrolysis of water into hydrogen and oxygen.
In the Sabatier reaction, methane is produced from hydrogen and CO₂.
Synthetic methane can be fed into the gas grid without any adjustments.
Hydrogen is called “green” when it is produced with renewable electricity.
On the way from electricity to gas and back to electricity, about 60 to 70 per cent of the energy is lost.
PEM stands for proton exchange membrane.
At the Gösgen hydropower station, Hydrospider has been producing hydrogen for lorries since around 2020.

abschnitte.text: Wind and sun do not always supply electricity when it is needed. **Power-to-gas** converts surplus electricity into a gas that can easily be stored and transported. This gas can later supply electricity, heat or fuel again. That is why it is called an **energy store**.

In the first step, electricity splits water into **hydrogen** and oxygen; this is called **electrolysis**. A widespread type of device is the PEM electrolyser, named after its proton exchange membrane. If the electricity comes from renewable sources, it is called **green hydrogen**. Hydrogen can be used directly in fuel cell vehicles.

Hydrogen cannot simply be mixed into any gas grid. That is why it can be converted with carbon dioxide into **methane**, the main component of natural gas. This conversion is called the **Sabatier reaction**, after the French chemist Paul Sabatier. The synthetic methane fits into the existing gas grid without any adjustments.

In Switzerland there is often more electricity from hydropower and the sun in summer than is needed. In winter, on the other hand, electricity is short. Power-to-gas could store **summer surpluses** as gas for the winter. One example is Hydrospider's plant at the **Gösgen hydropower station** with 2 MW of electrolysis capacity, whose hydrogen powers lorries.

The big advantage is that gas can be stored for months, which is hardly possible with batteries. One disadvantage is the **conversion losses**. On the way from electricity to gas and back to electricity, you get only about 30 to 40 per cent of the energy back. That is why power-to-gas is worthwhile mainly where there is no simpler solution, for example for lorries, industry or winter electricity.

begriffe.erklaerung: Splitting a substance such as water with the help of electricity.
The lightest gas, which can serve as an energy carrier.
Flammable gas, the main component of natural gas.
Chemical reaction that makes methane from hydrogen and CO₂.
Device that produces electricity from hydrogen and oxygen.

gewusst: Paul Sabatier received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1912.
When hydrogen is used in a fuel cell, the only exhaust is water.
A kilogram of hydrogen contains almost three times as much energy as a kilogram of petrol.

teile.einleitung: Space travel means travelling and doing research outside the Earth's atmosphere in space, with rockets, satellites, space probes and space stations. Since 1957 people have been sending devices into space, and since 1961 people themselves have been flying there too. Switzerland takes part in many space missions.
wichtigste: In 1957 Sputnik 1 was the first artificial satellite to orbit the Earth.
In 1961 Yuri Gagarin was the first person to fly into space.
In 1969, with Apollo 11, people landed on the Moon for the first time.
Rockets fly by the principle of recoil, even in empty space.
In 1992 Claude Nicollier was the first Swiss person to fly into space.
The University of Bern built the solar wind sail that was set up on the Moon during Apollo 11.
Switzerland is a founding member of the European Space Agency ESA.

abschnitte.text: A **rocket** burns fuel and pushes hot gases out backwards with great force. This pushes it forwards; this is the **principle of recoil**. It works even in empty space, because the rocket does not need to push against the air. You can compare it with a blown-up balloon that whizzes away when you let go. To orbit the Earth, a spacecraft needs about 28,000 kilometres per hour.
