On 4 October 1957 the Soviet Union sent **Sputnik 1** into space, the first artificial satellite. On 12 April 1961 **Yuri Gagarin** became the first person to fly into space, circling the Earth once. The USA responded with the Apollo programme. On 20 July 1969 Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin became the first people to walk on the Moon. By 1972 a total of twelve people had been on the Moon.

The University of Bern built the **solar wind sail** that was set up on the Moon during Apollo 11 in 1969. It caught tiny particles from the sun and was the first experiment the astronauts set up on the Moon. In 1992 **Claude Nicollier** became the first Swiss person to fly into space, and he went into space four times in all. On one mission he also helped to repair the Hubble Space Telescope. Switzerland is a founding member of **ESA**, the European Space Agency.

Thousands of **satellites** orbit the Earth today. They transmit television and telephone calls, take weather pictures and help with navigation by GPS. Space probes fly to other planets, for example the Voyager probes, which have been travelling since 1977. Rovers drive on Mars and examine rocks. Many devices contain parts from Swiss companies and universities.

Since November 2000 people have been living permanently on the **International Space Station ISS**. It orbits the Earth at a height of about 400 kilometres, roughly every 90 minutes. In **weightlessness** the astronauts float, and even water drops form balls. The astronauts carry out research there and do sport every day so that their muscles do not get weak. With the Artemis programme, the USA and its partners want to bring people to the Moon again.

begriffe.erklaerung: Device that orbits the Earth or another heavenly body in space.
Something is pushed forwards because it pushes gas out backwards.
State in which you float in space.
Uncrewed spacecraft that flies into space to other heavenly bodies.
European Space Agency, of which Switzerland is a member.

gewusst: The University of Bern's solar wind sail was even set up before the American flag.
On the ISS the astronauts see about 16 sunrises every day.
Sputnik 1 was only about the size of a beach ball and sent beeping sounds to Earth.

teile.einleitung: Information theory is a field of mathematics that studies how information can be measured, compressed and transmitted reliably. It was founded in 1948 by the American Claude Shannon. Without it, there would be no internet, no mobile phones and no streamed videos in their present form.
wichtigste: Claude Shannon founded information theory in 1948 with the paper A Mathematical Theory of Communication.
Information is measured in bits.
A fair coin toss has an entropy of 1 bit; a coin that always shows heads has 0 bits.
An event with a probability of 1/8 provides 3 bits of information.
For one of 26 equally likely characters you need about 4.7 bits.
Redundancy is the part of a message that is not needed for its content.
In channel coding, redundancy is added deliberately in order to detect and correct transmission errors.
The Shannon-Hartley formula C = B · log2(1 + S/N) gives the most a channel can transmit.

abschnitte.text: **Claude Shannon** (1916 to 2001) was an American mathematician and engineer. He worked at Bell Laboratories, the research laboratory of a large telephone company. In 1948 he published the paper A Mathematical Theory of Communication. In it he described exactly, for the first time, what information is mathematically.

The basic unit of information is the **bit**, the answer to a yes-or-no question. The less likely an event is, the more information it contains. An event with a probability of 1/8 provides 3 bits, because you need three yes-or-no questions to guess one of 8 results. A message that you already know for certain beforehand, on the other hand, contains no new information.

**Entropy** tells you how much information a source provides on average. A fair coin toss has exactly 1 bit; a coin with two heads has 0 bits, because the result is always clear. With 26 equally likely letters it is about 4.7 bits per character. In real texts, however, some letters such as E occur much more often, so the entropy is lower.

Many messages contain **redundancy**, that is, parts that are not needed for the content. That is why you can often still read a sentence when some letters are missing. In source coding, redundancy is removed so that files become smaller, as with ZIP files. Morse code already used this idea, because the frequent E consists of just a single short tone.

When transmitting by radio or cable, noise causes errors. That is why in **channel coding** redundancy is added deliberately, for example check digits. In this way the receiver can recognise errors and often even correct them. That is why a QR code can still be read when part of it is dirty.

Shannon showed that every transmission path has a highest possible data rate, the **channel capacity**. The Shannon-Hartley formula calculates it from the bandwidth and the ratio of signal to noise. So more bandwidth or a stronger signal allows more data per second. Engineers still use this limit today when building mobile networks, Wi-Fi and fibre-optic networks.

begriffe.erklaerung: Smallest unit of information, a yes-or-no answer or a 0 or 1.
Measure of how much information a source provides on average.
Part of a message that is not strictly needed for the content.
Random disturbances that distort a signal.
The largest amount of data a transmission path can manage per second.

gewusst: In his spare time Claude Shannon built a mechanical mouse that could learn its own way through a maze.
Because language has a lot of redundancy, you can often understand a text even when many letters are missing.
Every mobile phone call and every streaming video uses error correction based on the ideas of information theory.

teile.einleitung: Mobile communications is the technology with which mobile phones make calls, send messages and go online using radio waves. A dense network of aerials makes sure you can be reached almost everywhere, even on a moving train. Since the first car phones, mobile communications has developed enormously through several generations from 1G to 5G.
wichtigste: Mobile phones are connected to the mobile network via base stations.
With handover, a call is passed to the next radio cell.
SIM stands for subscriber identity module.
The SMS was introduced with the second-generation GSM standard.
The first SMS was sent in 1992 and read “Merry Christmas”.
4G refers to the LTE standard.
Roaming means that the phone uses another company's network abroad.
The emergency number 112 works throughout Europe, also from a mobile phone.

abschnitte.text: A mobile network is divided into many small areas called **radio cells**. Each cell has a **base station** with aerials, often on roofs or masts. Your phone talks by radio to the nearest base station, and from there the call usually continues by cable. In cities the aerials stand close together, because many people are making calls at the same time there.

When you make a call on a train, you keep leaving one radio cell and entering the next. With **handover**, the network passes your call to the new cell in a flash without it dropping. Abroad, your phone uses another company's network through **roaming**. This can cost extra, so it is worth checking your contract before the holidays.

The first generation (1G) was analogue and was used mainly for car phones; in Switzerland it was called Natel. With **GSM** around 1990 came the second generation, digital and with SMS. Later came UMTS (3G), LTE (4G) for fast internet and 5G, which was introduced in Switzerland from 2019. Each generation brought more speed and room for more devices.

In 1973 the engineer **Martin Cooper** made the first call with a hand-held mobile phone in New York. On 3 December 1992 the first SMS was sent; it read “Merry Christmas”. At the time hardly anyone imagined that text messages would one day be so popular. Today the mobile network mainly carries data for apps, videos and messaging services.

In Switzerland it is mainly Swisscom, Sunrise and Salt that run their own mobile networks. For a phone to be allowed onto the network, it needs a **SIM card**, which identifies the customer. Switzerland has stricter radiation limits for aerials than many other countries. In an emergency you can get help on 112 even without credit.

begriffe.erklaerung: The area supplied by a single mobile phone aerial.
An aerial site through which mobile phones are connected to the network.
Passing a call on to the next radio cell.
Using another company's mobile network, usually abroad.
A small chip card that registers your phone with the network.

gewusst: Natel was originally an abbreviation for “Nationales Autotelefon” (national car telephone).
Many new phones have a built-in eSIM instead of a plastic card.

teile.einleitung: Artificial intelligence, AI for short, is a branch of computer science that has computers solve tasks that would otherwise need human intelligence. These include understanding language, recognising images, playing games or making decisions. Today AI is found in voice assistants, translation programs and chatbots.
wichtigste: AI has computers solve tasks that would otherwise require human thinking.
The term “artificial intelligence” was established as a field of research at the Dartmouth Conference in 1956.
In 1950 Alan Turing proposed a test of whether a machine can answer like a human.
In the mid-1960s Joseph Weizenbaum wrote the chat program ELIZA.
In 1997 the IBM computer Deep Blue defeated the world chess champion Garry Kasparov.
In 2016 DeepMind's program AlphaGo defeated the Go professional Lee Sedol.
Today's large language models are based on the transformer architecture from 2017.

abschnitte.text: Artificial intelligence refers to computer programs that recognise patterns, learn and solve problems. Many of today's AI systems learn from huge amounts of data instead of having every rule programmed into them; this is called **machine learning**. But an AI does not think like a human and has no feelings. It calculates which answer is most likely to fit. That is why it can also make mistakes that sound confident.

In 1950 the British mathematician **Alan Turing** proposed the **Turing test**. In it, a person is supposed to find out through a text conversation whether they are talking to a human or a machine. In 1956 the term “artificial intelligence” was established as a field of research at the Dartmouth Conference in the USA. In the mid-1960s Joseph Weizenbaum wrote the chat program ELIZA. Many people believed ELIZA really understood them, even though the program only followed simple rules.

In 1997 the IBM computer **Deep Blue** defeated the world chess champion Garry Kasparov in a match. To do so, Deep Blue calculated millions of moves per second. The board game Go was considered much more difficult for computers. In 2016 the program **AlphaGo** from the company DeepMind defeated the Go professional Lee Sedol. AlphaGo had previously learnt from millions of games and also played against itself.

In 2017 researchers presented the **transformer** architecture in the paper “Attention Is All You Need”. Today's large **language models**, which can write texts, answer questions and translate, are based on it. They were trained on huge amounts of text. Since about 2022 millions of people have been using such chatbots. But you should always check their answers critically, because they can be wrong too.

AI helps doctors recognise diseases on X-rays and researchers find new medicines. At the same time there are questions about **data protection**, fairness and fake images, so-called deepfakes. In 2024 the European Union adopted an **AI Act** that classifies AI systems by their risk. The more dangerous an application can be, the stricter the rules that apply. Switzerland is also discussing how it wants to regulate AI.

begriffe.erklaerung: An exact step-by-step set of instructions for a computer.
Test of whether a machine can be told apart from a human in conversation.
AI that has learnt to understand and write texts.
Image, video or audio faked with AI that seems real.

gewusst: In the board game Go there are more possible positions than there are atoms in the visible universe.
Weizenbaum was shocked at how seriously people took his simple program ELIZA, and he later became a critic of AI.
At ETH Zurich and EPFL in Lausanne there is intensive research into artificial intelligence.

teile.einleitung: A microprocessor is a tiny chip that, as the calculating centre of a computer, carries out all the instructions. It is also called a processor or CPU. It is found not only in computers and mobile phones but also in cars, washing machines and games consoles.
wichtigste: A microprocessor is the calculating centre of a computer on a single chip.
The Intel 4004 of 1971 is considered the first commercially available single-chip microprocessor.
Moore's law states that the number of transistors per chip doubles about every two years.
The arithmetic logic unit carries out calculations and comparisons.
The cache is a fast buffer memory for frequently needed data.
At 3 gigahertz, one clock cycle lasts about 0.33 nanoseconds.
RISC stands for reduced instruction set computer.

abschnitte.text: A microprocessor consists of billions of tiny **transistors**. The **arithmetic logic unit**, ALU for short, carries out calculations and comparisons. The control unit fetches the instructions and tells the other parts what to do. **Registers** briefly store the numbers that are being worked on at that moment. The cache serves as a fast buffer memory for frequently needed data.

A processor works to the rhythm of a **clock**. At a clock speed of 3 gigahertz there are three billion cycles per second. One clock cycle then lasts only about 0.33 nanoseconds. In this time light travels only about 10 centimetres. Modern processors have several **cores**, which work on different tasks at the same time.

The **Intel 4004** of 1971 is considered the first commercially available single-chip microprocessor. It had about 2,300 transistors and was developed for a desktop calculator. Gordon Moore predicted that the number of transistors per chip would double regularly. In its best-known form, this **Moore's law** says they double about every two years. Today top chips have many billions of transistors.

Most computers follow the **von Neumann architecture**, in which instructions and data are in the same memory. Processors differ in their instruction set. **RISC** stands for reduced instruction set computer, that is, computers with few, simple instructions. ARM processors in mobile phones follow this principle and use very little power. Many PCs, on the other hand, use the x86 architecture of Intel and AMD.

More cores do not automatically make a program as fast as you like. **Amdahl's law** describes how the part that cannot be parallelised limits the speed-up. If 90 per cent of a program can be parallelised, at most a 10-fold speed-up is possible with any number of cores. This is because the remaining 10 per cent must always run one step after another. That is why clever programming is also important for fast computers.

begriffe.erklaerung: Abbreviation for central processing unit.
How many working steps a processor makes per second.
Very fast small buffer memory in the processor.
Independent processing unit inside a processor.
All the instructions a processor understands.

gewusst: The Intel 4004 was only about the size of a fingernail and as powerful as the huge valve computer ENIAC.
A modern car often contains more than 50 small processors.
Processors get so warm when calculating that they need heat sinks or fans.

teile.einleitung: Nanotechnology is the science and technology of tiny structures only a few nanometres in size. A nanometre is a billionth of a metre, about 100,000 times thinner than a hair. In this world of atoms and molecules, substances often behave quite differently from how they behave on a large scale.
wichtigste: A nanometre is 10⁻⁹ metres, a billionth of a metre.
In 1959 Richard Feynman gave the famous lecture “There's Plenty of Room at the Bottom”.
In 1981 Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer developed the scanning tunnelling microscope at the IBM research laboratory in Rüschlikon.
The lotus effect is the self-cleaning of surfaces thanks to nanostructures.
Graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms.
The best-known fullerene consists of 60 carbon atoms and looks like a football.
Small particles have a very large surface area relative to their volume.

abschnitte.text: The word **nano** comes from the Greek word for dwarf. A **nanometre** is 10⁻⁹ metres, a billionth of a metre. A human hair is about 80,000 to 100,000 nanometres thick. An atom is about 0.1 to 0.3 nanometres in size. People usually speak of nanotechnology for structures between 1 and 100 nanometres.

In 1959 the physicist **Richard Feynman** gave the lecture “There's Plenty of Room at the Bottom”. In it he imagined building things atom by atom. In 1981 Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer at the IBM research laboratory in **Rüschlikon** on Lake Zurich developed the **scanning tunnelling microscope**. With it, individual atoms on a surface could be made visible for the first time. The two received the Nobel Prize in Physics for it in 1986.

If you divide a substance into tiny particles, the **surface area** grows a great deal. If you cut a cube with 1 cm edges into cubes with 1 mm edges, the total surface area grows by a factor of 10. With nanoparticles this effect is much greater still. That is why they often react more strongly with other substances. As nanoparticles, gold can even look red instead of golden yellow.

The best-known **fullerene** consists of 60 carbon atoms and looks like a football. **Graphene** is a single layer of carbon atoms arranged like honeycomb. It is extremely tear-resistant and conducts electricity very well. Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov received the Nobel Prize in Physics for graphene in 2010. Carbon nanotubes are rolled-up sheets of graphene.

abschnitte.titel: Nature as a model and everyday life
abschnitte.text: Lotus leaves stay clean because tiny bumps on their surface make water roll off and carry dirt away. This **lotus effect** is used for self-cleaning paints and glass. Nanoparticles are found in some sun creams, computer chips and medicines. Researchers are also investigating whether nanoparticles can be harmful to people and the environment. In Switzerland, ETH, EPFL and Empa, among others, carry out research in this field.

begriffe.erklaerung: A billionth of a metre.
Device with which individual atoms can be made visible.
A layer of carbon only one atom thick.
Ball-shaped molecule made of carbon atoms.
Self-cleaning of a surface thanks to tiny structures.

gewusst: Around 1990 IBM researchers wrote the company name IBM with 35 individual atoms.
A fingernail grows by about one nanometre per second.
As early as the Middle Ages, gold nanoparticles coloured church windows red without anyone knowing it.

teile.einleitung: The Pilatus Railway is the steepest rack railway in the world. It runs from Alpnachstad on Lake Lucerne up Mount Pilatus near Lucerne. Since 1889 it has carried visitors up the mountain with very special technology.
wichtigste: The Pilatus Railway reaches a maximum gradient of 48 per cent.
Its rack system was developed by the engineer Eduard Locher.
In the Locher system the cogwheels engage the rack from the sides.
The valley station is in Alpnachstad in the canton of Obwalden.
The railway climbs about 1,600 metres in height.
The track gauge is 800 mm.
The Pilatus Railway has run on electricity since 1937.

abschnitte.text: The **valley station** is in **Alpnachstad** in the canton of Obwalden, right on the shore of Lake Alpnach, part of Lake Lucerne. The line is about 4.6 kilometres long and leads through forests, over rocks and through tunnels up to Pilatus Kulm. On the way the railway climbs about 1,600 metres. The journey takes about half an hour.

On normal rack railways, a cogwheel engages a toothed rack from above. But on such a steep gradient the wheel could jump out. That is why the Zurich engineer **Eduard Locher** invented a rack with teeth on both sides. Two horizontally mounted **cogwheels** engage it from the sides and so hold the car securely.

The greatest **gradient** is 48 per cent. This means that over 100 metres of horizontal distance the railway rises by 48 metres. No other rack railway in the world is so steep. The narrow track gauge of 800 mm helps the railway to be built even along narrow rock faces.

The Pilatus Railway opened in 1889 and at first ran on **steam**. Since 1937 it has run on electricity, which is quieter, cleaner and faster. In the 2020s new, modern railcars came into service. In winter the line is usually closed because of snow and the danger of avalanches.

At the top, on **Pilatus Kulm**, there are hotels, restaurants and a wide view over the Alps and the Swiss Plateau. You can do a round trip: by boat to Alpnachstad, up by rack railway and down by cable cars to Kriens. An old legend tells of **dragons** said to have lived in the caves of Pilatus. That is why the dragon is still a symbol of the mountain today.

begriffe.erklaerung: Railway in which a cogwheel engages a toothed rack to climb steep stretches.
Rail with teeth between the running rails.
How steeply a line rises, given as a percentage.
Distance between the two rails.

gewusst: The Pilatus Railway is the only railway built with the Locher system.
The railway was built in only about three years, from 1886 to 1889.
Because the cars travel so steeply, their seating compartments are arranged one above the other like steps.

teile.einleitung: A hammer is a tool used mainly for knocking in nails. It consists of a heavy head and a handle you hold it by. The hammer is one of the oldest tools of humankind.
wichtigste: A hammer is used mainly for knocking in nails.
A hammer consists of the hammer head and the handle.
With the split side of a claw hammer you can pull nails out.
The rubber mallet has a soft head so that nothing gets scratched.
A sledgehammer is so heavy that you swing it with both hands.
The blacksmith strikes glowing iron with a hammer on an anvil.
When hammering, safety glasses protect your eyes from splinters.

abschnitte.text: A hammer has a heavy **head** made of steel and a **handle**, usually made of wood such as ash or of plastic. The flat striking surface on the head is called the face. On the other side there is often a narrow edge, the peen, or a split claw. The head sits firmly on the handle and is secured with a wedge.

The hammer uses **leverage**: the further back you hold the handle, the more swing the head gets. That is why you hold it at the end of the handle when you want to strike hard. On impact, the head passes all its energy of movement to the nail in a short time. This creates a large force that drives the nail into the wood.

There are hammers for almost every job. The **claw hammer** has a split claw at the back for pulling out nails. The **rubber mallet** is soft and is used, for example, when laying tiles. The heavy sledgehammer is used for knocking down walls, and geologists use a special hammer to split rocks.

The blacksmith heats iron in the fire until it glows and becomes soft. Then he lays it on the **anvil**, a heavy block of steel, and shapes it with powerful hammer blows. In the past, horseshoes, tools, knives and railings were made like this. In Switzerland, at the Ballenberg open-air museum, you can still watch old craftsmen at work.

When hammering you wear safety glasses, because splinters of wood, stone or metal can fly into your eye. At the start you hold the nail with two fingers and strike lightly at first. As soon as it is in, you take your fingers away. A hammer with a loose head is dangerous and must be repaired.

Even in the Stone Age, people struck stones against other stones, bones or nuts. Later they fixed stones to wooden handles; these were the first real hammers. With the age of metals, hammers made of bronze and iron appeared. Today there are also machines that work on the hammer principle, such as the **pneumatic drill** on building sites.

begriffe.erklaerung: Heavy block of steel on which the blacksmith works metal.
A long lever makes a movement more powerful or faster.
Split end of the hammer head for pulling out nails.
Short, heavy hammer used, for example, for striking a chisel.

gewusst: In the human ear there are three tiny bones, and one of them is called the hammer.
In Norse legend the god Thor owns a magic hammer called Mjölnir.
In the hammer throw in athletics, a metal ball on a wire is hurled.

teile.einleitung: The Industrial Revolution was a huge upheaval that began in Great Britain around 1760. Machines, factories and steam power gradually replaced work by hand. People's lives changed more than at any time since the invention of farming.
wichtigste: The Industrial Revolution began in Great Britain in the 18th century.
The cotton industry is considered the first leading sector of industrialisation.
Steam engines, coke and iron made new machines and structures possible.
In 1830 the railway line between Liverpool and Manchester opened.
Poverty, housing shortages and child labour were called the social question.
Early Swiss factories used mainly water power, because the country had hardly any coal.
The Swiss Federal Factory Act of 1877 introduced, among other things, the eleven-hour day.

abschnitte.text: The Industrial Revolution began in Great Britain, above all in the **cotton industry**. New spinning machines such as the spinning jenny and mechanical looms made yarn and cloth much faster than people could by hand. Instead of at home, people now worked in large **factories**. Great Britain had plenty of coal, iron ore, capital and a large sea trade. This made the country the pioneer.

In 1709 **Abraham Darby** in Coalbrookdale first used coke instead of charcoal to produce iron. This made it possible to make much more iron. In 1779 the **Iron Bridge** was built in Shropshire, the first large bridge made of cast iron. From 1769 James Watt made decisive improvements to the **steam engine**. Soon steam engines were driving pumps, looms and locomotives.

In 1830 the first intercity railway to run on a timetable with steam locomotives only was opened between **Liverpool and Manchester**. Railways carried goods and people much faster than horse-drawn carts. From England, industrialisation spread to Belgium, France, Germany and the USA. In Switzerland, the first railway running entirely within the country opened in 1847: the Spanisch-Brötli-Bahn from Zurich to Baden. The world moved closer together.

For many workers life was hard. They often worked 14 hours a day, and **children** also had to toil in factories. In the cities there were housing shortages, dirt and disease. These problems were called the **social question**. In 1845 Friedrich Engels described the hardship in his book “The Condition of the Working Class in England”.

Switzerland was one of the early industrial countries in Europe. Because there was hardly any coal, **water wheels** on rivers such as the Töss, Aabach or Limmat drove the first spinning mills. The textile industry was important, later engineering, watches and chemicals. As early as 1815 the Zurich government banned factory work for children under nine. The **Swiss Federal Factory Act** of 1877 brought the eleven-hour day and a ban on factory work for children under 14.

In the long run the Industrial Revolution brought more prosperity, better goods and new jobs. Workers joined together in **trade unions** and fought for better conditions. At the same time, humans began burning coal, and later oil, in large quantities. This is one cause of today's **climate change**. Our modern life with factories, trains and cities has its roots in this period.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large business in which goods are made with machines.
A fuel made from hard coal that burns very hot.
A branch of the economy that drives development.
The hardship of working people in the 19th century.
An association of employees that stands up for their rights.

gewusst: The Iron Bridge in England still stands today and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The Spanisch-Brötli-Bahn got its name from a pastry from Baden that could be brought quickly to Zurich on it.
Before there were factories, many families in eastern Switzerland spun and wove at home as cottage industry.

teile.einleitung: A pumped storage power station is a giant battery made of water. When there is plenty of spare electricity, it pumps water into a reservoir high up, and when a lot of electricity is needed, it lets the water flow back down through turbines. With its mountains and reservoirs, Switzerland is especially well suited to this.
wichtigste: A pumped storage power station is often called a water battery.
It needs at least two basins at different heights.
When a lot of electricity is needed, the water flows through the turbines.
Part of the energy is lost during pumping and in the turbines.
With more solar and wind power, pumped storage power stations are becoming more important.
Nant de Drance in Valais went into operation in 2022 and has an output of 900 megawatts.
The Linth-Limmern power station in the canton of Glarus uses the Muttsee as its upper basin.

abschnitte.text: A pumped storage power station consists of at least **two basins**, an upper and a lower one, connected by pipes or tunnels. Between them are machines that can pump water or produce electricity. Because it can store energy and release it again, it is also called a **water battery**. It stores the energy as the potential energy of the water pumped up.

When there is too much electricity in the grid, for example on sunny middays, the electricity drives large **pumps** that carry water upwards. When a lot of electricity is needed, for example in the evening, the water flows down and turns **turbines**, which produce electricity with generators. Switching over takes only a few minutes. In this way the power station helps to keep the grid in balance.

During pumping and generating, part of the energy is lost as friction and heat. So you get back only about three quarters to four fifths of the electricity put in. Even so, it is worthwhile, because electricity is worth different amounts at different times. For electricity from **sun and wind**, which varies with the weather, such storage is especially valuable.

The **Nant de Drance** pumped storage power station in the canton of Valais went fully into operation in 2022. It uses the two reservoirs Emosson and Vieux Emosson near the border with France. Its machines stand in a huge **cavern** deep inside the mountain. With an output of 900 megawatts it is one of the most powerful installations in Europe.

The **Linth-Limmern** pumped storage power station is in the canton of Glarus. Its upper basin is the Muttsee, whose dam stands at about 2,500 metres, and the lower one is Lake Limmern. There are also pumped storage power stations in the Grimsel area in the Bernese Oberland and in other places in the Alps. With them Switzerland can store electricity temporarily for its neighbouring countries.

begriffe.erklaerung: A wheel with blades that is turned by water and drives a generator.
A large, artificially excavated hollow in the rock.
A lake artificially held back by a dam.
Energy that something has because it is high up.

gewusst: The whole Nant de Drance power station is underground; from outside you only see the two reservoirs.
At about one kilometre, the Muttsee dam is one of the longest dams in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: A power loom is a machine that weaves cloth without a person having to put in every thread by hand. It was patented by Edmund Cartwright in 1785 and fundamentally changed the world of work. Its story tells of the beginning of industrialisation, but also of the hardship and protest of hand weavers.
wichtigste: In 1785 Edmund Cartwright patented a power-driven loom.
In 1733 John Kay invented the flying shuttle.
In weaving, warp threads cross with weft threads put in crosswise.
From 1811 the Luddites in England destroyed textile machines in protest.
In the Uster fire of 1832, home weavers in the Zurich Oberland set fire to a mechanical weaving mill.
Modern weaving machines such as the air-jet loom work without shuttles.

abschnitte.text: In weaving, many lengthwise threads are stretched side by side; this is the **warp**. Some of them are lifted, creating a gap called the shed. A crosswise thread, the **weft**, is passed through this shed. Then it is beaten into place, and the warp threads change position, so that a firm cloth is created.

For centuries weaving was done by hand, often at home in the living room. In 1733 John Kay invented the **flying shuttle**, with which the weft thread could be shot back and forth much faster. Because weavers now needed more yarn, there was a shortage of yarn, which led to the invention of spinning machines. In 1785 the English clergyman **Edmund Cartwright** patented a loom driven by a power source. Later steam engines and water wheels provided the energy.

The machines worked faster and more cheaply than the hand weavers, who lost their income as a result. In England, from 1811 the **Luddites** destroyed textile machines in protest. In Switzerland, in November 1832 home weavers set fire to the Corrodi und Pfister mechanical weaving mill in Uster; this event is called the **Uster fire**. In Silesia there was a weavers' uprising in 1844, which Gerhart Hauptmann later depicted in the play “The Weavers”.

At the beginning of the 19th century the Frenchman Joseph-Marie Jacquard developed a control system with **punched cards** that allowed patterns to be woven automatically. In the 1890s the Northrop loom changed the weft bobbin automatically, so that one person could look after many looms. In the 20th century shuttleless machines appeared. The Winterthur company Sulzer built projectile weaving machines, and the **air-jet loom** shoots the thread through the shed with a jet of compressed air.

The power loom was one of the key machines of **industrialisation**. Factories sprang up, people moved from the countryside to the cities, and cloth became affordable for many. In eastern Switzerland and the Zurich Oberland, the textile industry shaped whole regions for a long time. The punched cards of the Jacquard loom are even considered early forerunners of computer programming.

begriffe.erklaerung: The lengthwise threads stretched in the loom.
The crosswise threads passed through the warp.
A device that carries the weft thread through the shed.
The period in which machines and factories replaced work by hand.
English workers who destroyed machines in protest.

gewusst: Edmund Cartwright was actually a clergyman and had no training as an engineer.
Modern air-jet looms can put in more than a thousand weft threads per minute.
After the Uster fire, those involved were put on trial and some were given long sentences.

teile.einleitung: An operational amplifier is a small electronic component that amplifies the difference between two voltages very strongly. It is one of the most important building blocks of electronics and is found in audio equipment, measuring instruments and sensors. With a few resistors it can be wired so that it gives exactly the amplification you want.
wichtigste: An operational amplifier has two inputs and one output.
An ideal operational amplifier has an infinitely large input resistance.
With negative feedback, a voltage of 0 V settles between the inputs.
An inverting amplifier with 10 kΩ and 47 kΩ amplifies by a factor of minus 4.7.
A voltage follower has a gain of 1.
Without negative feedback it works as a comparator.
The µA741, introduced by Fairchild in 1968, became a classic.
The name comes from mathematical operations in analogue computers.

abschnitte.text: An operational amplifier, op-amp for short, is a **differential amplifier**. It has a non-inverting input (+), an inverting input (minus) and an output. It amplifies the difference between the two input voltages, often by a hundred thousand times. Today it is usually found in a circuit as a tiny chip with a few connecting legs.

Because the gain is so huge, part of the output signal is fed back through a resistor to the minus input. This is called **negative feedback**. The amplifier then adjusts its output so that there are practically 0 volts between the two inputs. In this way the external resistors alone decide how strongly the signal is amplified, and the circuit becomes very precise.

For the **inverting amplifier**: gain equals minus R2 divided by R1, so with 10 kΩ and 47 kΩ it is minus 4.7. For the non-inverting amplifier you calculate 1 plus R2 divided by R1; with 1 kΩ and 9 kΩ that gives 10. The **voltage follower** amplifies exactly once, but relieves the load on the signal source. If you put a capacitor in the feedback path, you get an integrator.

To calculate circuits easily, people imagine an ideal operational amplifier. It has an infinitely large gain and an infinitely large **input resistance**, so no current flows into the inputs. Its output resistance is zero. Real components come surprisingly close to this ideal.

The name comes from the 1940s, when people did calculations with **analogue computers**. There such amplifiers carried out mathematical operations such as adding, integrating and multiplying by a number, at first still with valves. Later they were built with transistors and as integrated circuits. In 1968 the company Fairchild brought out the **µA741**, which became the most widely used classic.

Operational amplifiers amplify the weak signals from microphones, guitar pickups and sensors. In thermometers, scales and medical devices they help with precise measurement. As a **comparator** without negative feedback, an op-amp compares two voltages and, for example, switches on a light when it gets dark. They also play a big part in filters for music systems.

begriffe.erklaerung: The electrical pressure that drives current through a wire, measured in volts.
A component that slows down the flow of current, measured in ohms.
Part of the output is fed back to calm the circuit and make it precise.
A circuit that shows which of two voltages is larger.

gewusst: The name operational amplifier was coined by the engineer John Ragazzini in 1947.
The µA741 has been made for more than 50 years and is still well known to many electronics hobbyists.

teile.einleitung: Hydraulics is the technology of transmitting and multiplying forces with liquids. It makes use of the fact that liquids can hardly be squeezed together. Thanks to hydraulics, a digger can lift tonnes of earth and a car can be braked with light pressure on the pedal.
wichtigste: Hydraulics makes use of the fact that liquids can hardly be squeezed together.
Pressure spreads equally in all directions in a liquid, as Blaise Pascal discovered.
Hydraulic systems usually use oil.
In a hydraulic cylinder, the pressure of the liquid pushes a piston out.
A hydraulic press multiplies the force, but in return the distance at the small piston becomes longer.
1 bar equals 100,000 pascals.
Diggers usually move their arm with hydraulic cylinders.

abschnitte.text: The word hydraulics comes from Greek, where “hydor” means water. It refers to machines that transmit forces with a liquid. Because liquids can hardly be squeezed together, a liquid passes on any pressure immediately. If air is used instead of a liquid, it is called **pneumatics**.

In the 17th century the French scientist **Blaise Pascal** discovered that pressure in an enclosed liquid spreads equally in all directions. Pressure is force divided by area. In his honour, the unit of pressure is called the **pascal**. One bar is 100,000 pascals, which is about the air pressure at sea level.

A **hydraulic press** has a small and a large piston connected by liquid. If you press on the small piston of 2 square centimetres with 50 newtons, a force of 2,500 newtons acts on the large piston of 100 square centimetres. The area is 50 times bigger, so the force is too. But in return you have to push the small piston 50 times further than the large one moves, because energy cannot be gained.

A **pump** puts the liquid under pressure, often several hundred bar. Hoses and pipes carry it to where it is used, and valves control where it flows. In the **hydraulic cylinder**, the liquid pushes a piston out. **Oil** is usually used, because it lubricates the parts at the same time and protects them from rust.

Diggers, cranes, tractors and dustcarts move their arms with hydraulic cylinders. The brakes of a car also work hydraulically; the foot presses on the brake pads via brake fluid. In garages, hydraulic lifts raise whole cars. The landing gear of aircraft and many bike brakes also use hydraulics.

begriffe.erklaerung: Force acting on a certain area.
Movable part in a cylinder that is pushed by the liquid.
Unit of pressure, named after Blaise Pascal.
Technology that transmits forces with compressed air instead of liquid.

gewusst: With a hydraulic press, a person can move loads as heavy as a car using little force.
The Englishman Joseph Bramah patented the hydraulic press in the 18th century.
A digger can control several hydraulic cylinders at once so that the boom, arm and bucket move together.

teile.einleitung: A smart grid is a power grid in which generation, storage and consumption are coordinated using communication technology. It helps to make good use of electricity from sun and wind, even though this is not always produced evenly. Smart electricity meters, batteries and controlled appliances are important building blocks of it.
wichtigste: In a smart grid, generation, storage and consumption are coordinated using communication technology.
According to the Electricity Supply Ordinance, Swiss grid operators must replace 80 per cent of meters with smart meters by the end of 2027.
A prosumer uses electricity and also produces electricity themselves, for example with a solar system.
Load management deliberately shifts consumption to times when plenty is available.
A virtual power station is a group of many small installations that are controlled together.
For decades Swiss grid operators have switched electric water heaters on and off centrally using ripple control.
Decentralised installations feeding into lower grid levels make running the grid more demanding.
With digitalisation, the risk of cyber attacks on the control technology grows.

abschnitte.text: In the past electricity flowed almost only in one direction: from large power stations along lines to homes. In a **smart grid**, power stations, storage and consumers constantly exchange data. In this way the grid knows where and how much electricity is being produced and used at any moment. The aim is that exactly as much electricity is always fed into the grid as is used.

Today many Swiss roofs have **solar panels** that feed electricity into the grid. Someone who uses electricity and also produces it is called a **prosumer**, a word mixed from producer and consumer. Because this electricity is fed into lower grid levels, it sometimes flows in the opposite direction from before. In addition, the sun does not always shine, and at midday there is often more electricity than is needed at that moment.

A **smart meter** is a digital electricity meter that measures consumption precisely and sends the data automatically. In Switzerland, according to the Electricity Supply Ordinance, grid operators must have replaced 80 per cent of meters by the end of 2027. This lets households see more precisely when they use how much electricity. Grid operators can then plan the grid better.

With **load management**, consumption is shifted to times when plenty of electricity is available. Examples are electric water heaters, heat pumps or electric cars that run or charge when a lot of solar power is being produced. In Switzerland there has long been **ripple control** for this: signals sent over the power grid switch water heaters on and off centrally. Modern systems do this much more finely and quickly.

Many small installations such as solar roofs, batteries and combined heat and power units can be linked together to form a **virtual power station**. Central software then controls them together like one large power station. Pumped storage power stations in the Alps also help to store electricity and release it when needed. In future, electric car batteries could also feed electricity back into the grid.

Because many devices are networked in a smart grid, the risk of **cyber attacks** on the control technology rises. A successful attack could, in the worst case, lead to power cuts. That is why data must be encrypted and systems well protected. Data protection is also important, because consumption data reveals a lot about everyday life in a household.

begriffe.erklaerung: An intelligent power grid, “intelligentes Stromnetz” in German.
Digital electricity meter that sends data automatically.
Someone who uses electricity and also produces electricity themselves.
Deliberately shifting electricity use to favourable times.
Older technology that switches appliances centrally using signals in the power grid.

gewusst: Many Swiss electric water heaters have heated mainly at night for decades, because ripple control switches them on then.
On sunny middays, some European countries can have so much solar power that the electricity price on the exchange drops below zero.
An electric car with a full battery could supply a family house with electricity for several days.

teile.einleitung: Hans Hilfiker was a Swiss engineer and designer. In 1944 he designed the famous SBB station clock, which is now seen as a symbol of Swiss punctuality. He also helped to set the dimensions of Swiss kitchens.
wichtigste: Hans Hilfiker was born in Zurich in 1901 and died in 1993.
He studied electrical engineering at ETH Zurich.
In 1944 he designed the well-known SBB station clock.
The red second hand recalls the signalling disc of the stationmaster.
At every full minute the second hand stops for about 1.5 seconds.
Hilfiker helped shape the Swiss kitchen standard with appliances 55 centimetres wide.
From 1958 he was director of the Glarus company Therma.

abschnitte.text: Hans Hilfiker was born in **Zurich** in 1901. He studied electrical engineering at **ETH Zurich** and became an engineer. Later he worked for the Swiss Federal Railways, SBB. There he looked after technical equipment in stations, for example clocks and lighting.

In 1944 Hilfiker designed the **SBB station clock**, with a white face, black bars instead of numbers and black hands. It is easy to read even from a long way off. Later the red **second hand** with the round disc was added. It recalls the signalling disc with which the stationmaster gave a train the signal to depart.

The second hand takes only about 58.5 seconds to go round once. Then it stops at the top, at twelve, for about 1.5 seconds. It waits for an electrical pulse from a central **master clock**, which then makes the minute hand jump forward one step. In this way all the clocks in the stations run exactly the same, and trains can leave on time.

Hilfiker also worked on kitchens. He helped to develop the **Swiss kitchen standard**, according to which cookers, fridges and cupboards are 55 centimetres wide. This means appliances from different makers fit into every kitchen. From 1958 he ran the company **Therma** in Schwanden in the canton of Glarus as its director; it made kitchen appliances.

Today the station clock is considered a classic of Swiss design and hangs in museums. Since the 1980s the watch company Mondaine has sold wristwatches in this style. In 2012 an American technology company used the design in an app. According to media reports, it then paid the SBB about 20 million francs.

begriffe.erklaerung: Central clock that gives the exact time to many other clocks.
In the past, the head of a station, who gave trains the signal to depart.
Shaping objects so that they are attractive and practical.
A rule that sets how big something should be or how it should be built.

gewusst: Hans Hilfiker's station clock does not have a single number on its face.
The 55-centimetre kitchen standard applies in Switzerland, while 60 centimetres is usual in many European countries.
The brief pause of the second hand looks as if the clock is taking a breath.

teile.einleitung: A satellite dish is a bowl-shaped aerial that collects radio waves just as a concave mirror collects light. It is best known as the dish on the roof of a house for television. Huge dish aerials also serve as radio telescopes or for communicating with space probes.
wichtigste: A satellite dish receives television programmes from satellites.
It has the shape of a shallow bowl, more precisely a paraboloid.
The satellites orbit high above the Earth in space.
In Switzerland the dishes point roughly south.
Nothing may stand in front of the dish, otherwise the signal does not arrive.
Heavy rain or snow can disturb reception.
The small head in front of the dish catches the collected signals.

abschnitte.text: The curved bowl has the shape of a **paraboloid**. All waves that hit it head-on are reflected so that they meet at one point, the **focal point**. That is where the small receiving head, the **LNB**, sits. It amplifies the weak signals and sends them by cable to the receiver by the television.

Television satellites orbit about 36,000 kilometres above the equator. They move exactly as fast as the Earth turns, so they seem to stand still. This orbit is called **geostationary**. Because these satellites are above the equator, dishes in Switzerland must point roughly south and slightly upwards.

Radio waves from space are very weak and need a clear line of sight. Trees, houses or a balcony in front of the dish can block reception. Heavy rain, snow on the dish or a violent thunderstorm also weaken the signal. Then the picture can freeze briefly or disappear completely.

In **Leuk** in Valais there are many huge dish aerials. A ground station for **satellite communications** is located there, through which data, telephone calls and television signals are exchanged with satellites. The valley is sheltered, and the aerials have a good view of the sky. Big dishes need to be aimed precisely so that they hit the right satellite.

Huge dish aerials serve as **radio telescopes**, with which researchers receive radio waves from distant stars and galaxies. Space agencies use large dishes to talk to space probes travelling far out in the solar system. Directional radio links and radar also use the same trick. The bigger the dish, the weaker the signals it can catch.

begriffe.erklaerung: Curved bowl shape that collects waves at one point.
The point at which all the reflected waves meet.
Receiving head in front of the dish that catches and amplifies the signals.
Satellite orbit in which a satellite seems to stand still as seen from Earth.

gewusst: A satellite dish works on the same principle as the mirror in a torch, only the other way round.
A signal from a television satellite takes about a quarter of a second to reach your home.
Many satellite dishes are slightly oval because the receiving head is mounted off to one side.

teile.einleitung: Machine learning is a branch of artificial intelligence in which computers learn from examples instead of having every rule programmed into them. The program looks for patterns in data by itself and can then make predictions for new cases. This is how computers recognise spam, faces or spoken words.
wichtigste: In machine learning a computer learns from examples instead of fixed rules.
In supervised learning the model learns from examples with known correct answers.
In reinforcement learning an agent learns through rewards for its actions.
The k-means algorithm groups data into k clusters.
If a model only memorises the training data, this is called overfitting.
A test data set checks how well the model works on unknown data.
In 1958 Frank Rosenblatt presented the perceptron, an early artificial neuron.

abschnitte.text: Instead of telling a computer exactly what a cat looks like, you show it thousands of pictures of cats and other animals. The program works out for itself which features are important. The result is called a **model**. The examples it learns from are called **training data**. The more good and varied examples there are, the better the model usually learns.

In **supervised learning** the correct answer is known for each example, for instance “spam” or “not spam”. In unsupervised learning there are no answers; the program looks for groups by itself. A well-known method for this is the **k-means algorithm**, which divides data into k clusters. In **reinforcement learning** an agent tries out actions and receives rewards or penalties. This is how programs learnt, for example, to master video games.

**Neural networks** are loosely inspired by the brain and consist of many connected artificial neurons. In 1958 Frank Rosenblatt presented the perceptron, an early model of an artificial neuron. Each connection has a weight that is adjusted during training. The **backpropagation** algorithm calculates how much each weight contributes to the error. Networks with very many layers are called deep learning.

Part of the data is held back during training; this is the **test data set**. It is used to check how well the model works on unknown data. If a model only memorises the training data, it does badly on new data; this is called **overfitting**. There are measures such as precision for assessing it. If a spam filter marks 50 emails as spam and 40 of them really are spam, its precision is 80 per cent.

Machine learning is found in spam filters, translation programs and face recognition on mobile phones. Streaming services use it to suggest films you might like. In medicine it helps to detect tumours in images. Weather forecasts are also increasingly being improved with learning models. It is important that the data is fair, otherwise the model takes over **prejudices** from the data.

begriffe.erklaerung: The result of learning, with which the computer makes predictions.
Examples from which a model learns.
When a model only memorises and fails on new data.
A group of similar data points.
Computing model made of many connected artificial neurons.

gewusst: The perceptron of 1958 ran on a specially built machine that captured images using 400 light sensors.
Some models have billions of weights, all of which are adjusted during training.
A model that has only seen pictures of dogs on grass sometimes recognises grass instead of dogs.

teile.einleitung: The Gösgen nuclear power station is one of Switzerland's nuclear power stations and stands in Däniken in the canton of Solothurn. Its 150-metre cooling tower with its cloud of steam can be seen from far around. In a normal year it produces about 8 billion kilowatt hours of electricity.
wichtigste: The Gösgen nuclear power station lies on the River Aare in Däniken in the canton of Solothurn.
It has a pressurised water reactor supplied by the company Kraftwerk Union (KWU).
The reactor has a thermal output of about 3,000 megawatts.
The net electrical output is about 1,010 megawatts.
The natural-draught cooling tower is 150 metres high.
Alpiq holds 40 per cent and manages the business.
Nuclear safety is supervised by the Swiss Federal Nuclear Safety Inspectorate ENSI.

abschnitte.text: The Gösgen nuclear power station stands in the municipality of **Däniken** in the canton of Solothurn, between Olten and Aarau. It lies right on the **Aare**. The Aare supplies water with which the cooling circuit is topped up. The huge cooling tower shapes the landscape of the lower Niederamt. You can see it from a long way off from the motorway and the train.

Gösgen has a **pressurised water reactor**, supplied by the German company Kraftwerk Union (KWU). The reactor core contains 177 **fuel assemblies** with uranium. The water in the reactor is under such high pressure that it does not boil despite the great heat. Via steam generators it passes its heat on to a second circuit, where steam is produced for the turbine. The thermal output is about 3,000 megawatts.

The heat gives a net electrical output of about **1,010 megawatts**. So only about a third of the heat becomes electricity; the rest goes into the air via the cooling tower. In a normal year of operation Gösgen produces about **8 billion kilowatt hours** of electricity. In theory that is enough for very many Swiss households. After Leibstadt, Gösgen is the second most powerful nuclear power station in Switzerland.

The power station was built in the 1970s and went into commercial operation in 1979. It is owned jointly by several energy companies and cities. The largest share, 40 per cent, is held by **Alpiq**, which also manages the business. The plant is regularly shut down for a few weeks to change fuel assemblies and check parts. These shutdowns are called **overhauls**.

Nuclear safety is supervised by **ENSI**, the Swiss Federal Nuclear Safety Inspectorate. It checks whether all safety regulations are being followed. A nuclear power station in Switzerland may run as long as it is safe; there is no fixed maximum operating life. Around the power station, monitoring stations constantly measure radioactivity. For emergencies, people in the surrounding area have been given **iodine tablets**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A reactor in which the water is under high pressure and does not boil.
A bundle of fuel rods containing uranium.
A unit for large outputs, one million watts.
The federal authority that supervises the safety of nuclear power stations.
A planned shutdown for maintenance and checks.

gewusst: The Gösgen cooling tower is 150 metres high, which makes it taller than the Prime Tower in Zurich.
The cloud of steam above the cooling tower consists only of water that has evaporated.
A natural-draught cooling tower needs no fans; the warm air rises by itself, as in a chimney.

teile.einleitung: A short circuit happens when electric current takes a shortcut without flowing through a device. Because there is almost no resistance in the way, a huge current suddenly flows. This can make wires hot and even start fires, which is why fuses protect every house.
wichtigste: In a short circuit, the resistance in the circuit is almost zero.
That is why a very large current flows, which heats wires strongly.
Without a fuse, an overheated wire can start a fire.
Fuses and circuit breakers cut off the current very quickly in a short circuit.
When a live conductor touches the metal casing of a device, this is called an earth fault.
Never carry batteries loose in your pocket with coins or keys, because metal can short-circuit the terminals.

abschnitte.text: Normally current flows from the positive terminal through a device, for example a lamp, and back again. The device slows the current down; it has a **resistance**. In a **short circuit**, the outgoing and return wires touch directly, and the current bypasses the device. In a house, it is typically the **live conductor** and the neutral conductor that touch. Because almost nothing slows the current down, it rises suddenly.

According to **Ohm's law**, current equals voltage divided by resistance. A socket in Switzerland has 230 volts. If the short-circuited wire had a resistance of only 0.1 ohms, 2,300 amperes would flow without a fuse. A kettle, by comparison, needs only about 10 amperes. Such a large current makes wires glowing hot in a short time.

The great heat can melt the plastic insulation of the cables and start fires. Often a bright **electric arc** also forms, a spark that can melt metal. In an **earth fault**, the casing of a device is suddenly live, and anyone who touches it can get an electric shock. Even small batteries can become dangerous if a key connects their terminals, because they then get very hot.

Every household installation is protected by **fuses**. In the past these were mainly fuses with a thin wire that melts through when too much current flows. Today **circuit breakers** are mostly used, which can simply be switched back on after they trip. A residual current device, RCD for short, also switches off if current flows away through a person or a casing. These protective devices are required in Switzerland for new installations.

If a plugged-in device is smoking, first switch off the power, for example at the fuse box, without touching the device. If something is burning, call the fire brigade on 118. If a fuse keeps tripping immediately, a **qualified electrician** should look for the fault. Children should never tinker with sockets, cables or fuse boxes themselves.

begriffe.erklaerung: An unwanted direct connection through which current flows past the device.
How strongly something slows down electric current, measured in ohms.
A protective part that switches off the current when it becomes too large.
When a live wire touches the metal casing of a device.
A bright, very hot spark that jumps through the air.

gewusst: Electric welding deliberately uses an arc similar to a short circuit to melt metal.
A circuit breaker can trip within a few thousandths of a second in a short circuit.
In everyday German, people also speak of a “Kurzschluss” (short circuit) when someone acts without thinking.

teile.einleitung: Nikola Tesla was a brilliant inventor and engineer who greatly shaped electrical engineering. Without his ideas on alternating current and the electric motor, our electricity supply would look different today. Tesla, born in 1856, lived most of his life in New York and died there in 1943.
wichtigste: Nikola Tesla was born in 1856 in what is now Croatia.
In 1884 he came to New York and worked briefly for Thomas Edison.
He developed the induction motor, which runs with a rotating magnetic field.
George Westinghouse bought his patents for alternating current machines.
The so-called War of the Currents was about whether direct current or alternating current would win.
In the mid-1890s a large hydropower station using his system went into operation at Niagara Falls.
The unit tesla for magnetic flux density is named after him.

abschnitte.text: Nikola Tesla was born on 10 July 1856 in **Smiljan**, a village in what is now Croatia. His family was Serbian, and his father was a priest. Tesla studied engineering in Graz and then worked in Budapest and Paris. In 1884 he emigrated to New York, where he spent most of his life.

In New York Tesla at first worked for the famous inventor **Thomas Edison**. Edison backed direct current, while Tesla was convinced of alternating current. The two did not get on, and after a short time Tesla went his own way. He set up his own laboratory and applied for many patents.

Tesla developed an **induction motor**, which runs with a rotating magnetic field, and a whole system for alternating current. The industrialist **George Westinghouse** bought his patents. There followed the **War of the Currents**, a fierce dispute over whether direct current or alternating current was better. Alternating current won, because it can be transmitted over long distances with transformers.

In 1893 Westinghouse lit up the World's Fair in Chicago with Tesla's alternating current. In the mid-1890s a large hydropower station using Tesla's system went into operation at **Niagara Falls**. From there electricity was carried as far as the city of Buffalo. This was a breakthrough for the modern electricity supply.

With the **Tesla coil**, Tesla produced very high voltages with impressive sparks and flashes of lightning. He dreamt of sending electricity and messages around the world without wires, and for this he built the Wardenclyffe Tower near New York. But the project failed because the money ran out. Tesla died poor and withdrawn on 7 January 1943 in a hotel room in New York.

Today the unit **tesla** for magnetic flux density is named after him. A well-known electric car company also bears his name. Belgrade's airport is called Belgrade Nikola Tesla Airport, and there is a Tesla Museum in Belgrade. Tesla's induction motor still drives countless machines today, including many locomotives.

begriffe.erklaerung: Current that changes its direction many times per second.
Current that always flows in the same direction, as from a battery.
A right that protects an invention for a period of time.
A device that raises or lowers electrical voltage.

gewusst: Tesla is said to have had an amazing memory and to have designed machines entirely in his head first.
During his life Tesla held several hundred patents in various countries.

teile.einleitung: The wheel is a circular disc that turns around an axle in the middle. It is one of the most important inventions of humankind, because wheels make it easy to move heavy things. Whether bicycle, car, train or clock, wheels turn everywhere.
wichtigste: A wheel is circular and turns around an axle.
With wheels, things roll instead of being dragged.
The wheel was invented about 5,500 years ago.
Very old wooden wheels have been found in Swiss pile-dwelling settlements.
The thin rods of a bicycle wheel are called spokes.
Around the outside of a bicycle wheel there is a rubber tyre.
Wheels are also found in machines and clocks, for example as gearwheels.

abschnitte.text: A wheel turns around an **axle**, a rod in the middle. Because the wheel rolls instead of sliding, there is much less friction. That is why you can move much heavier loads on a cart than you could carry. The larger a wheel, the more easily it rolls over stones and holes. The middle part in which the axle sits is called the **hub**.

The wheel was invented about 5,500 years ago, that is, around 3500 BC. Probably the **potter's wheel** came first, in Mesopotamia, today's Iraq. At about the same time, wheels on carts appeared in various regions of Europe and Asia. The first wheels were heavy discs made of wooden planks. One of the oldest known wooden wheels was found in a marsh near Ljubljana in Slovenia.

Very old wooden wheels have also been found in Switzerland, in **pile-dwelling settlements**. These villages stood on lake shores thousands of years ago, for example on Lake Zurich. Because the wood lay in damp ground without air, it was preserved. Some of the wheels are almost 5,000 years old. Since 2011 the pile dwellings around the Alps have been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

Around 2000 BC wheels with **spokes** were invented. They were much lighter and made fast chariots possible. A bicycle wheel has thin metal spokes between the hub and the edge, the rim. Around the outside is a rubber **tyre**, which is filled with air and cushions bumps. The air-filled tyre for bicycles was developed by John Boyd Dunlop in 1888.

Wheels are not found only on vehicles. **Gearwheels** pass on movement in clocks, bicycle gears and machines. Water wheels and windmills used the power of water and wind early on. Steering wheels, Ferris wheels and turbines are also based on the principle of the wheel. Swiss watches contain tiny gearwheels made so precisely that they run accurately for years.

begriffe.erklaerung: Rod around which the wheel turns.
Middle part of the wheel in which the axle sits.
Thin rod between the hub and the rim.
Force that arises when things rub against each other and slows movement down.
Prehistoric villages with houses on wooden piles on lake shores.

gewusst: The Incas and Maya in America knew wheels on toys but did not use wheeled carts.
The wheel was probably invented after the potter's wheel, not before it.
The rim is the outer ring of a wheel on which the tyre sits.

teile.einleitung: Industry 4.0 describes factories in which machines, workpieces and computers are connected with each other via the internet. The machines constantly exchange data and can partly control themselves. The number 4.0 stands for the idea that this is seen as the fourth industrial revolution.
wichtigste: Industry 4.0 means networking machines, sensors and workpieces in the factory.
The term was presented to a wide public at the Hannover Messe trade fair in 2011.
In English it is also called the Industrial Internet of Things.
A digital twin is a virtual copy of a real machine with its real-time data.
Predictive maintenance uses sensor data to recognise when a machine is about to fail.
Cobots are robots that work directly with people without a safety fence.
The goal of “batch size 1” means making one-off items as cheaply as mass-produced goods.

abschnitte.text: The number recalls the version numbers of software. The **first industrial revolution** brought steam engines and mechanical looms from the 18th century. The second followed with electricity and the assembly line. The third brought computers and automation from the 1970s. The **fourth** now connects all machines via the internet.

abschnitte.titel: Machines that talk to each other
abschnitte.text: In a networked factory, machines have many **sensors** that measure, for example, temperature, pressure or vibrations. Such systems made of mechanics, sensors and software are called **cyber-physical systems**. So that machines from different makers understand each other, shared languages such as the **OPC UA** standard are needed. For wireless connections, 5G mobile communication is considered important because of its very short delays. Even a workpiece can carry a chip that tells the machine how it should be processed.

A **digital twin** is an exact copy of a machine or a whole factory in the computer. It is constantly fed with the real measurement data. In this way changes can first be tried out on the computer before they are put into practice in the real factory. Engineers can see on the screen how every machine is doing. As a result, faults can be spotted earlier.

In the past, machines were maintained according to fixed schedules or only when they broke down. With **predictive maintenance**, computers analyse the sensor data. If a bearing, for example, vibrates more than usual, the system reports that it is about to fail. Then the part can be replaced in good time. This saves money and prevents the whole production line from standing still.

**Collaborative robots**, cobots for short, work right next to people without a safety fence. They sense when they touch a person and stop immediately. A cobot can, for example, hold heavy parts while a person assembles them. A big goal of Industry 4.0 is **batch size 1**: every product can be individual and still be made cheaply. Many Swiss companies, for example in the engineering and watch industries, are also relying on such networked factories.

begriffe.erklaerung: A measuring probe that detects, for example, heat, pressure or movement.
A virtual copy of a real machine in the computer.
A robot that works closely with people.
Maintenance that predicts failures from data.
The number of identical items made in one run.

gewusst: With Industry 4.0, a customer can put their product together online, and the factory makes exactly that one item.
The term Industry 4.0 comes from Germany and is often simply taken over in English.
A cobot can be programmed by a person simply showing it a movement by guiding its arm.

teile.einleitung: A maglev train is a train that does not roll on wheels but is held floating above its guideway by magnets. Because no wheels rub, it can travel very fast and quietly. The speed record for rail vehicles is held by a Japanese maglev train at 603 km/h.
wichtigste: Maglev trains float above their guideway without touching it.
The Transrapid is driven by a linear motor.
In the Transrapid, electromagnets are pulled up towards the guideway from below.
The Transrapid in Shanghai links the city with Pudong airport.
Since 2015 Japan has held the record of 603 km/h with the SCMaglev.
Because there is no contact with the guideway, maglev trains suffer less wear.

abschnitte.text: Magnets can attract or repel each other, and that is exactly what maglev trains use. In the German **Transrapid**, the train wraps around the guideway, and electromagnets are pulled up towards the guideway from below. A computer constantly controls the gap so that the train floats about one centimetre up. This is called **electromagnetic suspension**.

The Japanese **SCMaglev** uses **superconducting magnets**, which are strongly cooled. When the train moves, currents arise in coils in the guideway that repel it and lift it. But this electrodynamic suspension only works above a certain speed, so the train needs wheels for starting and braking. In 2015 it reached 603 km/h on a test track, the world record for rail vehicles. A line for this system is being built between Tokyo and Nagoya.

A maglev train is driven by a **linear motor**. You can imagine it as an electric motor that has been unrolled and laid out flat. A travelling magnetic field in the guideway pulls the train forwards or brakes it. Because nothing touches, there is hardly any **wear** on wheels and rails.

In 1934 the German Hermann Kemper was granted a patent for a maglev train. In Germany the Transrapid was tested for decades on a test track in the **Emsland** region. There in 2006 a train collided with a maintenance vehicle, and 23 people were killed. After that the test track was closed, and no line was built in Germany.

The best-known line is the **Shanghai Transrapid**, which has linked the city with Pudong airport since the early 2000s. It covers the roughly 30 kilometres in a few minutes. Slower maglev lines run, for example, in South Korea and China as local transport. In Switzerland a maglev in tunnels was planned under the name **Swissmetro**, but the project was never carried out. Because construction and the guideway are very expensive, most countries continue to rely on high-speed trains with wheels.

begriffe.erklaerung: A train that is held up in the air above its guideway by magnets.
An electric motor that produces a straight rather than a rotating movement.
A material that, when strongly cooled, conducts electricity with no resistance at all.
The track above which the maglev train floats.
The wearing down of parts through friction and use.

gewusst: For a long time the Shanghai Transrapid ran in scheduled service at up to 431 km/h, making it the fastest scheduled train in the world.
During the record run at 603 km/h, the Japanese train covered almost 170 metres in one second.
A maglev train has no wheels to squeal; at high speed it is loud mainly because of the rushing air.

teile.einleitung: A hand mixer is an electric kitchen appliance that you hold in your hand and use to mix dough, beat egg whites or whip cream. Two fast-turning beaters do in a few minutes what would take a lot of strength and time by hand. It is part of the basic equipment of many Swiss kitchens.
wichtigste: A hand mixer is an electric mixing device that you hold in your hand.
It usually has two beaters that turn against each other.
A hand mixer is the fastest way to whip cream.
For heavy doughs there are special dough hooks.
The speed can be set in several stages.
When whipping, a lot of air is beaten into the cream or egg white.
Before inserting or changing the beaters, you must pull out the plug.

abschnitte.text: A hand mixer consists of a casing with a handle, an **electric motor** and two openings for the attachments. The motor drives the two **beaters** via gearwheels, and they turn in opposite directions. You can usually choose three to five speeds. Unlike a **food processor**, you hold the hand mixer yourself and move it through the bowl.

When whipping cream, the beaters stir lots of tiny **air bubbles** into the liquid. The fat droplets in the cream gather around the bubbles and hold them in place. In this way liquid cream turns into an airy, firm mass, **whipped cream**. It works best with well-chilled cream, and you should not whip it for too long, otherwise it turns into butter.

The normal wire **beaters** are suitable for cream, beaten egg whites, creams and runny batters such as cake mixture. For heavy doughs, such as bread or plaited loaf dough, you use spiral-shaped **dough hooks**. Some devices also have a blender stick as an attachment. Egg whites can only be beaten until stiff if there is no yolk and no fat in the bowl.

In the past everything was mixed by hand with a **whisk**, which took a lot of strength and stamina. At the beginning of the 20th century the first electric mixers appeared in the USA, at first as large stand machines for bakeries. Later the devices became smaller, lighter and cheaper. From the middle of the 20th century, hand mixers found their way into many households, including in Switzerland.

The beaters turn very fast and can catch fingers, hair or cables. That is why you only insert or change the beaters when the **plug is pulled out**. You start on a slow setting so that nothing splashes out of the bowl. Children should first use the hand mixer together with an adult.

begriffe.erklaerung: An attachment made of bent wire that beats air into liquids as it turns.
A spiral-shaped attachment for kneading heavy dough.
A motor that converts electrical energy into rotation.
Cream that has become light and firm by being beaten with air.

gewusst: If you whip cream for too long, it turns into butter.
The two beaters of a hand mixer turn in opposite directions.
Cream roughly doubles in volume when whipped, because a lot of air gets into it.

teile.einleitung: In communications engineering, modulation means imprinting a useful signal such as speech, music or data onto a carrier wave. Only then can information be sent over long distances by radio, cable or light. Radio, mobile phones, Wi-Fi and television all work only thanks to modulation.
wichtigste: In modulation, a useful signal is imprinted onto a carrier signal.
In the receiver, the useful signal is recovered by demodulation.
High carrier frequencies can be transmitted well with handy aerials.
A modem is a modulator and demodulator in one device.
In phase-shift keying (PSK) the phase of the carrier is changed; in QAM, amplitude and phase.
The multi-carrier method OFDM is used in Wi-Fi, DAB+ and LTE.

abschnitte.text: A **carrier wave** is an even, fast oscillation, for example a radio wave. On its own it contains no information. In **modulation**, one of its properties is changed in time with the useful signal, for example its strength, its frequency or its phase. The receiver recognises these changes and turns them back into music, speech or data; this is called **demodulation**.

A sound signal oscillates only a few hundred to a few thousand times per second. To transmit such low frequencies, you would need huge aerials. High frequencies, on the other hand, can be sent out well with handy **aerials**. In addition, many stations can be given different carrier frequencies so that they do not interfere with each other.

In **amplitude modulation**, AM for short, the strength of the carrier wave changes in time with the sound; this is how medium-wave and long-wave transmitters worked. In **frequency modulation**, FM for short, the frequency changes slightly instead. FM was used for VHF radio and is less prone to noise. In Switzerland the SRG switched off its VHF transmitters at the end of 2024 and has since broadcast digitally via DAB+.
