In digital transmission, bits are sent, that is, zeros and ones. In phase-shift keying (PSK), the phase of the carrier jumps back and forth between fixed values. **Quadrature amplitude modulation** (QAM) changes amplitude and phase at the same time; with 64-QAM there are 64 different states, and each symbol carries 6 bits. The multi-carrier method **OFDM** spreads the data over many carriers at once and is used in Wi-Fi, DAB+ and LTE.

A **modem** is a device that modulates and demodulates data; its name is made up of modulator and demodulator. In the past, modems connected computers to the internet over the telephone line and whistled audibly as they did so. Today there are modems in every internet router and every mobile phone. Remote controls, satellites and optical fibres also use modulation to transmit information.

begriffe.erklaerung: An even oscillation onto which information is imprinted.
Recovering the information from the modulated wave.
The strength or height of an oscillation.
How often something oscillates per second, measured in hertz.
A device that modulates and demodulates data for transmission.

gewusst: The German abbreviation UKW stands for “Ultrakurzwelle”, very high frequency (VHF).
The whistling and hissing noises of old internet modems were audible modulation.
Even the Morse signals of the first radio operators were a very simple form of modulation, in which the carrier was just switched on and off.

teile.einleitung: A refrigeration machine is a machine that removes heat from a space and releases it somewhere else. The best-known example is the fridge in the kitchen. It works like a heat pump and needs energy to do so, usually electricity.
wichtigste: A refrigeration machine pumps heat from a cold place to a warmer one.
In the evaporator, the refrigerant absorbs heat from the cold compartment.
The expansion valve lowers the pressure and temperature of the refrigerant.
At the back, a fridge gives off the heat it has removed plus the electrical energy it has taken in.
The Montreal Protocol of 1987 led to the ban on CFC refrigerants.
Most European household fridges today use isobutane.
In 1930 Albert Einstein and Leó Szilárd patented a fridge with no moving parts.

abschnitte.text: On its own, heat always flows from warm to cold. A **refrigeration machine** manages to pump heat in the other direction, out of a cold space into the warmer surroundings. For this it needs work, usually from an electric motor. Examples are fridges, chest freezers, air conditioning and cooling systems for artificial ice rinks.

A **refrigerant** that evaporates easily circulates in the machine. In the **evaporator** inside the fridge it evaporates and absorbs heat, just as sweat cools the skin as it evaporates. A compressor squeezes the vapour together, which makes it hot. In the condenser at the back it gives off the heat to the kitchen and turns liquid again; then the **expansion valve** lowers the pressure and temperature, and the cycle starts again.

A fridge that removes 300 watts of heat from inside and takes in 100 watts of electricity gives off 400 watts of heat to the kitchen. That is why a kitchen does not get cooler if you leave the fridge door open; it even gets warmer. How well a refrigeration machine works is shown by its **coefficient of performance**. An ideal machine between 250 kelvin and 300 kelvin would have a coefficient of performance of 5, so it would pump five times as much heat as the energy it uses.

In the past **CFCs** were often used as refrigerants. These substances destroy the ozone layer, which protects us from harmful UV radiation. With the Montreal Protocol of 1987, many countries agreed to ban CFCs. Today most household fridges in Europe contain the natural refrigerant **isobutane**.

Research into refrigeration machines was already going on in the 19th century. In the 1870s the German engineer **Carl von Linde** built one of the first reliable compression refrigeration machines, at first for breweries. In 1930 the physicists **Albert Einstein** and Leó Szilárd patented a fridge with no moving parts. Before refrigeration machines, people kept things cool with natural ice, which was sawn out of lakes in winter and stored in ice cellars.

begriffe.erklaerung: Substance that evaporates and turns liquid again in the cycle, and so carries heat.
Part in the cold compartment in which the refrigerant evaporates and absorbs heat.
Pump that squeezes the gaseous refrigerant together.
Ratio of the heat pumped to the energy used.
Chlorofluorocarbons, refrigerants used in the past that harm the ozone layer.

gewusst: The back of a fridge gets warm because the heat from inside is given off there.
A heat pump that heats a house works on exactly the same principle as a fridge.
Even Albert Einstein invented a fridge.

teile.einleitung: Josephine Cochrane was an American inventor who built the first practical dishwasher. In 1886 she received a patent for it. Her idea still makes work in the kitchen easier for millions of people today.
wichtigste: Josephine Cochrane invented the dishwasher.
In 1886 she received the patent for her machine.
She got the idea because her valuable china was damaged during washing up.
In her machine, soapy water sprayed from nozzles onto wire baskets holding the dishes.
In 1893 she presented the machine at the World's Fair in Chicago.
At first it was mainly hotels and restaurants that bought her machines.
She lived and worked in the USA.
Her great-grandfather John Fitch is known for an early steamboat.

abschnitte.text: Josephine Cochrane was born in 1839 in the state of **Ohio** in the USA and died in Chicago in 1913. Her father was an engineer, and her great-grandfather **John Fitch** had built an early steamboat back in the 18th century. She married a wealthy man and lived in Illinois. She liked to invite guests and used her valuable china for them.

When washing up by hand, plates and cups from her precious china kept getting broken. Cochrane was annoyed by this and wanted a machine that washed faster and more gently. After her husband's death in 1883 she was also in debt and needed money. So she began to put her idea into practice in earnest.

Cochrane measured every piece of china exactly and built matching **wire baskets** for plates, cups and saucers. The baskets sat on a wheel in a boiler. While the wheel turned, hot **soapy water** sprayed from nozzles onto the dishes. A mechanic helped her build it, and in 1886 she received the **patent**.

At the **World's Fair in Chicago** in 1893, Cochrane presented her machine to a huge audience. Restaurants on the exhibition grounds used it to wash their dishes, and the invention won an award. After that it was mainly **hotels and restaurants** that ordered the machines, because they were too big and too expensive for normal households. She founded her own company to make the machines.

Only from the middle of the 20th century did dishwashers become common in private households too. Today most Swiss kitchens have a dishwasher, often in the Swiss standard width of 55 centimetres. Modern machines often use less water than washing up by hand. Over several stages, Cochrane's company later became a well-known American brand of kitchen appliances.

begriffe.erklaerung: A right that secures an invention for its inventor for a certain time.
Large international exhibition at which countries show new inventions.
Narrow opening from which water or air sprays out under pressure.
Fine, white and valuable material for crockery.

gewusst: Josephine Cochrane is said to have declared that if nobody else would invent a dishwasher, she would do it herself.
Her family name was actually spelt Cochran; she added the e at the end herself.
In 2006 Cochrane was inducted into the American National Inventors Hall of Fame.

teile.einleitung: Power electronics is the part of electrical engineering that switches and converts large amounts of electrical power with semiconductors. It is found in phone chargers, electric cars, solar systems and locomotives. Its trick: electronic switches go on and off thousands of times per second.
wichtigste: Power electronics converts electrical energy with semiconductor switches.
Important components are diodes, thyristors, MOSFETs and IGBTs.
With pulse-width modulation, an average voltage is set by switching on and off rapidly.
Switched-mode power supplies work with low losses, because the transistors are only ever fully on or fully off.
A frequency converter controls the speed of a three-phase motor.
Silicon carbide and gallium nitride are becoming established as new semiconductor materials.

abschnitte.text: Electricity does not always come in the form a device needs. The socket supplies 230 volts of alternating current, but a mobile phone battery needs only a few volts of direct current. **Power electronics** converts the energy: from alternating to direct current, from high to low voltage or into a different frequency. Unlike the electronics in computers, this is not about data but about **energy**.

The most important tools are electronic switches made of **semiconductors**. A **thyristor** can be switched on with a trigger pulse, but cannot be switched off again via its control connection. The **IGBT** combines the easy control of a MOSFET with the high current capacity of a bipolar transistor and is found in many trains and electric cars. Newer components made of silicon carbide and gallium nitride switch faster and get less warm.

One basic trick is **pulse-width modulation**: a switch goes on and off many thousands of times per second. The longer it stays on each time, the higher the average voltage. An ideal step-down converter with 48 volts at the input that is switched on 25 per cent of the time supplies 12 volts. Because the transistors are only fully on or fully off, hardly any heat is produced and the device wastes little energy.

Every modern charger is a small **switched-mode power supply**, which is why it is light and handy. An **inverter** turns the direct current from a solar system into alternating current for the household grid. A **frequency converter** controls the speed of motors in lifts, pumps and heat pumps by changing frequency and voltage. LED lamps, induction hobs and e-bikes also need power electronics.

In locomotives and trams, power electronics controls the motors and recovers electricity when braking. Very large converters connect power grids with each other or transmit electricity as direct current over long distances. In Switzerland, companies such as ABB, which has its headquarters in Zurich, develop such installations. Without power electronics, the energy transition with sun, wind and electric mobility would hardly be possible.

begriffe.erklaerung: A material such as silicon that conducts or blocks current depending on its state.
A semiconductor switch that switches on with a pulse.
A transistor for large currents, as found in trains and electric cars.
A device that converts direct current into alternating current.
Switching on and off rapidly to set an average voltage.

gewusst: An old power supply with a heavy transformer often weighed many times as much as a modern switched-mode power supply.
The quiet whistling of some chargers or trams comes from the fast switching of the power electronics.
Gallium nitride chargers are especially small because they can switch very fast.

teile.einleitung: An optical fibre, often simply called glass fibre, is a hair-thin thread of glass or plastic through which light is guided. With flashes of light, such fibres transmit huge amounts of data over thousands of kilometres. The internet, the telephone network and television today rely largely on optical fibres.
wichtigste: An optical fibre consists of a core and a cladding with a lower refractive index.
The light is held in the core by total internal reflection.
A single-mode fibre has a core diameter of about 9 micrometres.
The attenuation of quartz glass is lowest at a wavelength of around 1,550 nanometres.
Erbium-doped fibre amplifiers amplify the light directly in the fibre.
With wavelength division multiplexing, many light signals of different colours run through one fibre at the same time.

abschnitte.text: An optical fibre has an inner **core** and an outer **cladding**. The core has a higher **refractive index** than the cladding. If the light hits the boundary between core and cladding at a shallow angle, it is reflected back completely; this is called **total internal reflection**. In this way the light zigzags through the fibre, even round bends.

In **multimode fibres** the core is thicker, and the light can travel along many paths. Because some paths are longer, the light pulses become wider, which is called modal dispersion, and over long distances they blur. A graded-index fibre reduces this, because its refractive index gradually decreases from the centre of the core outwards. For long distances, **single-mode fibres** with a core of only about 9 micrometres are used, in which the light has only one path.

Even in the best glass, light gets weaker along the way; this is called **attenuation**. Quartz glass attenuates least for light with a wavelength of around 1,550 nanometres, which lies in the infrared and is invisible to us. At 0.2 decibels per kilometre, 10 per cent of the light power still arrives after 50 kilometres. **Erbium-doped fibre amplifiers** then amplify the light directly in the fibre without converting it into electricity.

With **wavelength division multiplexing**, many light signals of different wavelengths are sent through the same fibre at once. In this way a single fibre carries huge amounts of data per second. Submarine cables with optical fibres connect all the continents and carry most of the world's internet traffic. In Switzerland too, houses are increasingly being connected directly with optical fibre, which is called fibre to the home.

As early as the 19th century it was shown that light can be guided in a jet of water. In 1966 Charles Kao realised that very pure glass could carry light over long distances. He received the Nobel Prize in Physics for this in 2009. From the 1970s it became possible to make such pure glass, and soon the first fibre-optic lines were laid. Optical fibres are also used in medicine, for example in the **endoscope**, with which doctors look inside the body.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number that shows how strongly a substance bends light.
Complete reflection of light at a boundary.
How much a signal weakens along the way.
A very thin optical fibre in which the light can take only one path.
A thousandth of a millimetre, about a tenth of a hair.

gewusst: The core of a single-mode fibre is thinner than a human hair.
Optical fibres are not affected by interference from lightning and electrical fields.
Light in an optical fibre travels about 200,000 kilometres per second.

teile.einleitung: A light switch is the small switch on the wall that you use to turn the light on and off. It closes or breaks the circuit to the lamp. Behind the simple button there is more technology than you might think, from dimmers to motion sensors.
wichtigste: A light switch closes or breaks the circuit.
With a dimmer you can make the light brighter or darker.
A motion sensor switches the light on by itself when someone moves.
With two special switches you can switch the same lamp from two places.
A push button only supplies current while you press it, for example for the doorbell.
If wires are sticking out of a switch, touch nothing and fetch an adult.

abschnitte.text: Current only flows when the **circuit** is closed. In a light switch, two metal contacts press against each other when you switch it on, and current can flow to the lamp. When you switch off, the contacts are separated and the circuit is broken. The switch is usually placed in the **live conductor** so that the lamp really is free of voltage when switched off.

In a long corridor you want to be able to switch the light on and off at both ends. For this, two **two-way switches** connected by two wires are used. Each switch can close or open the circuit, no matter which way the other one is set. For three or more switching points there is the intermediate switch.

A **dimmer** controls the brightness by reducing the power to the lamp. Not every LED lamp can be dimmed; it says so on the packaging. A **push button** only supplies current while you press it, as with the doorbell. In a **stairwell**, push buttons often switch on a timer that turns the light off again after a few minutes so that no electricity is wasted.

A **motion sensor** uses a sensor to detect the heat radiation of people and switches the light on by itself. It is found in garages, cellars and at house entrances. Some light switches have a small glow lamp or an LED so that you can find them more easily in the dark. Smart switches can be controlled by app or voice command.

Behind every light switch there are wires carrying 230 volts, and that is deadly dangerous. If the cover is missing or wires are sticking out, you must touch nothing and fetch an adult immediately. In Switzerland, repairs to switches may only be carried out by **qualified electricians**. You should not operate switches with wet hands.

begriffe.erklaerung: The closed path along which current flows from the source to the device and back.
A switch with which you can adjust the brightness.
A switch that only supplies current as long as you press it.
A switch with which, together with a second one, you can switch from two places.
A sensor that detects movement and switches the light on.

gewusst: Before there was electric light, people put out candles and paraffin lamps by hand; light switches have only existed since the late 19th century.
The click of a switch comes from a small spring that quickly presses the contacts together or separates them.
An ordinary light switch is built so that it can be switched on and off many thousands of times.

teile.einleitung: In physics and engineering, noise is the name for random, disorderly disturbances that accompany every electrical signal. You hear it, for example, as hissing on the radio between two stations. Noise can never be avoided completely, because it comes from the movement of tiny particles, but engineers have many tricks to keep it small.
wichtigste: Thermal noise comes from the heat motion of the charge carriers.
Thermal noise power is calculated with P = k · T · B.
White noise has the same power density at all frequencies.
With pink noise, the power density falls in proportion to 1/f.
Shot noise arises because electric charge consists of individual electrons.
A signal-to-noise ratio of 30 dB corresponds to a power ratio of 1,000 to 1.
In 1964 Penzias and Wilson discovered the cosmic background radiation through a puzzling noise.

abschnitte.text: Noise is a **random signal** that is laid over a useful signal such as music, speech or measurement data. You hear it as hissing or crackling and on old televisions you see it as flickering snow. It arises in all electronic components because electrons are constantly moving about in a disorderly way. The weaker a signal is, the more the noise disturbs it.

**Thermal noise** arises because the charge carriers in a resistor jiggle about because of heat. The warmer it is, the stronger it becomes. The noise power is P = k · T · B, where k is the Boltzmann constant, T the temperature in kelvin and B the bandwidth. That is why the receiving amplifiers of large radio telescopes are strongly cooled, often with liquid helium.

In **white noise** the power is spread equally over all frequencies, just as white light contains all colours. In **pink noise** the power density falls in proportion to 1 over f, so low notes are stronger. It sounds softer, rather like rain or a waterfall. **Shot noise** arises because current consists of individual electrons that arrive irregularly like grains of shot.

How good a signal is, is described by the **signal-to-noise ratio**, usually in decibels. 10 dB means a signal ten times stronger, 30 dB a power ratio of 1,000 to 1. The noise figure of an amplifier shows how much it worsens this ratio. That is why good amplifiers for mobile phones, satellites and radio make as little noise as possible.

abschnitte.titel: A noise from the Big Bang
abschnitte.text: In 1964 Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson in the USA were looking for the cause of a puzzling noise in their large horn aerial. They even cleaned pigeon droppings out of the aerial, but the noise remained. In the end it turned out that it came from every direction in space: it was the **cosmic background radiation**, an afterglow of the Big Bang. The two received the Nobel Prize in Physics for this in 1978.

begriffe.erklaerung: Information that is transmitted by cable or radio.
How often an oscillation happens per second, measured in hertz.
A unit used to give ratios of powers or loudness.
The range of frequencies a device handles.
A unit of temperature that starts at 0 at absolute zero.

gewusst: A small part of the snow on old television screens really did come from the cosmic background radiation.
Some people fall asleep more easily with white or pink noise because it covers up disturbing sounds.

teile.einleitung: Velcro is a fastening made of two strips of fabric that stick together when pressed. It was invented by the Swiss engineer George de Mestral, who copied the idea from the burdock plant. Today it is found on shoes, jackets, bags and even in space travel.
wichtigste: The burdock plant gave the inventor the idea.
A Velcro fastening consists of one strip with tiny hooks and one with loops.
It stays closed when you press both sides together.
When opened it makes a ripping sound.
In English it is often simply called Velcro.
It is often found on children's shoes.
Astronauts also use it on the space station.

abschnitte.text: In the 1940s the Swiss engineer **George de Mestral** from the canton of Vaud went for a walk with his dog. Afterwards many **burdock** burrs were stuck in his clothes and in the dog's fur. Under the microscope he saw that the burrs have tiny hooks that catch in loops. This gave him the idea of building a fastening on this model.

A Velcro fastening consists of two strips. On one there are lots of small, hard **hooks**, on the other soft **loops**. If you press both together, thousands of hooks catch in the loops and the fastening holds. If you pull them apart, they come loose with a typical ripping sound.

It took several years for de Mestral to find the right material. Cotton did not work well; only with the plastic **nylon** were the hooks stable enough. At the beginning of the 1950s he applied for a patent for his invention. He formed the name Velcro from the French words “velours” for velvet and “crochet” for hook.

Velcro fastenings are found on **children's shoes**, because children can close them without tying laces. They are also practical on jackets, bags, blood pressure cuffs and sports guards. On the **space station**, astronauts fix objects with Velcro tape so that nothing floats away in weightlessness. Over time fluff and hairs collect in the hooks, which you can remove with a brush or a comb.

Velcro is a famous example of **bionics**. In bionics, researchers copy solutions from nature and apply them to technology. Other examples are surfaces that make water roll off like a lotus leaf. In this way the burdock shows how a small observation on a walk can become an invention used all over the world.

begriffe.erklaerung: Plant whose fruits stick to fur and clothes with tiny hooks.
Tough plastic from which fibres and tapes are made.
Science that uses ideas from nature for technology.
Protective right for an invention.

gewusst: The burdock uses its hooks so that animals carry its seeds far away.
Velcro is a Swiss invention.
Velcro is actually a brand name, but in English it is used for almost all hook-and-loop fastenings.

teile.einleitung: A high-rise building is a building with very many storeys that reaches far up into the sky. Especially tall ones are called skyscrapers. The tallest building in Switzerland is the Roche Tower Building 2 in Basel.
wichtigste: A high-rise is a building with many storeys.
Very tall high-rises are called skyscrapers.
High-rises are built mainly where there is little space in cities.
The tallest building in the world is in Dubai (as of 2025).
The tallest building in Switzerland is the Roche Tower Building 2 in Basel (as of 2025).
Tall high-rises sway a little in strong wind.
Red lights on the roof warn aircraft at night.

abschnitte.text: In big cities land is scarce and expensive. If you build upwards, you can fit many **flats** and offices onto a small area. The individual levels are called **storeys**. The district of **Manhattan** in New York is famous for its many high-rises. Cities such as Hong Kong, Shanghai and Dubai also have impressive skylines.

High-rises only became possible when two inventions came together. A **steel frame** carries the weight, so the walls no longer have to support everything. And safe **lifts** carry people up comfortably; Elisha Otis presented the first safety device against lifts falling in the 1850s. The Home Insurance Building in Chicago of 1885 is considered one of the first skyscrapers. In 1931 the Empire State Building was completed in New York, and for a long time it was the tallest building in the world.

A very tall high-rise **sways** a little in strong wind; this is normal and intended. Some towers have heavy pendulums at the top that dampen the swaying. For emergencies every high-rise needs a protected **stairwell** as an escape route, because lifts must not be used in a fire. There are also sprinkler systems and fire walls. Red lights on the roof warn aeroplanes and helicopters at night.

The tallest building in the world is the **Burj Khalifa** in Dubai, which opened in 2010. It is 828 metres tall, more than twice as tall as the Eiffel Tower in Paris. Most skyscrapers today are being built in Asia and the Middle East. Many countries compete to own the tallest building. Records often last only a few years, until a new tower is even taller.

In Switzerland a building counts as a high-rise from about 25 to 30 metres, depending on the canton. The tallest building is the **Roche Tower Building 2** in Basel at 205 metres, which was completed in 2022. Next to it stands the slightly smaller Building 1 from 2015. In Zurich the **Prime Tower** at 126 metres is well known. For a long time relatively few high-rises were built in Switzerland, but today more are being built because people want to save building land.

begriffe.erklaerung: A very, very tall high-rise building.
One level or floor in a building.
A load-bearing framework of steel girders inside a building.
A safe way outside in case of danger.

gewusst: The Burj Khalifa has more than 160 storeys.
The English word “skyscraper” literally means something that scratches the sky.
The fastest lifts in the world travel upwards at more than 70 kilometres per hour.

teile.einleitung: A mobile phone, in Switzerland often called a “Handy” or “Natel”, is a telephone without a cable that you can take anywhere. Today's smartphones are small computers with a camera, internet and countless apps. The first devices, on the other hand, were big, heavy and very expensive.
wichtigste: To make calls, a mobile phone needs a SIM card.
With the emergency number 112 you can get help throughout Europe.
The microphone makes sure the other person hears your voice.
You take photos with the built-in camera.
The bars at the top of the screen show how good the reception is.
The first mobile phones were big and heavy.
In the cinema you put your phone on silent, and when cycling you do not look at it.

abschnitte.text: A mobile phone connects to the mobile network by radio. For this to work it needs a **SIM card**, which identifies your connection. The bars at the top of the screen show how good the **reception** is. A **smartphone** is a mobile phone with a large touchscreen on which you can install apps.

A mobile phone contains a screen, a **battery**, a small computer chip, aerials, a loudspeaker and a **microphone**. The microphone picks up your voice, and the loudspeaker plays the other person's voice. On top of this come cameras, sensors for movement and light, and satellite positioning. All these parts need many raw materials such as copper, gold or cobalt.

In 1973 the engineer Martin Cooper made the first call with a hand-held mobile phone. The first mobile phone you could buy, the Motorola DynaTAC of 1983, weighed almost a kilogram and was as big as a brick. In the 1990s mobile phones became small and cheap, and people sent text messages. From 2007 smartphones with touchscreens took over.

With a mobile phone you make calls, write messages, take photos and videos, listen to music or find your way with the map app. You type a short message and send it. Many people also use it to pay in shops or buy a train ticket. In an emergency you dial **112**; in Switzerland there are also 117 for the police, 118 for the fire brigade and 144 for the ambulance.

In the cinema, the theatre and lessons you put your phone on **silent**. When cycling and crossing the road you do not look at your phone, because otherwise you cannot see the traffic. You do not share personal data, passwords or photos of other people without permission. And every now and then a break from the screen is good for your eyes and your head.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mobile phone with a touchscreen, internet and apps, almost like a small computer.
A rechargeable battery that supplies the phone with power.
How strong the radio connection between phone and aerial is.
A small program on the phone, for example a game or a timetable.

gewusst: Old mobile phones do not belong in the rubbish, because valuable metals such as gold can be recovered from them.
Today's smartphones are much more powerful than the computers used to control the first Moon landing in 1969.

teile.einleitung: The Chapel Bridge in Lucerne is a covered wooden bridge over the River Reuss and one of the best-known landmarks of Switzerland. It was built about 650 years ago and is considered one of the oldest surviving covered wooden bridges in Europe. Together with the octagonal Water Tower, millions of people photograph it every year.
wichtigste: The Chapel Bridge crosses the Reuss in Lucerne, where the river flows out of Lake Lucerne.
It was built around 1365, which makes it about 650 years old.
In the past it served not only for crossing but also for protecting the town.
Triangular paintings from the 17th century showing scenes from history hang in the roof.
In a fire in August 1993 a large part of the bridge was destroyed.
By spring 1994 the bridge had already been rebuilt.
The Water Tower next to the bridge is even older than the bridge itself.

abschnitte.text: In Lucerne the **Chapel Bridge** connects the old town with the other bank of the **Reuss**. It does not run straight but slightly diagonally and with bends across the river. Today it is just over 200 metres long; in the past it was even longer. The bridge is covered with a tiled roof that protects the wood from rain. It takes its name from the nearby St Peter's Chapel.

In the Middle Ages Lucerne was surrounded by **town fortifications**. The Chapel Bridge was part of them and protected the town against attacks from the lake. That is why the parapet on the lake side is higher than on the other side. In the middle of the Reuss stands the octagonal **Water Tower**, which was built around 1300. Over time it served as a watchtower, archive, treasury and even a prison.

Under the roof of the bridge hang triangular wooden panels with paintings, the so-called **gable paintings**. They were painted from about 1611, many of them by the Lucerne painter Hans Heinrich Wägmann. The pictures show scenes from Swiss history and from the lives of Lucerne's patron saints. Anyone walking across the bridge could look at a kind of picture story. Originally there were well over a hundred such paintings.

In the night of 18 August 1993 a fire broke out on the Chapel Bridge. The exact cause was never fully explained; carelessness is suspected, such as a discarded cigarette. A large part of the wooden bridge and many of the valuable gable paintings burned. The people of Lucerne were shocked, and **rebuilding** began immediately. By April 1994 people could already walk across the bridge again, and some charred paintings still hang there today as a reminder.

The Chapel Bridge is one of the most photographed structures in Switzerland. It is very often shown with the Water Tower on postcards, chocolate packaging and souvenirs. In summer many flower boxes decorate the parapet. Not far away is the Spreuer Bridge, another old wooden bridge with paintings of a dance of death. For Lucerne the Chapel Bridge is an important symbol and a draw for visitors from all over the world.

begriffe.erklaerung: Bridge with a roof that protects the wood from the weather.
Walls, towers and gates that protected a town from enemies in the past.
Triangular painting that hangs under the gable of the roof.
River that flows out of Lake Lucerne in Lucerne.

gewusst: The Water Tower stands in the water and was never used as a water reservoir; it gets its name from its location.
After the fire of 1993 the bridge was rebuilt in only about eight months.

teile.einleitung: Smoke signals are one of the oldest ways of sending messages over long distances. With fire and smoke, people were able to warn of dangers thousands of years ago. Smoke signals still exist today, for example at the election of a pope in Rome or in distress at sea.
wichtigste: For smoke signals you need a fire and, for example, a blanket.
They are made on hills so that they can be seen from far away.
In fog, smoke signals are hard to see.
In Switzerland such signal fires on hills were called Hochwachten.
On the Great Wall of China, smoke and fire signals warned of enemies.
White smoke in Rome means that a new pope has been elected.
One disadvantage is that you can only communicate a little.

abschnitte.text: You light a **fire** and put damp grass or green twigs on it so that lots of smoke is produced. If you briefly hold a blanket over it and pull it away again, individual **puffs of smoke** rise. In this way you can form agreed signals, for example one, two or three puffs. At night you see the bright fire instead of the smoke.

Smoke signals only work if they can be seen. That is why they are lit on **hills**, mountains or towers. The next station passes the signal on, so that a message races through the country like a **relay**. But in fog, rain or strong wind this does not work well.

In ancient China, guards on the **Great Wall** already warned of approaching enemies with smoke and fire. There were also chains of signals in ancient Greece and in the Roman Empire. Some Indigenous peoples of North America also used smoke signals to communicate across wide plains. A disadvantage was always that only simple, previously agreed messages could be sent.

In the old Swiss Confederation there were **Hochwachten** (signal posts) on many hills. These were posts with piles of wood that were lit in an emergency. The state of Bern in particular built up a dense network in the 17th century. In this way troops could be alerted in a short time when there was danger, and place names such as “Hochwacht” still recall these posts today.

When the cardinals in Rome elect a new pope in the **conclave**, they burn the ballot papers. Black smoke from the chimney of the Sistine Chapel means that nobody has been elected yet. White smoke announces that there is a new pope. At sea, people in distress use an orange **smoke flare** to show that they need help.

begriffe.erklaerung: Sign that conveys an agreed message.
Old signal post on a Swiss hill with a fire for raising the alarm.
Gathering of the cardinals to elect a new pope.
Distress signal that produces coloured smoke.

gewusst: For the election of a pope, chemicals are now added to the fire so that the colour of the smoke is clear.
The Swiss Hochwachten were placed so that each station could see at least one other.
Scouts also sometimes learn to give simple signals with smoke and a blanket.

teile.einleitung: The Crocodile is one of the most famous locomotives in the world and a symbol of the Swiss railway. From 1919 the SBB used the powerful electric locomotive mainly on the Gotthard to pull heavy goods trains over the steep mountain line. It owes its nickname to its long, flat shape, which recalls a crocodile.
wichtigste: The first SBB Crocodile locomotives ran from 1919.
They were used mainly on the Gotthard Railway.
Their main job was pulling heavy goods trains.
The long, flat bonnets recall a crocodile.
The locomotive consists of three parts joined by hinges so that it can go round tight bends.
The power of the motors is transmitted to the wheels via rods.
The SBB built 33 of the Ce 6/8 II class.

abschnitte.text: The Crocodile is an electric locomotive built for the SBB in the 1920s. The best-known classes are called **Ce 6/8 II** and Ce 6/8 III. The figure 6/8 means that 6 of the 8 axles in total are driven. Such a locomotive is almost 20 metres long and weighs well over 100 tonnes.

At the front and back the locomotive has long, low **bonnets**, which contain the motors. In the middle sits a taller box with the driver's cabs. From the side this looks like a flat crocodile with a long snout. That is how the locomotive got its nickname, which is now known all over the world.

The Crocodile is built from three parts connected by **joints**. This means it can lean into the many tight bends of the Gotthard line. The large motors do not turn the wheels directly but drive several wheels at once via **connecting rods**, similar to a steam locomotive. These rods can be seen moving up and down as it runs.

The Gotthard Railway has long, steep ramps and many spiral tunnels. After the line was electrified from 1920, the SBB needed locomotives that could pull heavy goods trains safely up the mountain. The Crocodile was ideal for this because it had a great deal of pulling power. Often two Crocodiles ran together at the head of a long train.

The locomotives were made in Swiss factories. The **Swiss Locomotive and Machine Works** (SLM) in Winterthur built the mechanical parts. The electrical equipment came from Maschinenfabrik Oerlikon in Zurich. So the Crocodile was an example of the strength of Swiss industry.

From the 1960s the Crocodiles were gradually replaced by more modern locomotives. A few have been preserved and still run on special trips today. One stands in the Swiss Museum of Transport in Lucerne. The Crocodile is also very popular as a model railway, especially with collectors.

begriffe.erklaerung: A vehicle that pulls or pushes a train.
A bar that connects two wheels.
A rod that transmits the power of the motor to the wheels.
A train that carries goods instead of people.

gewusst: The Rhaetian Railway in the Grisons also has Crocodile locomotives; they are smaller and run on narrow gauge.
For many railway fans all over the world, the Crocodile is the most beautiful electric locomotive ever built.

teile.einleitung: A marshalling yard is a large station just for goods wagons. There, arriving trains are split up, the wagons are sorted by destination and put together into new trains. It works like a gigantic sorting machine for the railway.
wichtigste: A marshalling yard sorts goods wagons and puts them together into new trains.
The wagons roll over a small hill, the hump.
Rail brakes slow down the rolling wagons.
Before the wagons roll off, the coupling between them must be released.
The most important Swiss marshalling yard for single wagons is in the Limmat valley.
It stretches across the cantons of Aargau and Zurich and has 64 sorting tracks.
Marshalling yards are especially important for single wagonload traffic.

abschnitte.text: Many companies do not send a whole train, but only individual goods wagons. These wagons have very different destinations. In the **marshalling yard** they are re-sorted so that all the wagons for the same region end up in one train. This traffic is called **single wagonload traffic**.

An arriving train is first placed on the **arrival tracks**. Then staff release the **couplings** between the wagons. A locomotive slowly pushes the train over the **hump**, a small artificial hill. Once at the top, the wagons roll down one by one by gravity.

Behind the hump, automatically set **points** steer each wagon onto the right **sorting track**. So that the wagons do not crash into each other too fast, **rail brakes** press against the wheels from the side. Computers calculate how heavy each wagon is and how strongly it must be braked. When all the wagons for one track are together, they are coupled again and sent off as a new train.

The largest and most important marshalling yard in Switzerland is in the **Limmat valley** between Dietikon, Spreitenbach and Killwangen. It stretches across the cantons of Zurich and Aargau and went into operation at the end of the 1970s. With 64 sorting tracks it can sort a great many wagons every day. Other important yards are, for example, near Basel and near Lausanne.

A goods train replaces many lorries on the road. This saves energy, relieves the motorways and causes fewer exhaust fumes. For rail freight to work, efficient marshalling yards are needed. In Switzerland they are run by SBB Cargo.

begriffe.erklaerung: Moving, separating and re-forming wagons.
Small hill over which goods wagons roll down one by one.
Device beside the rails that slows down rolling wagons.
Track on which wagons with the same destination are collected.
Freight traffic in which individual wagons are sent instead of whole trains.

gewusst: On its journey a goods wagon may roll through several marshalling yards before it reaches its destination.
On the hump, gravity is enough to keep wagons weighing many tonnes rolling without a locomotive.
The Limmattal marshalling yard is several kilometres long.

teile.einleitung: A cable is a line that carries electricity, signals or data from one place to another. Inside there are metal wires or glass fibres, and outside a plastic sheath protects them. Cables are everywhere, but you have to be careful with electricity, because a damaged cable can be deadly.
wichtigste: A cable carries electricity, signals or data.
The plastic sheath protects against electric shocks.
A device with a damaged cable must not be used any more.
Cables should not be laid under carpets or trapped in doors, because they can be damaged and overheat.
A cable reel must be fully unwound before you connect a powerful appliance.
Tall pylons carry the power lines across the country.
Near power lines and overhead railway lines there is a danger to life.

abschnitte.text: Inside, a power cable usually has several **cores** made of copper, because copper conducts electricity very well. Each core is insulated with plastic so that the wires do not touch. On the outside there is a further plastic sheath, the **insulation**, which protects against electric shocks and damage. In Switzerland the protective earth conductor is green and yellow, the neutral conductor blue and the live conductor usually brown.

Besides power cables there are cables for data, such as network cables, USB cables or aerial cables. Modern **fibre-optic cables** transmit data as light signals through wafer-thin glass fibres. Huge submarine cables lie on the sea floor and connect continents for the internet. The first telegraph cable across the Atlantic was laid as early as 1858, but it only worked for a few weeks.

High-voltage lines carry electricity from power stations over long distances. They hang on tall frames, the **pylons**. Some lines are also laid as underground cables. Above the SBB tracks hangs the **overhead line**, at a voltage of 15,000 volts, which supplies the trains with electricity.

A damaged cable where you can see the wires can cause an **electric shock**, so you stop using the device. Cables under carpets or trapped in doors get squashed and can overheat and start a fire. Never fly kites near power lines. Climbing onto stationary railway wagons is deadly dangerous, because electricity can jump across from the overhead line over a distance.

With an **extension cable**, a device can stand further away from the socket. A cable reel must be fully unwound before you connect a powerful appliance such as a fan heater, otherwise it can get hot. Always pull the plug and not the cable when unplugging a device. Cables should not be kinked or laid over sharp edges.

begriffe.erklaerung: Single insulated wire in a cable.
Plastic sheath that does not conduct electricity and protects against electric shocks.
Wafer-thin glass fibre that transmits data as light.
Very high electrical voltage, as in overland power lines or overhead railway lines.

gewusst: By far the largest share of international internet traffic flows through submarine cables on the sea floor.
With an overhead railway line you do not have to touch it to be injured, because the electricity can jump through the air.
A cable reel left wound up can get so hot that the plastic melts.
